obverse: Head of Hercules right, club on shoulder; three value dots behind
reverse: Prow right; C.ABVRI / GEM above, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this quadrans as tribus notis signatus (three value dots marking the denomination). He calls the prow type ratitus, deriving the term from ratis (ship/raft). Connects C. Aburius Geminus via Livy to a Roman legation sent to Masinissa and Carthage.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; GEM behind
reverse: Mars in quadriga right, holding trophy, shield, reins and spear; C.ABVRI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the GEM abbreviation as Geminus or Gemellus. He connects C. Aburius Geminus via Livy to the embassy sent to Masinissa and Carthage, treating this denarius as the primary monument of the moneyer.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma; GEM behind
reverse: Sol in quadriga right; M.ABVRI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Aburius M.f. Geminus as a second member of the gens and cites Livy to connect him to a praetorship. He distinguishes the Sol reverse from the Martian quadriga of coin 2, treating both as separate Aburian monuments.

obverse: Draped female bust right (Luna or Diana); crescent behind
reverse: Three standing female figures (triple cult statue)
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the three standing female figures on the reverse as the Heliades — the sisters of Phaethon transforming into larch trees — connecting the cognomen Lariscolus to larix (larch). Modern scholarship identifies the reverse figures as a triple Diana. He cites this as a striking interpretive case.

identification: BAR Issue 21; HGC 2, 178 — Manlius Acilius, quaestor, Sicily c. 208-200 BC
obverse: Head of Asklepios right, wearing tainia
reverse: Serpent-entwined staff (rod of Asklepios); MN·A·CILI
orsini_comment: Orsini calls this primo aereo nummo (the first bronze coin) of the Acilii and derives the nomen Acilius from Greek akesimos (healer), connecting the gens to Aesculapius. He attributes the coin to a quaestor serving in Sicily during the Hannibalic war.

obverse: Laureate head of Salus right; legend around
reverse: Standing female figure (Valetudo) leaning on column, holding snake; MN.ACILIVS.III.VIR.VALETV
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the Salutis and Valetudinis legend types to the temples of Salus and Valetudo on the Quirinal. He identifies the moneyer Mn. Acilius Glabrio as tresvir monetalis, reading the III.VIR.VALETV legend on the reverse.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; star behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; M·ACILI below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the myrtle wreath on the reverse as signifying an ovation (not a full triumph) and attributes the coin to the consul who served with M. Porcius Cato in 639 AUC (115 BC). He connects the Jupiter quadriga to the consular triumph.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; M.AEMILI(O) legend around
reverse: Deity in quadriga/triga right, ROMA in exergue; winged figure (Victory/Cupid) above
orsini_comment: Orsini admits uncertainty ('quarto denario mihi quidem obscurum est'), tentatively attributing this fourth Acilius denarius to Mn. Acilius Glabrio who triumphed over the Aetolians. He acknowledges the attribution is conjectural for want of clearer legend evidence.

obverse: Legend in three lines AVGVSTVS / TRIBVNIC / POTEST within a laurel wreath (no head)
reverse: S.C large in centre; Q.AELIVS.LAMIA / III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Aelius Lamia as one of the IIIvir monetales under Augustus and discusses the priestly simpulum type, connecting the Lamia family to augural and pontifical offices visible in the coin imagery.

moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
obverse: Clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio) holding a caduceus; LAMIA SILVS ANNIVS around
reverse: S.C large in centre; III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the college of L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, and C. Annius as IIIIviri A.A.A.F.F. He discusses the simpulum as a symbol of pontifical office and the quadrans denomination as the smallest Augustan bronze issue.

moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
obverse: Apex and lituus (priestly/augural implements); ANNIVS LAMIA SILVS around
reverse: S.C large in centre; IIII.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini records L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, and C. Annius as joint issuers. He interprets the reverse priestly implements as marking the holders of pontifical functions within the Augustan college of moneyers.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; value mark behind
reverse: Dioscuri galloping right; P·PAETVS below, ROMA in exergue (tablet)
orsini_comment: Denarius of P. Aelius Paetus (Crawford 233/1). Obverse: helmeted head of Roma right with value mark behind. Reverse: the Dioscuri on horseback galloping right, P·PAETVS below and ROMA on a tablet in exergue. A standard Roman-magistrate Dioscuri type within Orsini's Aelia commentary.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Dioscuri galloping right; C·AL below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini uncertain ("incertum ad quem spectet"), tentatively C. Ailius. His note that silver coinage did not yet exist is incorrect — the denarius was introduced in 211 BC and Crawford 75/1b is dated 209-208 BC. Notably, this coin was struck in Sicily during the Second Punic War, making it one of the earliest Roman denarii and a military issue — not a Rome mint coin. The X (denarius value mark) appears on the actual coin but was not engraved by Orsini. The Sicilian mint context is historically significant: Roman forces were consolidating control of Sicily after Marcellus's capture of Syracuse (212 BC), and field coinage was needed to pay troops.

obverse: Head right; BALA behind
reverse: Biga of stags right; C.ALLI behind
orsini_comment: Denarius of C. Allius Bala (Crawford 336/1), placed by Orsini in the Aelia section under his equation of the Allia with the Aelia. Obverse: female head right with BALA behind. Reverse: Diana in a biga of stags right, C·ALLI behind.

moneyer: M. Aemilius Scaurus & P. Plautius Hypsaeus
obverse: Kneeling figure right beside camel; M.SCAVR / AED.CVR above; REX ARETAS below
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga left, hurling thunderbolt; P.HVPSAEVS / AED.CVR; C.HVPSAE.COS / PREIVE / CAPTV in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Aretas kneeling type in relation to M. Aemilius Scaurus's aedileship. He connects the Nabataean king's submission to Scaurus's eastern campaigns and reads the joint legend with P. Plautius Hypsaeus, citing their shared praetorship.

obverse: Laureate head right; star before, ROM behind
reverse: Equestrian statue: rider on horseback atop an arched base inscribed LEP; M·AEMILIO around
orsini_comment: Denarius of M. Aemilius Lepidus (Crawford 291/1). Obverse: laureate head right, star before and ROM behind. Reverse: an equestrian statue of a rider on horseback set atop an arched base inscribed LEP, with M·AEMILIO around. The type commemorates the Aemilii Lepidi rather than the Scaurus camel/Venus issue.

obverse: Laureate head right; symbol behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right; M.LEPIDVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses M. Aemilius Lepidus (61 BC) in connection with the young Lepidus who killed an enemy and saved a citizen at age fifteen, citing Valerius Maximus III.1. He reads the horseman reverse as commemorating an equestrian honour of the gens.

obverse: Laureate/diademed female head right; symbols in field
reverse: Horseman galloping right; M.LEPIDVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this as a second specimen of M. Aemilius Lepidus (Crawford 419/1), grouping it with coin 3 as showing the same equestrian type. His discussion draws on Cicero, Plutarch, and Appian for the Lepidan branch of the Aemilii.

obverse: Veiled head of the Vestal Aemilia right
reverse: Façade of the Basilica Aemilia (Aemilia et Fulvia); AIMILIA / REF within; M·LEPIDVS; S·C
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Basilica Aemilia on this reverse, connecting the REF (refecit) inscription to L. Aemilius Lepidus Paullus's rebuilding of the building. He cites the clupei (shields) displayed there as commemorating Aemilian triumphs.

obverse: Diademed female head right (Alexandria); ALEXANDR around
reverse: Two standing figures (Lepidus crowning Ptolemy); S.C in field; M.LEPIDVS / PON.MAX around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the crowning of Ptolemy scene for M. Aemilius Lepidus's denarius of 61 BC. He connects the ALEXANDR legend and the S.C to Lepidus's role in the east, reading the type as commemorating a diplomatic mission.

obverse: Veiled female head right (Concordia); PAVLLVS LEPIDVS CONCORDIA around
reverse: Trophy with two captive figures at base; TER / PAVLLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads TER as standing for triple triumph and identifies the two captive figures at the base of the trophy as Perseus and his sons. He cites Plutarch and Livy on L. Aemilius Paullus's Macedonian triumph over Perseus.

obverse: Veiled female head right with diadem; legend around
reverse: Puteal Scribonianum (decorated well-head); PVTEAL.SCRIBON around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Puteal Scribonianum, identifying this monument on the reverse as the Puteal Scribonianum (well-head) dedicated in the Forum. He connects L. Scribonius Libo to the Aemilian plate by virtue of the Puteal's association with the family.

obverse: Bare male head right; LEPIDVS.PON.MAX around
reverse: Bare male head right; CAESAR.IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this joint issue of the triumvir Lepidus with Octavian, noting the LEPIDVS.PON.MAX legend establishing his pontificate. His discussion of Lepidus focuses on the political rather than the military role within the triumvirate.

obverse: Bearded male head right; jug behind; lituus before
reverse: Horseman galloping right with spear; P.SEPVLLIVS / MACER around
orsini_comment: Orsini includes this Caesar coinage among the Aemilian plate via P. Sepullius Macer's role as Caesarian moneyer. He connects the reverse horseman to a military memorial and notes the Saturn/Jupiter head on the obverse.

obverse: Eagle and praefericulum (jug); AN.IMP in field
reverse: Priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex); LEP.IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex) on the reverse as emblems of the triumvir Lepidus's pontifical office. He reads the eagle with praefericulum as linking Lepidus to augural authority.

identification: RPC I 528 — M. Aemilius Lepidus (triumvir), Cabellio (Gallia Narbonensis)
metal_mismatch: AR→AE (Orsini's engraving tags AR; coin is bronze)
obverse: Head of Apollo right; CABE (= Cabellio, the mint)
reverse: Cornucopia within laurel wreath; LE-PI (= Lepidus)
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 11) calls this his 'fourth denarius' and reads CABE as «Cabae», a city he places in the province of Africa, administered by M. Aemilius Lepidus under the triumviral division of the empire; he takes the crown as decreed to Lepidus and the cornucopia as indicating the fertility of the place («copiae cornu ad indicandam loci ubertatem»). His attribution to Lepidus is sound, but the mint is Cabellio in Gallia Narbonensis (Gaul), not Africa.

obverse: Bare male head left; M.LEPIDVS.III.VIR.R.P.C around
reverse: Standing nude youthful figure leaning on a spear, holding an attribute; L.MVSSIDIVS.T.F.LONGVS IIII.VIR.A.P.F legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Marcus Aemilius Lepidus as triumvir (III.VIR.R.P.C) on this denarius. He connects the Mars reverse type to Lepidus's military campaigns and reads the legend as establishing his triumviral authority.

obverse: Bare male head right
reverse: Draped female figure (Fortuna/Concordia type) standing, holding small Victory in right hand and cornucopia in left; VARVS / C.VIBIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini places this L. Mussidius Longus issue within the Aemilian plate in the context of the triumviral series. He discusses the Victory or warrior holding trophy and palm as a standard triumviral military type.

obverse: L·BVCA: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem.
reverse: Sulla reclining; on right, Luna; behind, Victory with outspread wings holding a staff. (the dream of Sulla)
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this L. Aemilius Buca denarius as part of the Caesar series. He notes Buca as one of Caesar's monetales in 44 BC and discusses the Venus obverse as alluding to Caesar's claimed Julian descent.

obverse: Laureate head right; DICT.PERPETVO / CAESAR around
reverse: Standing female figure (Ceres or Venus) holding sceptre and cornucopia; L.BVCA behind
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Aemilius Buca's role as Caesarian moneyer, noting the DICT.PERPETVO legend establishing Caesar as dictator in perpetuity. He reads the Ceres or Venus reverse as part of the wider Caesarian iconographic programme.

obverse: CAESAR·IM·P·M: Wreathed head of Caesar right.
reverse: L·AEMILIVS BVCA: Venus standing left, holding Victory in right hand and sceptre in left.
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this L. Aemilius Buca denarius as a monument to Caesar's cosmic claims: he interprets the naked figure holding globe and branch as representing Caesar's universal dominion (BVCA / L.AEM legend confirmed).

obverse: Laureate head right; CAESAR around
reverse: Two clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio); L.AEMILIVS / BVCA.IIIVIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this L. Aemilius Paullus/Buca shared issue, noting the dextrarum iunctio (clasped hands) as symbolising political concordia. He reads the BVCA.III.VIR legend as establishing Buca's moneyer title alongside Paullus.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right with crest and visor
reverse: Victory in biga right; S.AFRA / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini debates whether the Afranii were patrician or plebeian, ultimately classifying them as plebeian. He reads the S as the praenomen Spurius and notes this abbreviation is paralleled in the Postumii. He connects Sp. Afranius to the Republican biga denarius type.

obverse: Head of Janus bifrons
reverse: Prow right; S.AFRA above
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this Janiform as (Crawford 206/2) as the bronze companion to the denarius. He reads the S.AFRA legend and identifies Sp. Afranius as the issuer, treating both coin 1 and coin 2 as monuments of the same moneyer.

identification: Bolskan (Hispania Citerior) AR denarius, c. 150–100 BC — ACIP 1412–1417; CNH pp. 210–212
obverse: Bare male head right; Iberian legend behind (appears as ARSA or similar)
reverse: Horseman galloping right, wearing helmet, holding spear/lance; Iberian legend in exergue below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Iberian horseman type to L. Afranius serving as Cn. Pompey's legate in Hispania during the Sertorian campaigns. He connects the reverse cavalry scene to L. Afranius's military role in Spain, drawing on Livy and Appian for the context.
orsini_error: Orsini misattributes a Bolskan (Iberian, Hispania Citerior) denarius to gens Afrania, reading the north-eastern Iberian script as the Latin name AFRA; the coin is not Roman. An understandable error — Iberian script was not deciphered until 1922 — but a genuine misattribution.

obverse: Bust of Venus, right, draped and wearing diadem. C·CAESAR IMP·COS·ITER
reverse: Trinacrus, left, placing right foot on prow and holding triskeles in right hand and cloak in left hand. A·ALLIENVS PRO·COS
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse bust as Persephone, patron goddess of Sicily, and interprets the reverse Trinacrus as tria crura (three legs), the heraldic emblem of the island. He cites Hirtius (the continuator of Caesar's Gallic commentaries) as the source for Allienus as praetor governing Sicily.

obverse: Draped female bust right; legend around C·ANNI·T·F·T·N·PRO·COS·EX·S·C
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; Q above; C·TARQVITI·P·F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Annius T.f. T.n. as holding proconsular authority against Sertorius and reads the caduceus and scales as symbols of peace and justice in his command. He cites Sallust's Historiae for the Sertorian context of the Spanish campaigns.

moneyer: C. Annius / L. Fabius L.f. Hispaniensis
obverse: Laureate female bust right; S.C behind
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; L.FABI.L.F / HISP below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue with L. Fabius Hispaniensis, noting the proconsular command against Sertorius. He reads the Victory in quadriga as a military memorial type and connects the L.FABI.L.F / HISP legend to the joint magistracy in Spain.

moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
obverse: Simpulum and lituus; SILIVS ANNIVS LAMIA around
reverse: Large S·C in centre; III·VIR / A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Annius as part of the college of L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, and C. Annius as IIIIviri A.A.A.F.F. He treats the simpulum reverse as marking the pontifical dimension of the Augustan moneyer college.

moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
obverse: Clasped hands holding winged caduceus; LAMIA·SILIVS·ANNIVS around
reverse: S.C large in centre; III·VIR / A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini records the joint issue of Lamia, Silanvs, and C. Annius with the dextrarum iunctio obverse and S.C reverse. He connects the IIII.VIR A.A.A.F.F. legend to the Augustan monetary reform and the clasped hands to concordia imagery.

moneyer: C. Annius T.f.T.n. / C. Tarquitius P.f.
obverse: Single draped female bust right; legend around C·ANNIVS·T·F·T·N·PRO·COS
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; HISP above; L·FABI·LF in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue of C. Annius with C. Tarquitius P.f., citing Sallust's Historiae for Tarquitius's presence in Spain under Pompeian command. He reads the Victory quadriga as part of the anti-Sertorian military series.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; C.ANTES below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini equates the Antestia gens with Antistia and notes the spelling variation across inscriptions and manuscripts. He reads GRAG as a dimidiatum cognomen Graecum (half-Greek name), interpreting it as Gragulus rather than Gragus.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Two horsemen (the Dioscuri) galloping right; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Antestius tentatively as the consul mentioned by Dio (book XLVII) paired with M. Licinius. He notes this horseman/Dioscurus type as the primary Antestian monument on the plate.

obverse: Head right with star or control mark
reverse: Two horsemen (the Dioscuri) galloping right, stars above; C·ANTESTI below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini groups this as a die variant of the C. Antestius denarius, treating coins 2 and 3 as two specimens of the same issue. He confirms C.ANTESTI in the legend and reads the horseman reverse as a Dioscurian type.

obverse: Bare head right (Augustus?); legend around
reverse: Column or altar with priestly implements; ANTISTIVS.REGINVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Antistius Reginus from Caesar's Bellum Gallicum (book VI) as the probable father of this moneyer, but explicitly withholds certainty: 'in re tam dubia nihil audeam affirmare'. He does not attribute the pontifical implements to this coin; those appear on coin 2 (the Vetus denarius).

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 410 — C. Antistius Reginus
obverse: Bare head right (Augustus?); legend around
reverse: COS / IMP.CAESAR.AVG legend; implements
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the pontifical instruments on the reverse of this denarius as evidence of Antistius Vetus's pontificate: 'Instrumenta pontificalia, quae in altera denarii parte impressa sunt, Antistii pontificatum indicant', citing Velleius lib. II. He notes C. Antistius Vetus as consul with D. Laelius Balbus, anno DCCXLVII, and quotes the Pliny epigramma (lib. XXXI, cap. I).

obverse: Bare male head right; RESTIO behind
reverse: Standing figure (Hercules) holding club and trophy
orsini_comment: Orsini states that Restio's portrait appears on this first denarius ('cuius imago in primo denario impressa est') and discusses him as the author of the lex sumptuaria, citing Gellius and Macrobius. He makes no specific claim about the Hercules reverse being emblematic of sumptuary legislation.

obverse: Jugate (conjoined) laureate heads of the Dei Penates right; DEI PENATES (D.E.I. / PENATES) legend; C.ANTI behind
reverse: Hercules holding cornucopia and patera
orsini_comment: Orsini states that the Penates images are on the REVERSE ('in altera secundi denarii parte') of this coin, not the obverse. He presents two possible reasons for their inclusion — family origin from Lanuvium (citing Varro and Paedianus) or Restio's law touching on religion — but commits to neither ('fortasse'). He does not describe the other side's figure as Hercules here, nor link Hercules to the household cult.

obverse: Bucranium (bull skull) facing; C.ANTIVS above
reverse: Flaming altar (thymiaterion); RESTIO around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the bull's head crowned with a garland ('bouis caput insula redimitum') to the Saecular Games (Saeculares ludi), at which this animal was sacrificed, and infers that a member of the Restio family served as quindecemuir at those games. He mentions no capis, lituus, or other implements; the coin is identified only by the bull's head and its Saecular-games connection.

obverse: Bare head of M. Antonius right; M·ANT·IMP·AVG·III·VIR·R·P·C·M·NERVA·PROQ·P
reverse: Bare head of L. Antonius right; L·ANTONIVS·COS
orsini_comment: Orsini opens his Antonian section citing Plutarch, Dio, and the Philippics. He reads this denarius as a joint issue between M. Antonius and a fellow triumvir and discusses Antony as Pontifex, noting the augural and pontifical legends.

obverse: Bare head right with slight drapery; legend around partially visible
reverse: Victory standing right on globe, holding wreath and palm; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the Victory on globe to Antony's claim of universal dominion. He draws on Velleius's account of Antony as Liber Pater (Dionysus) and reads the reverse as a triumviral propaganda monument.

obverse: Bare head right; M·ANTONIVS / III·VIR·R·P·C around
reverse: Pietas standing facing beside a lighted altar; PIETAS / COS in fields
orsini_comment: Orsini reads IMP.TERT and PIETAS.COS as establishing Antony's third imperatorship and his claim to Pietas. He connects the trophy reverse to Antony's eastern campaigns and cites Plutarch and Appian on the triumvir's military career.

obverse: Head wearing petasus right; C·ANTONIVS·M·F·PRO·COS around
reverse: Priestly implements: simpulum, aspergillum, axe, apex; legend: PONTIFEX
orsini_comment: Orsini's Dionysiac/Sol observations (pp. 18–19) are made collectively about the plate, not coin-by-coin. He cites Velleius on Antony presenting himself as Liber Pater ('cũ ante nouũ fe Liberũ patrem appellari iufisset... curru uelut Liber pater uectus esset Alexãdriae,' p. 19) and Dio lib. XLVIII on Antony as Osiris/Dionysus ('Aυτòς μἐν ὅσιρις & διονύσιος,' p. 19). These general remarks illuminate the plate as a whole. Individual comments attributing Sol iconography to coins 5 and 6 specifically, or Liber Pater to coin 7, are inferences, not Orsini's coin-by-coin statements. The comments for coins 4–7 should reflect that Orsini's Dionysiac/solar text applies to the plate generally ('Ad primũ uero & reliquos, spectãnt illa ex lib. l').

obverse: Laureate head facing right; legend around: III.VIR.R.P.C.COS.DESIG.ITER.ET.TERT
reverse: Nude male figure (Sol) standing facing, right arm raised holding object; legend around: M.ANTONIVS.M.F.M.N.AVGVR.IMP.TER
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Sol figure on the reverse as part of Antony's Dionysiac-solar iconography. Drawing on Velleius, he discusses Antony's identification with Liber Pater and connects this type to the eastern solar cult in Antony's ideology.

obverse: Bare head right; legend: IMP
reverse: Temple facade with four columns; radiate head of Sol within temple; legend: III VIR R.P.C. arranged around temple
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this temple-reverse type with radiate Sol within the façade as evidence of Antony's eastern religious associations. He reads the IMP legend as establishing imperatorship and connects the Sol imagery to Antony's Hellenistic divine claims.

obverse: Bare head right; no legend clearly visible
reverse: Radiate and draped bust right (Sol/Helios type); legend around: M·ANTONIVS·III·VIR·R·P·C
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the radiate Sol bust on the reverse as part of Antony's sustained identification with eastern solar and Dionysiac deities. He connects this to Plutarch's account of Antony presenting himself as a new Dionysus in the east.

obverse: Laureate head right; legend around partially legible
reverse: Cista (cista mystica / altar) with a small bust above it, flanked by two coiled serpents; legend around: III VIR R P C
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this eastern issue of M. Antonius and records the double-head obverse as a joint issue. He draws on Appian and Dio for the context of Antony's eastern command and reads the laureate heads as establishing his triumviral authority.

obverse: Bare head right; legend partially visible
reverse: Double cornucopia; ΑΥΤΟ / ΚΡΑ (Greek)
orsini_comment: Orsini records this eastern issue with a double cornucopia and the Greek legend ΑΥΤΟ/ΚΡΑ (autokrator).

obverse: Laureate head right; legend around M·ANTONIVS·IMP·COS·DESIG·ITER·ET·TERT
reverse: Statue figure atop a cista, flanked by two coiled serpents; legend around III·VIR·R·P·C
orsini_comment: Orsini gives no individual comment on this cistophorus. His general discussion of Antony's eastern coins (pp. 19–21) concerns Dionysiac/Osiris imagery and the Armenia Devicta types; no coin-specific description of a cista mystica figure is offered anywhere in the Antonia section.

obverse: Bare/laureate head of Mark Antony right, Armenian tiara behind; legend around: ANTONI.ARMENIA.DEVICTA
reverse: Draped bust right (possibly Cleopatra); legend around: REGINAE.REGVM.FILIORVM.REGVM (partially legible)
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as the Cleopatra joint issue and notes the full titulature CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM on the reverse. He draws on Plutarch and Dio for the political significance of Antony's union with Cleopatra.

obverse: Bare head right; legend: M.ANTO.IMP
reverse: Bare head right; legend: CAESAR.DIC (portrait of Caesar)
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this early joint issue of M. Antonius with a Caesar portrait, treating M.ANTO.IMP and CAESAR.DIC as establishing the triumviral relationship. He cites the Philippics for the period before Caesar's assassination.

obverse: Single bare head right; legend around: M ANT IMP AVG III VIR R P C M BARBAT P
reverse: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the jugate busts as a joint triumviral issue and connects the CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C legend to the reconstitution of Roman authority after Philippi. He draws on Appian's Bella Civilia for the triumviral settlements.

obverse: Single bare head right; legend around: M ANT IMP AVG III VIR R P C L GELLI Q P
reverse: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue of Antony and Octavian (M.ANT.IMP and CAESAR.IMP) as a monument to the Second Triumvirate. He cites Appian and Dio on the Perusine war period and the uneasy alliance between the two triumvirs.

obverse: Bare head of Mark Antony right; M·ANTON·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C
reverse: Bare head of Octavian right; CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C
orsini_comment: Crawford 517/2 (M. Barbatius, 41 BC): two facing bare heads — M. Antonius (M·ANTON·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C) and Octavian (CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C) — a monument to the short-lived triumviral concord between Antony and Octavian, NOT a jugate Antony/Cleopatra type. (Re-identified from the former 543/1.)

obverse: Bare head right; legend around: ANT... IMP... III.VIR.R.P.C.
reverse: Prow of galley right; legend: AHENOBARVS.IMP; star above; legend below: CN.DOMITI (partially legible)
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus prow issue as part of the Antonian series. He notes the AHENOBARVS.IMP galley reverse as marking fleet command and connects it to the build-up of Antony's naval forces before Actium.

identification: Crawford 542/1 — Mark Antony with M. Silanus as quaestor pro consule, 33 BC
moneyer: M. Junius Silanus (quaestor pro consule under M. Antonius)
obverse: Bare head right; legend around: IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVG.VR.COS.DES...
reverse: Legend in two lines within plain field: M.SILANVS.AVG / Q.PRO.COS.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes M. Silanus as quaestor pro consule under M. Antonius and reads the legend M.SILANVS.AVG / Q.PR as establishing his subordinate command. He discusses the IMP.TER legend as marking Antony's third imperatorship.

obverse: Jug (praefericulum) between lituus and other priestly implements; legend around: III.VIR.R.P.C. / M.ANTON (partially legible)
reverse: Augural/priestly implements: lituus (left), jug/praefericulum (center) and winged caduceus (right); legend around: M ANTON IMP ITER (AVGVR)
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the priestly implements (jug, lituus) on the obverse and caduceus between cornucopiae on the reverse as emblems of Antony's pontifical office and claim to peace and plenty. He connects this to Antony's augurate.

identification: Crawford 546/2b — M. Pinarius Scarpus for Mark Antony, Cyrenaica, 31-30 BC
obverse: Bearded head right; legend around: ANTO.COS.III.IMP.IIII
reverse: Victory standing right, holding wreath and palm; legend around: SCARPVS.IMP / ANTONIO.AVG
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Pinarius Scarpus as a Caesarian/Antonian officer serving in Cyrenaica. He reads ANTO.COS.III.IMP.IIII and the Victory reverse as establishing Antony's authority in North Africa in the last phase before Actium.

obverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANTONIVS.AVG.IMP
reverse: Victory standing right within laurel wreath, holding trophy; legend partially visible
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this colonial/provincial issue as part of Antony's provincial programme. He reads M.ANTONIVS.AVG.IMP on the obverse and connects the Victory with trophy reverse to Antony's military command in the eastern provinces.

obverse: Bare head right; ANTON·AVG·IMP·III·COS·DES·III·III·V·R·P·C (partially legible)
reverse: Legend in field: ANTONIVS / AVG.IMP.III (text only within plain circle)
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the ANTONIVS / AVG.IMP.III legend and discusses this text-field reverse as an unusual Antonian issue. He connects it to the broader series of Antonian moneta struck in the east from 38 BC.

obverse: Bare male head right (Antony); no legend clearly visible
reverse: Galley/ship right; legend above: L.BIBVLVS
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers all discussion of Bibulus to the Calpurnia gens entry: 'De Bibulo, Fonteio, & Atratino, qui & ipsi Antonianarum partium fuerunt, non est hic locus scribendi: sed in Calpurnia, Fonteia, & Sempronia gentibus...diligenter à nobis indicabuntur.'

obverse: Single bare male head in profile; no clearly legible legend
reverse: Galley/ship right; legend: L.BIBVLVS (partially visible)
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers all discussion of Bibulus to the Calpurnia gens entry: 'non est hic locus scribendi.'

moneyer: M. Antonius and C. Asinius Gallus (Capito, propraetor)
obverse: Two heads right (jugate busts); legend around: ...PIVS.CAPI.TO.PRO.PR (partially legible)
reverse: Galley/ship right; legend around: M.ANT.IMP... COS.DESIG.ITER.ET.TER (partially legible)
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no individual comment on this coin. He defers discussion of Bibulus, Fonteius, and Atratinus to other gentes entries ('non est hic locus scribendi: sed in Calpurnia, Fonteia, & Sempronia gentibus...diligenter à nobis indicabuntur,' p. 22). No text on pp. 18–27 individually discusses Capito or attributes a 'jugate heads' reading to Orsini for this coin.

identification: RPC I, 1459 — Mark Antony and Octavia, with L. Sempronius Atratinus, fleet coinage, Achaea, 36 BC; bare head of Antony right + Octavia / quadriga of hippocamps with L·ATRATINVS·AVGVR
obverse: Two jugate heads (same direction, overlapping); legend above: M.AT.IMP.TER.COS
reverse: Marine creature (hippocampus or dolphin) with small Victory figure; legend around: L·ATRATINVS
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers discussion of Atratinus to the Sempronia gens entry: 'De Bibulo, Fonteio, & Atratino...non est hic locus scribendi.'

obverse: Bare head; capis (jug) in field before the face; CAESAR·DIC
reverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANTO.IMP... R.P.C. (partially legible)
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as a joint issue of M. Antonius and Octavian, noting CAESAR.DIC and M.ANTO.IMP as the paired legends. He connects the lituus on the obverse to Antony's augurate and discusses the early triumviral period before the break.

identification: Crawford 489/3 — M. Aemilius Lepidus (as triumvir), 42 BC
moneyer: M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Antonius (joint triumviral issue)
obverse: Bird (eagle) standing, jug before it; legend above: M.ATINI
reverse: Priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex); LEP·IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex) on the reverse as emblems of M. Aemilius Lepidus's pontifical authority (Pontifex Maximus). He reads this joint Lepidus/Antonius issue within his extended treatment of triumviral coinage.

moneyer: L. Munatius Plancus (for M. Antonius, at Lugdunum)
obverse: Bare head right; no legend clearly visible
reverse: Lion walking right; legend above: INAQ; legend below: LVGV; A and XL in field
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the lion as the emblem of the Lugdunum colony and identifies L. Munatius Plancus as involved in the colony's foundation (citing Dio XLV). He reads the lion as 'coloniae uetus insigne, à quo fortasfse nomen id, quod nunc uocatur traxit' (p. 23). He does not read or interpret the legend INAQ visible in the engraving, and does not identify it as a place name.

obverse: Bare head right; legend partially visible
reverse: Lion walking right; legend above: ANTONI; legend below: IMP
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the lion walking right with ANTONI / IMP as Antony's Lugdunum-type issue, discussing the lion as the emblem of the colony. He draws on Appian and Dio for the Lugdunum foundation and Antony's role in the Gallic command.

obverse: Jug and bird (eagle or raven) standing right; legend: M.A.IMP (partially legible)
reverse: Victory, right, crowning trophy
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the jug and raven/eagle obverse and the Victory crowning trophy reverse as emblems of Antony's augural and military authority. He reads the M.A.IMP legend and connects the bird to Antony's augurate office.

obverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANT.AVGVR.III.VIR.R.P.C.
reverse: Trophy of arms with shield and spear; legend: IMP.TER (with additional symbols)
orsini_comment: Orsini reads M.ANT.AVGVR.III.VIR.R.P.C as establishing Antony as augur and triumvir. He connects the trophy of arms with shield and spear to IMP.TER (third imperatorship) and discusses this within his account of Antony's Armenia campaign.

obverse: Laureate head right; legend around: IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVGVR.COS.DES (partially legible)
reverse: Trophy with captive at base; legend around: ...IMP... III.VIR.R.P.C. / ...ITER.ET.TER (partially legible)
orsini_comment: Orsini notes IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVGVR on the obverse and reads the trophy with captive as commemorating the Armenia campaign of 34 BC. He cites Plutarch and Dio on the capture of Artavasdes and connects the Armenia Devicta imagery to Antony's claims.

identification: Crawford 529/4b — Mark Antony and Octavian; Head of Concordia right, veiled / Two hands clasped round caduceus; AR quinarius, 39 BC
obverse: Veiled head of Concordia right; legend partially visible around
reverse: Two hands clasped round a winged caduceus (dextrarum iunctio); legend partially visible
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this quinarius type as part of the concordia series with clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio). He connects the caduceus to peace negotiations and reads the Concordia imagery as commemorating the reconciliation between Antony and Octavian at Misenum (39 BC).

identification: Crawford 529/2a — M. Antonius and Octavian, 41 BC
obverse: Bare head right; legend CAESAR IMP
reverse: Caduceus with wings; legend ANTONIVS IMP
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this joint Antony/Octavian quinarius as a monument to the triumviral concordia. He notes CAESAR IMP and ANTONIVS IMP as the paired legends and connects the caduceus reverse to the pact of Misenum (39 BC) discussed in Appian.

obverse: Head of M. Antonius right; lituus behind
reverse: Caduceus between two cornucopiae on globe; M·ANT·IMP III·VIR·R·P·C
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the caduceus between cornucopiae on globe as symbolising Antony's claim to peace and plenty. He notes M·ANT·IMP III·VIR and discusses the head of Antony with lituus (augurate symbol) as the obverse type.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Three legionary standards (aquila between two signa); CHORTIVM PRAETORIARVM
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the cohors praetoria as Antony's praetorian guard, noting its Scipionic precedent. He reads CHORTIS PRAETORIAE with the three standards as the emblem of Antony's personal escort, connecting it to Scipio Africanus's use of a praetorian cohort.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Three legionary standards; CHORTIS SPECULATORVM
orsini_comment: Orsini reads CHORTIS SPECULATORVM as the reconnaissance and intelligence unit of Antony's army. He discusses the three legionary standards and the galley obverse as marking this special cohort's place within the legionary series.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG II
orsini_comment: Orsini notes LEG II as the second legion in Antony's order of battle. He reads the galley obverse (ANT.AVG / III.VIR.R.P.C) as marking the fleet context and the aquila between two signa as the legion's standards.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG III
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG III in the legionary series. He treats the three standards as emblematic of the legion's identity and notes the galley obverse linking all legionary denarii to Antony's fleet command before Actium.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG IIII
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG IIII in sequence. He notes the consistent reverse type (aquila between two signa) across the legionary series and the galley obverse as the unifying element of Antony's army pay-coinage.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG V
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG V in the legionary sequence. His extended treatment of the legionary series notes the consistent obverse/reverse formula and the special designations (Classicae, Lybicae) for selected legions.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG VI
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG VI among Antony's legions. He discusses the legionary series collectively as a monument to Antony's army mobilised for the Actium campaign, drawing on Plutarch and Appian for the scale of the forces assembled.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG VI (variant with ANTONIVS VETVRS AVGVR)
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the fifth denarius of this plate as attesting Legio VI restored by Antoninus and Verus Augusti: 'VI. LEGIONEM ab Antonino & Vero Augustis restitutam fuifse, ex nullo Scriptorũ, praeterquàm ex quinti denarii infcriptione cognofcimus' (p. 25). He does not discuss a 'veteran-designation variant'; his remark concerns imperial restoration of the legion known only from this coin's inscription. The 'ab Antonino & Vero Augustis restitutam' refers to a later imperial restoration attested on the coin legend, not to Antony's own nomenclature for a veteran unit.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG VII
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG VII in sequence. He reads the three standards and aquila as the consistent badge of each Antonian legion and connects the galley obverse to the combined fleet-and-army command structure before Actium.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG VIII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG VIII in the legionary series. He treats these coins as a collective monument to Antony's army, noting the series as the most extensive Republican military coinage preserved in the numismatic record.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG IX
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG IX in sequence. He connects each legion to the broader narrative of Antony's campaign preparations, citing Plutarch's Life of Antony on the size of the forces marshalled for the war against Octavian.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG X
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG X in the series. He notes this as one of the core Antonian legions and discusses the legionary denarii collectively as evidence of the scale of Antony's military financing in the final civil war.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XI
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG XI in sequence. He reads all legionary reverses as following the same formula (aquila between two signa, legion number in legend) and treats the series as a systematic record of Antony's order of battle.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XII in the legionary sequence. He discusses the series collectively as the most complete surviving record of a Republican army's composition, connecting it to Plutarch and Appian on the Actium campaign.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XII ANTIQVAE
orsini_comment: Orsini states that Legio XII Antiquae is known solely from this coin: 'Legionis. XII. Antiquae, quae in huius tabellae denario notata est, nullus, quod sciam, ueterum scriptorum facit mentionem.' He makes no claim about it having an established history; on the contrary, he notes the complete absence of any ancient literary attestation.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XIII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XIII in the series. He reads the legion number and aquila type as consistent markers and connects the galley obverse to Antony's combined naval and land command at Actium.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XIV
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG XIV in sequence. He discusses these coins as army-pay coinage struck in quantity before Actium and connects them to Plutarch's account of the financial demands of Antony's eastern military establishment.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XV
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XV in the legionary series. He notes the aquila between two signa reverse and the galley obverse as the standard Antonian formula, reading the series as a comprehensive military pay record.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XVI
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG XVI in sequence. He treats all regular numbered legions as following the same formula and notes the special units (Classicae, Lybicae, Cohors Praetoria, Speculatorum) as the distinctive elements within the series.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XVII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XVII in the series, before the Classicae variant. He reads these in order and connects the series to his extended discussion of Antony's army and fleet, drawing on Plutarch, Dio, and Appian.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XVII CLASSICAE
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that Legio XVII Classica would have been entirely unknown but for this coin: 'Legio XVII Classica: in sexto huius tabellae denario signata, nisi antiquus hic denarius extaret, fuisset nobis prorsus ignota.' He does not explain what Classicae designates or identify it as a naval unit.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XVIII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XVIII in the regular sequence. He notes the consistent three-standards reverse across all legionary denarii and discusses the series as an unparalleled record of a late Republican army's order of battle.

identification: Crawford 544/38 — Mark Antony legionary denarius, LEG XXIII (RSC 55)
obverse: Praetorian galley right; ANT·AVG / III·VIR·R·P·C
reverse: Aquila (legionary eagle) between two standards; LEG XXIII (the engraving erroneously shows LEG XXIIII)
orsini_comment: Mark Antony legionary denarius (Crawford 544/38), praetorian galley / aquila between two standards, ANT·AVG·III·VIR·R·P·C. The reverse legion is LEG XXIII (the highest genuine legion in the series); the engraving erroneously adds a stroke, reading LEG XXIIII (not a real legion) — an engraver's error. (Re-identified from the former 544/11 / LEG XI.)
orsini_error: Engraver's error: reverse engraved LEG XXIIII (extra stroke). LEG XXIIII (24) is not a recognised legion in Antony's series — XXIII is the highest genuine number; higher numbers are dismissed as die-engraver's errors/forgeries. Read as LEG XXIII (Crawford 544/38).

identification: Crawford 364/1d — Q. Antonius Balbus, praetor, 83-82 BC
obverse: Bare head right with slight beard; S·C in field
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, holding thunderbolt; Q·A·BALB·PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini distinguishes Q. Antonius Balbus as a separate branch of the gens from the triumvir. He reads Q·A·BALB·PR as Quintus Antonius Balbus, Praetor, and connects the S·C in the field to senatorial authorisation of the issue in 83-82 BC.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XIIX
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XIX in the legionary series. He connects this to the Actium campaign and discusses the series collectively as a monument to Antony's army, noting the galley obverse as linking all legionary coins to the fleet context.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XVIII LYBICAE
orsini_comment: Orsini states Legio XVIII Lybicae is attested only in this coin ('nisi in hoc tantum denario, nulla alibi extat mentio') and guesses it was named from the region, as were the Cyrenaica, Scythica, and Macedonia legions mentioned by Dio lib. LV. He does NOT say the legion was recruited from or stationed in North Africa.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XIX
orsini_comment: Orsini records a second example of LEG XIX. He treats this as a duplicate issue of the same legion noted at coin 60, reading both as part of the same die series and noting the consistent aquila between two signa reverse.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XX
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XX in the legionary series. He discusses the series collectively as evidence of the unprecedented scale of Antony's military coinage, citing Plutarch and Appian on the size of the forces at Actium.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XXI
orsini_comment: Orsini lists LEG XXI in the sequence. He reads the three standards as the unit's emblem and connects the galley obverse to Antony's combined fleet command. He notes the cohors praetoria precedent from Scipio Africanus within his legionary commentary.

obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG XXII
orsini_comment: Orsini records LEG XXII as the final legion in the series. He concludes his Antonian treatment by noting the series as the most extensive mint output of any Republican commander, connecting its scale to the demands of financing the Actium campaign.

obverse: MESSALLA.APRONIVS / SISENNA.GALVS around; priestly implements
reverse: S.C large in centre; III.VIR / A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini records the joint issue by Sisenna and Aproni / Galvs as IIIviri monetales under Augustus (A.A.A.F.F.). The third named moneyer is Galvs (not Messalla). Orsini has little to say about the Apronii beyond identifying Galvs as probably the consul of anno DCCLX in the Capitoline tables and noting his connection to the Sulpicia family.

obverse: Helmeted bust right (Virtus); VIRTVS behind
reverse: Warrior raising up fallen figure (Sicilia); MN.AQVIL / SICIL around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Virtus/Sicilia type as commemorating Mn. Aquillius who suppressed the Sicilian slave revolt, correctly reading the SICIL legend. He reads the warrior raising up the fallen Sicilia figure as a monument to the victory over the slaves.

obverse: Head of Sol right
reverse: Luna in biga right; stars above; MN.AQVIL below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this Sol/Luna biga type as an earlier issue of the Aquillii, attributing it to Mn. Aquillius in the consular period. He connects the Sol head obverse and the Luna biga reverse to standard Republican astronomical imagery.

obverse: Bare head right; L.AQVILLIVS.FLORVS around
reverse: Kneeling figure (Armenian/Parthian) presenting/handing standard; CAESAR / DIVVS.F / ARMEN.CAPTA / SIGN.RECE around
orsini_comment: Orsini records L. Aquillius Florus as triumuir under Augustus and notes the flower on the coin reverse as referencing the cognomen Florus ('à flore quodam ea familia duxerat, florem ipsum cuiusmodi fuerit, in altera denarii parte indicauit'). He mentions that Dio lib. LI records the execution of Aquillii Flori, father and son, at Augustus's command. Orsini does not describe a kneeling figure with Parthian standards for this coin.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 309 — L. Aquillius Florus; Head of Augustus bare right / Open flower with six petals; AR denarius, Rome, 19–4 BC
obverse: Bare head right (Augustus); CAESAR behind/around
reverse: Open flower with petals (rosette/flower-star); L.AQVILLIVS.FLORVS / III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the flower reverse to the cognomen Florus, stating that 'à flore quodam ea familia duxerat, florem ipfum cuiufmodi fuerit, in altera denarii parte indicauit' (p. 29) — 'from some flower the family took [the cognomen], and indicated on the other side of the denarius what kind of flower it was.' He does not name Flora as a goddess or invoke her cult; he speaks only of 'some flower' (flore quodam) as the origin of the cognomen.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 301 — L. Aquillius Florus, moneyer, 19 BC (Virtus / Augustus in elephant biga)
obverse: Helmeted head right; L.AQVILLIVS.FLORVS.III.VIR around
reverse: Elephant walking left; AVGVSTVS above, CAESAR below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not provide a specific comment on this coin beyond the general discussion of L. Aquillius Florus as triumuir under Augustus and the Florus cognomen connected to the flower on the reverse. The specific claim about a helmeted head or Augustan military achievement is not attested in Orsini's text.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 303 — L. Aquillius Florus; Head of Sol radiate right / Slow quadriga right with grain stalks; AR denarius, Rome, 19–4 BC
obverse: Radiate head of Sol right; L·AQVILLI / FLORVS·III·VIR around
reverse: Sol in slow quadriga right, holding grain stalks (or whip); CAESAR·AVGVSTVS above; S·C in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Aquillius Florus's reverse type as depicting a flower referencing the cognomen Florus. He does not mention a bull or ox reverse for any Aquillian coin, nor does he call any of these issues a 'bronze' (the Florus denarii are silver). The specific 'bull or ox reverse' description is not grounded in Orsini's text.

obverse: Bare male head; M·ARRIVS / SECVNDVS around
reverse: Wreath at left; square frame enclosing sacrificial implements at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the military decorations on the reverse — clathros (lattice-work), hasta pura, and corona — arguing these were the dona with which Arrius was honoured for defending a camp gate, citing Horace (Ars Poetica) and Columella (VIII.3). He quotes Catullus Carmen 84 on Q. Arrius's aspirated pronunciation as prosopographic context. He leaves the identity of M. Arrius Secundus explicitly open ('incertum mihi'): he may be the person in Pedianus's argument to Verr. IV, or the Suriae praefectus.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 373 — C. Asinius Gallus; Head of Augustus bare right / Legend surrounding S·C; AE as, Rome, 16 BC
obverse: Bare head left; TRIBVNIC.POTEST.CAESAR.AVGVSTVS around
reverse: S·C within wreath; C.ASINIVS.GALLVS / III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Asinius Gallus as 'orator & poeta' and as the son of Asinius Pollio. He notes Pollio's consulship (anno DCCXIX with C. Marcius Censorinus) and his fame praised by Seneca, Pliny, and Suetonius. Orsini says Gallus 'signavit' these bronze coins but does not mention the title IIIvir monetalis.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 370 — C. Asinius Gallus; Oak-wreath between laurel branches / S·C; AE sestertius, Rome, 16 BC
obverse: OB / CIVIS / SERVATOS within an oak wreath
reverse: S.C; C.ASINIVS / GALLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini treats both Asinia bronzes as struck by C. Asinius Gallus ('signavit'). His text discusses Gallus and Pollio's biography; he does not describe the individual types of the two coins separately, and does not mention the oak-wreath, the OB CIVIS SERVATOS legend, or distinguish the two coins' reverses in his commentary.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; SARAN behind
reverse: The Dioscuri on horseback galloping right; M·ATIL below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Seranus/Saranus cognomen, citing Pliny (Lib. XVIII cap. III) for the serendo etymology but noting doubt about whether this applies to the Saranus form. He identifies two possible persons — M. Atilii Serani triumviri (anno DLXVIII) and C. Atilius consul (anno DCXLVII) — but explicitly states the identification is uncertain ('difficile est... affirmare'). He does not confidently assign the coins to M. Atilius Saranus.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Horseman in biga right; C.ATL / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini groups the Roma/horseman-type Atilian denarii together but explicitly declines to identify which specific moneyer they belong to ('difficile est, qui praecipue his denariis designentur, affirmare'). He discusses the Seranorum family etymology (Pliny) and the alternative Saranus inscription evidence without resolving the question.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; control marks
reverse: Horseman in biga or quadriga right; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini treats the Atilian denarii collectively and declines to specify which moneyer each belongs to. He does not invoke M. Atilius Regulus of the First Punic War in this context.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind; COTA behind
reverse: Horseman in biga right; M.AVRELI / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the COTA cognomen and identifies M. Aurelius Cotta as issuing this biga denarius. He connects the moneyer to the consular Cottae and provides prosopographic notes on the family without extended historical commentary.

obverse: Laureate head right within laurel wreath; star behind
reverse: Eagle with spread wings; L·COT in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the bearded, pileus-wearing bust as Vulcan, citing Virgil on Vulcan's sooty beard and Arnobius (lib. VI: 'cum pileo Vulcanus & malleo' — pileus and hammer, not tongs). He attributes the coin to L. Aurelius Cotta. He does not discuss the eagle reverse or connect it to any augural tradition.

moneyer: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, M. Aurelius Scaurus, L. Licinius Crassus
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; M·AVRELI around
reverse: Figure driving biga right; S·CARI / L·LIC·CN·DOM below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the third coin as possibly M. AVRELIVS SCAVRVS, consul suffectus in anno DCXLV with L. Hortensius, described as 'unicus in ea familia consularis.' He reads the legends visible in the plate (including the names of the collegiate moneyers) but does not name the college explicitly in his prose; his text focuses on Scaurus's identification.

obverse: Head of Mars right, wearing plumed helmet
reverse: Diana in biga of stags right, holding spear; L.AXSIVS.L.F below, NASO in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini admits to great difficulty with this family, writing in tanta praesertim huius familiae ignoratione (given such ignorance about this family). He discusses the archaic spelling AXSIVS and its possible connection to MAXIMVS. For the Diana/stag reverse, he cites Apollonius Rhodius (book III) and Callimachus on the stag-drawn chariot.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma left; TAMPIL behind
reverse: Apollo in quadriga right; M.BAEBQ.F / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Baebius Tampilus as consul in 181 BC with P. Cornelius Cethegus, noting his triumph over the Ligurians. He observes the spelling TAMPIL on the coin versus Tamphilus in the Capitoline tablets, noting the absence of aspiration in the coin legend.

obverse: Handwritten annotation (not a coin engraving): "tête de Jupiter"
reverse: Handwritten annotation: "TAN en monogramme / victoire couronnant un trophée / Jason / ROMA"
orsini_comment: Later annotator's note (French): obv «tête de Jupiter»; rev «TAM en monogramme, Victoire couronnant un trophée, ROMA» — Crawford 133/1, an anonymous denarius (154 BC) formerly attributed to M. Baebius Tampilus.

identification: Crawford 263/1 — M. Caecilius Q.f. Q.n. Metellus; Head of Roma right / Macedonian shield with elephant head within laurel wreath; AR denarius, 127 BC
obverse: Head of Apollo right, hair tied with band; behind small object
reverse: Macedonian shield decorated with elephant's head in center; laurel wreath border
orsini_comment: Orsini opens his extended treatment of the Metelli by attributing the Macedonian shield type to M. Caecilius Metellus, one of the four sons of Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus. He connects the elephant in the shield's centre to the Metellian triumphal tradition.

obverse: ROMA (upwards) / ROMA (downwards): Helmeted head of Roma right, with star on helmet flap. Border of dots.
reverse: M·METELLVS Q·F: Macedonian shield decorated with elephant's head at centre. Laurel-wreath border.
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this as a second monument of M. Caecilius Q.f. Q.n. Metellus. He discusses the four sons of Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus — Marcus, Caius Caprarius, Quintus Balearicus, and Lucius Diadematus — as the framework for his Metellian commentary.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: Biga of elephants right driven by a charioteer; C.M.TELLVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Victory/biga type to C. Caecilius Metellus Caprarius, identifying him as the second of the four Metellian sons. He connects the cognomen Caprarius to goat-herding imagery, drawing on the prosopographic tradition.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, holding thunderbolt and branch; Q·METE (Q. Caecilius Metellus); ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the Dioscuri type to Q. Caecilius Metellus and connects it to the gens's long tradition of Dioscurian reverse types. He identifies this as the issue of Q. Caecilius Metellus Balearicus, the third son of Macedonicus.

moneyer: Q. Caecilius Metellus / M. Calidius / Cn. Fulvius
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right with winged griffin crest; Q.MET behind
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the joint issue of Q. Caecilius Metellus with M. Calidius and Cn. Fulvius. He reads Q.MET in the legend and connects the Roma/Victory quadriga type to the magistracy shared among three monetales in 117-116 BC.

obverse: Bearded head of Jupiter right, laureate; Q.ME behind
reverse: Prow right; Q.MET / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze prow issue to Q. Caecilius Metellus, reading Q.MET / ROMA as the issuer's legend. He treats the Janiform Jupiter head and prow reverse as standard Republican bronze types of the Metellian magistracy.

moneyer: Q. Caecilius Metellus / M. Calidius / Cn. Fulvius
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA; X behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; CN.FOV / M.CALO / Q.MET below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue with M. Calidius and Cn. Fulvius (CN.FOV / M.CALOM legible). He reads Q.MET as Q. Caecilius Metellus and treats this variant as part of the same college issue as coin 5.

moneyer: L. Caecilius Metellus / C. Publicius Malleolus / A. Postumius Albinus
obverse: Laureate head right; L.METEL / A.ALB.S.F around
reverse: Roma seated holding spear, crowned from behind by Victory standing; C·MAL at left, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: The joint issue of L. Metellus, A. Postumius Albinus, and C. Publicius Malleolus (Crawford 335/1) is visible on the second Caecilia plate (p. 38, legend L.METEL / A.ALB.S.F / C.MA…). Orsini provides no prose discussion of this coin; his text on pp. 38–40 turns immediately to Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio and the African campaign coins. The coin appears on the plate without individual commentary from Orsini.

obverse: Head right with elephant skin headdress (Africa personified)
reverse: Elephant walking right; Q.C.M.P.I below
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the elephant reverse of Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius to the Jugurthine triumph and identifies the elephant-skin headdress as the personification of Africa. He reads Q.C.M.P.I as Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Imperator.

obverse: Laureate head right; Q.METEL / PIVS around
reverse: Elephant walking right; SCIPIO / IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Metellus Pius Scipio as imperator in Africa, demonstrating this from Caesar's own words in Bellum Civile III. He connects the elephant on the third and fourth denarii to Africa and the spica/aratrum on the sixth to Africa's fertility (via Claudianus). He does not say Orsini 'conflates' the moneyer and proconsul — Scipio was the commanding general who issued these coins in Africa.
orsini_error: Conflates the moneyer Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio with the proconsul of the same name

obverse: Bare head right
reverse: IMPER; lituus and praefericulum (priestly implements)
orsini_comment: Orsini reads IMPER with lituus and praefericulum as a second issue of Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius, connecting the priestly implements to the gens's pontifical tradition. He discusses the lituus as an augural symbol appropriate to the Metellian command.

moneyer: Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio / Eppius
obverse: Single head right; SCIPIO·IM / Q·METEL around
reverse: Single standing male figure (Genius/Hercules); LEG·F·C / EPPIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this joint issue of Metellus Scipio with Eppius (LEG.F.C / ENIVS), reading the two jugate heads and the standing figure on the reverse as a monument to the joint African command. He connects this to his treatment of Metellus Scipio at Thapsus.

moneyer: Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio / P. Licinius Crassus Iunianus
obverse: Genius of the African land (Genius Terrae Africae) standing right, holding attributes; G·T·A above; Q·METELLVS·PIVS·SCIPIO·IMP around
reverse: Victory standing left, holding wreath and resting on a shield; LEG·PRO·PR / P·CRASSVS·IVN around
orsini_comment: Coin of Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio (imperator in Africa, 47-46 BC) with his proquaestor P. Licinius Crassus Junianus: standing Genius Terrae Africae / Victory with shield. Orsini files it under the Caecilian section.

identification: Crawford 460/2 — Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio and P. Licinius Crassus Iunianus Damasippus; Bust of Jupiter right / Curule chair with scales on cornucopia; AR denarius, 47–46 BC
obverse: Bearded head of the African Genius (Jupiter-like) right; SCIP·IMP / METEL·PIVS around
reverse: Balance (scales) above a curule chair set on a cornucopia; LEG·PRO·PR / P·CRASSVS·IVN around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the bare head with METELLUS legend alongside the priestly implements (praefericulum, securis) and P.CRASSVS legend. He connects this to the African command series, grouping it with coins 12-13 as part of the Metellus Scipio/Crassus joint issues.

moneyer: Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio (imperator) with L. Licinius Crassus Iunianus (proquaestor pro praetore)
obverse: Turreted head of Genius Terrae Africae (Africa) right, corn-ear before; CRASS·IVN / LEG·PRO·PR around.
reverse: Trophy of arms; on left, lituus; on right, jug (praefericulum); METEL·PIVS / SCIP·IMP around.
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the turreted-head obverse with caduceus and the trophy reverse with SCIP IMP as a joint issue of Metellus Scipio (imperator) and L. Licinius Crassus Iunianus (proquaestor pro praetore, L.C.P.RO.PR). He connects the trophy to the African military command.

identification: Crawford 263/5 — C. Caecilius Metellus Caprarius, AE as, 125 BC
obverse: Bare head right
reverse: Prow right; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini includes this bronze of C. Caecilius Metellus Caprarius, placing it alongside coin 3. He reads the prow and ROMA reverse as standard Republican bronze types and treats this as the only bronze monument of the Caprarius branch on his plate.

identification: Crawford 174/1 — A. Caecilius (gens Caecilia); laureate head of bearded Janus / prow of galley right, A·CAE above, ROMA below (Æ as).
obverse: Janiform head (two heads back-to-back)
reverse: Prow right; A.CA / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini leaves it uncertain ('aeque mihi obscurum est') whether this bronze belongs to A. Caecina the Roman knight from Volaterrae (Cicero Fam. VI) or to his son, whom Orsini believes was consul suffectus in the XIII consulship of Augustus (anno DCCLI). He does not give '2 BC'; he says 'in XIII Consulatu' and calculates anno DCCLI with M. Plautius Silvanus as colleague.
orsini_error: Modern attribution Crawford 174/1 = A. Caecilius (gens Caecilia); Orsini placed the coin under gens Caecina (he himself flagged the attribution as obscure, 'aeque mihi obscurum est').

obverse: Bust of Apollo seen from behind, head turned left, holding thunderbolt; control marks
reverse: Two Lares Praestites seated facing, dog between; bust of Vulcan above; L.CAESI around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse bust as Veiovis, citing Gellius (V.12), and is uncertain whether the Caesii were patrician or plebeian. He identifies L. Caesius from Cicero's letters to Quintus (ad Q. Fratrem) and discusses the Lares Praestites with dog on the reverse via Plutarch on guardian dogs as household protectors.

moneyer: M. Calidius / Q. Caecilius Metellus / Cn. Fulvius
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Victory driving galloping biga right; M·CALID above, Q·MET·CN·FL in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Calidius as a patrician senator from Caesar's Bellum Civile (book I) and notes his praetorship in 696 AUC (57 BC). He cites Cicero's Brutus, where M. Calidius is praised as an outstanding orator of elegant and smooth style.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right; control mark behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right, holding palm; L·PISO·L·F / FRVGI below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi as consul in 620 AUC and interprets the horseman on the reverse as desultorius eques (vaulting rider), connecting it to the Ludi Apollinares established during Piso's consulship. He notes the Apollo head on the obverse as referencing the same games.

identification: Crawford 340/2 — L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi; Laureate head of Apollo right / Victory standing right with wreath; AR quinarius, 90 BC
obverse: Head right, laureate or diademed
reverse: Winged Victory standing, holding wreath; L.PI / SO in field, FRVGI below
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this quinarius as a second type of L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi. He connects the Apollo head to the Ludi Apollinares and reads the Victory/standing figure reverse as part of the same magistracy series, noting the large number of die variants Piso's issues present.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right; control mark behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right, holding spear
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this horseman type as one of L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi's die variants. He connects the large number of control marks to the scale of the issue but gives no explanation for the quantity and makes no reference to Social War financing.

obverse: Head right, laureate
reverse: Figure on horseback galloping right; F above
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to C. Calpurnius Piso L.f. Frugi and notes the many die variants as a continuation of the Piso tradition. He connects the Apollo head and horseman reverse to the Ludi Apollinares of the earlier Pisonum issues.

identification: Crawford 340/2 — L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi; Laureate head of Apollo right / Victory standing right with wreath; AR quinarius, 90 BC
obverse: Laureate head right; PISO before
reverse: Victory standing right holding wreath; FRVGI below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses C. Calpurnius Piso L.f. Frugi's Apollo/horseman types as a continuation of the Pisonum series. He notes the many die variants but says nothing about a plough on the reverse or an agricultural cognomen tradition for this specific type.

obverse: Head left, laureate; LPISO below
reverse: Horse galloping right; FRUGI below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this horseman variant for L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi. He discusses the Terminus head on the obverse as connected to Numa Pompilius's cult and explains the sacrificial instruments (simpulum, patera, culter) on associated types as also referencing Numa.

identification: RPC I, 4092 — L. Bibulus M.f. (L. Calpurnius Bibulus), fleet prefect under M. Antony; Head of Antony right / Half ship with boar's head right; L·BIBVLVS·M·F·PR·DESIG; AE fleet coinage, Syria
obverse: Head of male figure right, bare
reverse: Half-galley (prow) right with boar's-head protome; BIBVLVS above
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Calpurnius Bibulus as fleet prefect (praefectus classis) under Antony and connects the galley reverse to Antony's naval build-up. He notes the BIBVLVS legend and treats the ship type as a monument to the fleet prefecture.

identification: RPC I, 4091 — L. Bibulus M.f. (L. Calpurnius Bibulus), fleet prefect under M. Antony; Jugate heads of Antony and Octavia right / Ship under sail right with Medusa head; L·BIBVLVS·M·F·PR·DESIG; AE fleet coinage, Syria
obverse: Jugate heads of Antony and Octavia right
reverse: Galley (ship) right; L·BIBVLVS above
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the jugate heads and prow reverse for this second Bibulus issue. He discusses L. Calpurnius Bibulus's role in Antony's fleet command and reads the ship reverse as consistent with the fleet prefect's authority over the Antonian naval forces.

obverse: Standing figure left holding wreath and small object; bird (goose or duck) to right
reverse: Legend M.PISO.M.F / FRVGI within a wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses M. Pupius Piso within the Calpurnian section by adoption. For the Piso coins he describes the Terminus figure and sacrificial instruments: 'in primo denario integrum Termini fimulacrum, in altero caput tantum exprefsum eft: in utroque autem, ab una fimulacri, feu capitis parte, fimpulum; ab altera, corona fignata eft' (p. 46). He also mentions the Numa Pompilius family connection and discusses the simpulum, patera, and culter as sacrorum instrumenta referencing Numa. No dove or goose is mentioned by Orsini for any Piso coin.

obverse: Laureate head (Apollo) right; star and control mark in field
reverse: Legend within wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini records this second Pupius Piso issue with Roma head and wreath reverse. He treats M. Pupius Piso as connected to the Calpurnii by the shared Frugi cognomen and discusses the Roma/wreath type as a standard late Republican form.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; CN·CAE above, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Cn. Calpurnius as the earliest Calpurnian moneyer on the plate. He reads CN CA / ROMA and the Dioscuri galloping right as a standard Republican type of the mid-second century, noting the gens's consular connections.

obverse: Head of bearded figure right, laureate
reverse: Galley prow right; MAGN above, PRO.COS below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this MAGN PRO·COS type and says 'CN. PISONEM PROQ. opinor designari eum, qui Cn. Pompeii legatus in bello Piratico fuit.' He attributes the coin to Cn. Piso as Pompey's legate in the Piratic War but says nothing about the lion as a Pompeiian emblem.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 394 — Cn. Calpurnius Piso; Head of Augustus bare right / Head of Numa Pompilius bearded diademed right (Piso claimed descent from Numa); AE as, Rome, 16–15 BC
obverse: Head of bearded figure left; legend around border
reverse: Head of figure right, laureate; legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Cn. Calpurnius Piso's claim of descent from Numa Pompilius: he reads the Numa head on the reverse (with Cn. Piso's head on the obverse) as the moneyer honouring his legendary ancestor. He connects the Terminus cult and Numa reference to the Pisonum tradition.

obverse: Youthful bare/laureate head (Augustus) with legend around border
reverse: Large letters SC in center; legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini notes Cn. Calpurnius Piso as IIIvir monetalis with the large SC reverse. He discusses the A.A.A.F.F. inscription on related types as Aere Argento Auro Flando Feriundo and connects the Augustan moneyer to the Pisonum family.

obverse: Large letters SC within circular border with legend around
reverse: Wreath enclosing unclear text or monogram, with legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini records Cn. Calpurnius Piso IIIvir on this Augustan issue with the SC within wreath reverse. He connects the moneyer to the wider Pisonum family discussion and notes the IIIvir title on the coin as establishing magistracy.

moneyer: L. Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus / Q. Servilius Caepio
obverse: Bare head right; PISO above, CAEPIO below
reverse: Two seated figures; AD-FAV EMV EX SC around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the seated figures on the reverse as Cereales Aediles in the context of the grain commission, and names 'Pifo Caepionis collega, familia ortus eft plebeia' (p. 48) to explain why Piso — being of plebeian origin — held this magistracy rather than the patrician aedileship. He does not give the full names 'L. Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus' or 'Q. Servilius Caepio' nor state the date '100 BC' in his commentary on this coin.
orsini_error: Conflates L. Calpurnius Bibulus with Cn. Calpurnius Piso in the Augustan bronze attributions

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 416 — L. Caninius Gallus, 12 BC
obverse: Bare head right (Augustus); AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Kneeling figure holding trophy; L.CANINIVS.GALLVS.III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini enumerates four Caninian families (Rebili, Reguli, Galli, Labones) and identifies L. Caninius Gallus as IIIvir A.A.A.F.F. He reads the kneeling figure holding trophy on the reverse as commemorating the recovery of Parthian standards under Augustus.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 417 — L. Caninius Gallus, IIIvir monetalis, 12 BC
obverse: Bare head right (Augustus); AVGVSTVS behind
reverse: Altar or cista within wreath; AVGVSTVS / TR.POT; CANINIVS.GALLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the reverse of this second Caninius Gallus coin as a tabernaculum (military tent), designating the assault or siege of a town under Augustus: 'tabernaculù, quod est in secundo denario signatu, oppidi alicuius oppugnatione sub eodem Augusto designat.' He does not describe it as a tribunal or altar.

obverse: Draped female bust right (Victory or Diana)
reverse: Horseman in biga right; T.CARISI below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that no ancient writers mention the Carisia gens except Dio on T. Carisius. He reads the draped female bust as Victory or Diana and treats this biga type as the first of T. Carisius's diverse series of 46 BC.

obverse: Draped female head right; MONETA behind
reverse: Round domed temple (rotunda/shrine); T·CARISIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the MONETA bust as Juno Moneta (guardian of the mint) and reads the anvil, hammer, and tongs on the reverse as the implements of the mint itself. He connects the T.CARISIVS legend to the moneyer's role as monetary official.

obverse: Draped female head right
reverse: Sphinx seated right; T.CARISI below
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the sphinx on this T. Carisius denarius to Augustus's personal signet seal, explaining that Carisius struck the sphinx 'in Augusti gratiam.' He cites Suetonius (lib. II cap. V) for the fact that Augustus used a sphinx as his seal before switching to the image of Alexander and then his own portrait. Orsini's reading correctly attributes the sphinx to Augustus, not to Alexander.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind
reverse: Cornucopia on globe, sceptre and rudder within wreath; T.CARIS
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the helmeted ROMA bust and the sceptre/trophy within wreath as T. Carisius's martial type. He connects the reverse wreath to Victoria imagery and notes this as the fourth distinct reverse type Carisius produced in 46 BC.

obverse: Head of Apollo right, oak-wreathed; thunderbolt below
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; GAR·OGVL·VER (order varies by subtype)

obverse: Draped female bust right (Diana); bow and quiver behind
reverse: Running dog right; T.CA behind
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Diana/hound type of T. Carisius as struck for the Ludi Saeculares. He reads the bow and quiver on the obverse and the running hound on the reverse as Diana attributes appropriate to the secular games imagery.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 4A — P. Carisius legatus pro praetore; Head of Augustus bare right / Trophy on mound of shields; AR denarius, Emerita, 25–23 BC
obverse: Head of Augustus bare right; IMP CAESAR AVGVST around
reverse: Trophy erected on mound of shields; P CARISIVS LEG PRO PR around
