orsini_comment: Orsini discusses P. Carisius in Lusitania and notes his magistrate titles (legatus, pro praetore) on the provincial coinage. He connects the trophy on mound of shields reverse to the Cantabrian victory and reads the Emerita Augusta mint as evidence of the colonial foundation.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 9A — P. Carisius legatus pro praetore, AR denarius, 25–23 BC, Emerita
obverse: Bare head of Augustus right; IMP·CAESAR·AVGVST around
reverse: City wall with arched gateway and two towers; EMERITA above, P·CARISIVS·LEG·PRO·PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads P. Carisius's magistrate title (LEG AVG PRO PR) and discusses the city gateway on the reverse as evidence of the colonial foundation of Emerita Augusta. He connects the crossed weapons type to the Cantabrian wars.

obverse: Bare head of Augustus; IMP CAESAR AVGVST around
reverse: Shield with spear behind; legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini notes P. Carisius as legatus pro praetore of Augustus in Lusitania and reads the arms/trophy reverse as a monument to the Cantabrian conquest. He treats the Emerita mint issues as evidence of Augustus's colonial programme in Spain.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 1A — P. Carisius legatus pro praetore; Bare head of Augustus left / Victory standing right placing wreath on trophy; AR quinarius, Emerita, 25–23 BC
obverse: Bare head of Augustus right; AVGVSTVS.IMP.CAESAR around
reverse: Victory standing right placing wreath on trophy; P.CARISIVS.LEG.PRO.PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this quinarius of P. Carisius with Victory crowning a trophy. He reads it as a monument to the Cantabrian victory and connects the Victory type to the Augustan settlement of the western provinces under Carisius's propraetorian command.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 23 — P. Carisius, legatus pro praetore, Emerita mint, c. 25-23 BC
obverse: Bare head right; TRIB.POTEST.CAESAR.AVG around
reverse: P.CARISIVS / LEG / AVGVSTI (inscription only)
orsini_comment: Orsini notes P. Carisius LEG PRO PR on this bronze and discusses the Emerita mint as the colonial capital of Lusitania. He connects the civic imagery to the foundation of the colony and reads the coin as establishing the moneyer's provincial authority.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 2B — P. Carisius legatus pro praetore; Bare head of Augustus left / Round shield, spear-head and curved sword; AR denarius, Emerita, 25–23 BC
obverse: Bare head right (Augustus); IMP / CAESAR / AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Crossed weapons (pugio and caetra); P.CARISIVS / LEG.PRO.PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the round shield, spear-head, and curved sword on the reverse as captured Cantabrian arms. He connects the IMP CAESAR AVGVST obverse to the Augustan triumph and treats the weapons type as the most explicitly military of the P. Carisius series.

obverse: Veiled female head right (Vesta); VEST behind
reverse: Round temple (aedicula of Vesta); AC within
orsini_comment: Orsini says this first coin 'potest ad Q. CASSIVM referri,' noting Q. Cassius as Tribunus Plebis (anno DCCIX). He observes that the vessels and lituus on the coin indicate Q. Cassius's auguratus and pontificatus, but adds 'nihil (quod sciam) apud scriptores reperitur' about those offices — he can find nothing in the sources about them.

obverse: Head of Libertas right; LIBERT before, Q·CASSIVS around
reverse: Round temple (aedicula of Vesta); A C flanking at base
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this second Q. Cassius Longinus type as part of the same magistracy series. He notes the Vesta and temple types as chosen to reference the tribunician sacred inviolability that Q. Cassius was accused of violating.

obverse: Veiled female head left (Vesta)
reverse: Standing togate figure; LONGINVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this urn/voting type of Q. Cassius Longinus (Crawford 413) to the ballot laws of the Cassii. He reads the voting urn on the reverse as referencing L. Cassius Longinus's lex tabellaria on judicial voting, connecting the two branches of the family.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Libertas in quadriga right; C.CASSI / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini says this coin 'pertinet, in quo ponè Romae caput urna quaedam adiecta est, in quam tabellae à iudicibus coniicebantur, uel Absolutionis, uel Condemnationis' — a voting urn placed beside the head of Roma, into which judges cast their ballots of absolution or condemnation.

obverse: Veiled head right (Vesta); CASSIVS around
reverse: Round temple; IMP.CAES.TRIAN / AVG / AC around
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as a variant or duplicate of Q. Cassius Longinus's Vesta/temple type (Crawford 428/1). He treats it alongside coins 1-2 as part of the same Q. Cassius magistracy series, noting the consistent reverse iconography.

obverse: Laureate head of Libertas right; C·CASSEI·IMP
reverse: Crab holding aplustre in claws; rose and untied diadem on left; M·SERVILIVS LEG
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Cassius Longinus as the tyrannicide on this joint issue with M. Servilius as legate. He connects C. Cassius to the fleet command against Dolabella and the joint command before Philippi, drawing on Appian's Bella Civilia.

obverse: Head of Libertas right, wreathed; C·CASSI·IMP around
reverse: Aplustre (curved naval stern-ornament); M·SERVILIVS LEG around
orsini_comment: Orsini says five coins on this plate were struck by C. Cassius ('quinà C. CASSIO Caesaris percussore signati fint, dubitari nõ potest') and discusses C. Cassius's deeds after Caesar's assassination at length, citing Livy, Velleius, Dio, Appian, Plutarch, and Suetonius. He does not single out this coin as gold, nor does he remark on exceptional metal or connect the gold coinage specifically to the gravity of the Philippi command.

identification: Crawford 507/2 — P. Servilius Casca Longus under Brutus, 42 BC
moneyer: P. Servilius Casca Longus (as military moneyer for Brutus)
obverse: Head of bearded figure right, laureate; CASCA LONGVS around; trident symbol
reverse: Victory advancing right, holding wreath and palm branch; BRVTVS IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this issue of P. Servilius Casca Longus under Brutus as part of the libertarian/tyrannicide series. He connects P. Casca to the assassination of Caesar (citing Appian) and reads the coin as a monument to the Liberatores' cause.

obverse: Head of Libertas right, wearing diadem
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT in field
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue of C. Cassius Longinus with Lentulus Spinther (Crawford 500). He connects both men to the command against Dolabella and the preparations for Philippi, drawing on Appian's Bella Civilia for the civil war context.

obverse: Head of Libertas right; C·CASSI·IMP and LEIBERTAS around
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT in field
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as a second type in the Cassius/Lentulus Spinther joint series (Crawford 500). He connects both men to Cassius's fleet command against Dolabella and the preparations before Philippi, drawing on Appian's Bella Civilia. He does not use the framing 'senatorial resistance to the triumvirs'; the Republican cause is characterised through Cassius's personal military role and the tyrannicide tradition.

identification: Crawford 355/1f — C. Cassius and L. Salinius, AE as, 84 BC
obverse: Janiform (two-faced) bearded head
reverse: Prow of galley right; C·CASSI / L·SALIN above
orsini_comment: Orsini includes this bronze as (Crawford 355/1f) for C. Cassius with L. Salinius within the Cassia section. He reads it as an early Republican bronze issue and connects it to the plebeian Cassian tradition.

obverse: Head right, bare or lightly helmeted (helmet unclear in engraving)
reverse: Eagle with spread wings on thunderbolt; to left, lituus; to right, capis (jug); Q·CASSIVS around.
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this third Q. Cassius Longinus type (Crawford 428/3). He notes the eagle-on-thunderbolt or forum scene on the reverse as part of Q. Cassius's tribunician programme and connects the types to the lex Cassia tabellaria tradition.

obverse: Head of Liber right, ivy-wreathed; thyrsus over shoulder; no legend
reverse: Head of Libera left, vine-wreathed; L·CASSI·Q·F
orsini_comment: Denarius of L. Cassius Q.f. Longinus (Crawford 386/1). Obverse: ivy-wreathed head of Liber (Bacchus) right with thyrsus over the shoulder. Reverse: vine-wreathed head of Libera left, L·CASSI·Q·F. A Bacchic Liber/Libera pairing, not a Libertas/voting-urn ballot type.

obverse: Head of Ceres right, wreathed with grain; CAECIN(A) around.
reverse: Yoke of oxen left driven by ploughman; L·CASSI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini says this coin 'potest ad legem Cassiam frumentariam pertinere, latam in ipso consulatu à C. Cassio Varo Cos. cum M. Terentio Varrone Lucullo anno DCLXXX' — a grain law (lex Cassia frumentaria), citing Asconius in Verrina. He connects it to Cereris imago (Ceres's image) as appropriate to grain-law commemoration.

obverse: OB CIVIS SERVATOS — oak wreath between two laurel branches
reverse: SC in centre; C·CASSIVS·C·F·CELER·IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini records C. Cassius Celer as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus and notes the Augustan portrait on the obverse. He treats this bronze as the Augustan bookend to his Cassian treatment, contrasting it with the Republican ballot-law types.

obverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
reverse: SC in centre; C·CASSIVS·C·F·CELER·IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini records this second C. Cassius Celer bronze, noting the IIIvir monetalis title. He discusses the S.C and Augustan reverse as standard Augustan bronze formula and connects the moneyer to the Augustan collegiate system of the mint.

moneyer: C. Cassius Longinus (imp.) / Cornelius Lentulus Spinther (quaest.)
obverse: Tripod with cauldron and two laurel branches; C·CASSI IMP
reverse: Capis and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the tyrannicide C. Cassius Longinus on this first issue in the Cassius/Lentulus Spinther series (Crawford 500/1). He connects the issue to Cassius's fleet command and discusses the Republican cause, citing Appian and Cicero's Philippics.

obverse: Bust of Africa, right, draped and wearing elephant's skin
reverse: Curule chair, of which front legs are decorated with sculpted eagles and on which lies Corinthian helmet. L·CESTIVS C·NORBA PR S·C
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Cestius from Cicero (pro L. Flacco and Philippicae III) and Appian (Bella Civilia IV). He reads the inscription C. Cestius L.F. POB. EPVLO PR. TR. PL. and discusses the curule chair on the reverse as indicating praetorship, citing Varro on the sella curulis. He connects the elephant-skin headdress to Africa and Metellus Scipio.

obverse: Handwritten annotation (not a coin engraving): text notes on Norbanus/Cestius coins
reverse: No engraving — manuscript annotation only
orsini_comment: Later annotator's note (French) copying Mionnet (p. 28, ‘Raretés en or’) for the Cestia gold aureus — Cybele in a chariot drawn by two lions (Crawford 491/2): «Cybèle dans un char traîné par deux lions», AV, «200 fr» — Mionnet's 1847 valuation for that aureus.

obverse: Handwritten annotation (not a coin engraving): bibliographic/numismatic notes
reverse: No engraving — manuscript annotation only
orsini_comment: Later annotator's note (French) citing «Mionnet, Tome 1er, p. 28» for the gens Cestia — the Nero-era provincial bronzes (moyen and petit bronze) struck at Antioche, «de 2 à 24 fr», transcribed almost verbatim.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: Victory in galloping biga right, holding reins; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that no ancient writers mention the gens Cipia and argues it is the same family as Cispia without the S. He cites Cicero's oratione post reditum in senatu and oratione pro P. Sextio, and notes that the manuscript reading Mospius was corrected to M. Cispius by Manutio ("emendatur a Manutio M. Cifpius"), not by Orsini himself.

obverse: Handwritten note: 'N° 7 c. une / autre variété'
reverse: No engraving — blank circles
orsini_comment: Later annotator's note (French): «il y a une autre variété»; the right circle was left blank.

obverse: Bare male head right (Marcellinus); MARCELLINVS around
reverse: Figure standing within temple or shrine structure with columns; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to Cn. Lentulus Marcellinus ("sine dubio a Cn. Lentvlo Marcellino cusus est"), not P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus. He discusses the Marcellorum family tradition and reads the reverse type as a monument to M. Claudius Marcellus's Sicilian triumphs, noting the "tria crura" (Sicilian symbol) as expressing Marcellus's connection to Sicily.

obverse: Bearded head of Saturn right; harpa behind; NERI·Q·VRB around
reverse: Legionary eagle (aquila) between two standards; L·LENT·C·MARC / COS
orsini_comment: Denarius of Cn. Nerius, quaestor urbanus, 49 BC (legionary eagle between two standards, naming the consuls L. Cornelius Lentulus and C. Claudius Marcellus). Orsini files it in the Claudian section via the Marcellus name.

moneyer: L. Cornelius Lentulus Crus and C. Claudius Marcellus (cos.)
obverse: Head right; L·LENT·C·MARC·COS around
reverse: Standing figure facing, holding objects in both hands; rectangular object (altar or cippus) to right; star in field
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the joint issue of L. Cornelius Lentulus Crus and C. Claudius Marcellus (consuls of 49 BC). He discusses the two men's opposition to Caesar and reads the coin as a monument to the last Republican consuls before the civil war.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; modius (control) behind; ✱ below chin; X (value)
reverse: Victory in biga right; two corn-ears below; M·MARC; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: This denarius is in fact M. Marcius Mn.f. (Crawford 245/1): helmeted Roma with modius behind / Victory in biga, two corn-ears below, M·MARC, ROMA — the corn-ears alluding to a grain distribution by the moneyer's family. It is a gens MARCIA coin that Orsini filed under Claudia in error. (Re-identified from the former Pulcher 300/1.)
orsini_error: Orsini files this denarius of M. Marcius Mn.f. (Crawford 245/1, gens Marcia; legend M·MARC) under Claudia — a gens misattribution.

moneyer: Ap. Claudius Pulcher, T. Manlius Mancinus, Q. Urbinius
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right with feathered crest
reverse: Victory in triga right; AP·CL·T·MAL·Q·VR in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini places this Victory-in-triga denarius under Claudia on the strength of the legend AP·CL — Ap. Claudius Pulcher, lead moneyer of the joint issue AP·CL·T·MAL·Q·VR (Crawford 299/1a, 111 BC, with T. Manlius Mancinus and Q. Urbinius). The attribution is correct.

obverse: Bust of Diana right; S.C behind
reverse: Victory in biga right, galloping; LXXIIII above; TI.CLAVD.TI.F / A.N below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Ti. Claudius Ti.f. Ap.n. Nero's denarius (Crawford 383/1) as a monument of the Neronian branch of the Claudii. He reads the reverse type and connects the moneyer to the later Julio-Claudian house through the Tiberian lineage.

obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo?)
reverse: Crescent and five stars; P.CLODIVS / M.F below
orsini_comment: Orsini explicitly states he CANNOT determine what the Sol, Luna, and Mars imagery on P. Clodius M.F.'s coins means ("nec Solis mihi, nec Lunae, Martisq. simulacra in eius denariis expressa, quo pertineant, in tanta huius uiri ignoratione diuinare licet"). He does not identify an Apollo head as expressing Apolline devotion.

obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo?)
reverse: Single standing figure (Diana Lucifera) facing, holding long torch in each hand; M.F left, P.CLODIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini explains Diana's image on this P. Clodius M.F. coin by citing Callimachus's hymn to Diana and Sophocles (Trachiniae) on her bearing twin torches ("geminas faces manibus gestantem"). He does NOT frame this as part of a "triumviral programme of 42 BC."

obverse: CAESAR III·VIR·R·P·C: Bare head of Octavian right. Border of dots.
reverse: P·CLODIVS M·F: Pietas standing left, holding branch in right hand over a lit altar (stork at feet) and long sceptre in left. Border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes P. Clodius M.F. appears on coins "primo, secundo, tertio, & sexto" of the second plate but is otherwise unattested in ancient writers ("a nullo ueterum scriptorum, quos ego legerim, nominatur"). He does not use the language of a "triumviral monetary college."

obverse: Head of Flora right; flower symbol behind; C·CLODIVS C·F around
reverse: Claudia Pulchra seated left, holding culullus; VESTALIS legend
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses C. Clodius Vestalis within the Claudian plebeian section. He reads Crawford 512/2 and connects the moneyer to the Vestal connection implied by the cognomen, discussing the priestly family associations of the Clodii.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; quiver behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; C.PVLCHER below
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as a second specimen of C. Claudius Pulcher's Roma/biga type (Crawford 300/1), treating it alongside coin 4. He discusses the gens's patrician Pulchri tradition and notes the moneyer's place in the consular genealogy of the Claudii.

obverse: Clasped right hands holding caduceus; PVLCHER TAVRVS REGVLVS around
reverse: Large S·C; IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Augustan bronze of the moneyers Pulcher, Taurus and Regulus (IIIvir A.A.A.F.F): clasped hands holding a caduceus (concord) / large S C. Orsini files the moneyer in the Claudian section by name association.

obverse: Laureate head of Caesar right; CAESAR DICT·TER around
reverse: Standing Victory left; C·LOVIVS PRAEF around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Cluvius as praefectus urbis under Caesar, citing Dio lib. XLIII (no chapter specified). He notes the gens's origins in Puteoli from Cicero's epistle to Thermum and in oratione pro Q. Roscio calls a Cluvius equitem Romanum ornatissimum.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Victory in biga right; T.CLOVL / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini equates the Clovlia gens with the patrician Cloelia and cites Livy on the lex Canuleia and Dionysius lib. III on the family's Alban origin. He discusses T. Cloelius's connection to a Siculi cognomen and connects the spica symbol on the coin to possible Sicilian or frumentarian associations ("spica eius insulae peculiari symbolo T. Cloelium; qui denarium cudit, indicare uoluisse, credi potest"). He does NOT reference Dio or C. Cluvius as consul in 723 AUC — those belong to the Clovia section.

obverse: Laureate head right; F behind
reverse: Standing figure (Victory) crowning trophy; T.CLOVLI around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses only a single moneyer, T. Cloelius, in the Clovlia section and does not distinguish multiple coin types. He focusses on the question of which Cloelius struck the coin (the Tribunus militum consulari potestate of anno CCCIX who led the Ardea colony, or another Cloelius), and on the spica symbol as a possible indicator of Sicilian or frumentarian associations ('spica eius insulae peculiari symbolo T. Cloelium; qui denarium cudit, indicare uoluisse, credi potest'). He provides no description that would allow identification of a second distinct type. The Crawford number for this coin cannot be confirmed from Orsini's text.

identification: Crawford 517/5a — M. Cocceius Nerva (proquaestor pro praetore under Mark Antony), AR denarius, 41 BC
obverse: Bare head right (Mark Antony); M.ANT.IMP.III.VIR.R.P.C.M.NERVA.PROQ.P around
reverse: Bare head right (Antony); ANTONIVS.COS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the coin's portrait as M. Cocceius Nerva, consul with L. Gellius Poplicola in 717 AUC (37 BC by his reckoning), and cites Appian (Bella Civilia V) on his mediation between Antony and Octavian at Brundisium, and Horace (Satires I.5). Separately, Orsini speculates the coin was actually struck by L. Cocceius (M. Nerva's brother) as Antony's legatus pro praetore ("Antonii Legatus Pro Praetore... denarium cufit"). He does not conflate the Republican figure with the Emperor Nerva.

obverse: Bare head right; C·COEL·CALDVS / COS around
reverse: Trophies flanking a central standard; CALDVS·IIIVIR legend
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this denarius (Crawford 437/2) as struck by the grandson as IIIvir monetalis to honour his ancestor C. Coelius Caldus (consul 94 BC). He identifies the two bare heads as the consul and a family member and discusses the L.D. inscription as libero/damno (absolvo/condemno), relating it to the lex Cassia tabellaria.

obverse: Portrait head of C. Coelius Caldus (cos.) right; C·COEL·CALDVS COS around; L·D behind
reverse: Radiate head of Sol (Caldus IIIvir) right; CALDVS·IIIVIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses C. Coelius Caldus (cos.) and the Caldus IIIvir as the two generations commemorated. He connects the joint naming to the Republican practice of honouring consular ancestors on moneyers' coins and reads the reverse in connection with the family's voting-law associations.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma left; VII star behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; H above; C.COIL / CALD below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the early C. Coil. Cald. type (Crawford 318) as struck by the IIIvir in memory of his father and grandfather. He does NOT connect this early type to the Epulonum imagery — that interpretation (Jupiter on a couch) applies specifically to the fifth coin (IMP.A.X type) in relation to L. Coelius Caldus's Septemuirum Epulonum membership.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; control mark at right
reverse: Victory in biga right; CALD above; M in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini records this variant of Crawford 318 within the Caldus series. He treats it as a second example of the same type and discusses the Epulonum connection via L. Coelius Caldus's membership of the sacred college of seven.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (denominational mark) behind; border of dots.
reverse: Dioscuri galloping right; L·COIL ROMA legend; line border.
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Coelius as the earliest Coelian moneyer on the plate. He treats Crawford 154/1 as the founding monument of the Coelii in his numismatic record and connects the early issue to the gens's plebeian status and Roman citizenship.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right; A behind
reverse: Curule chair (sella curulis); C·CONSIDI above, PAETI below
orsini_comment: Orsini classifies the Considii as plebeian, citing Liuius lib. II and Dionyfius lib. IX. He does NOT definitively identify C. Considius Paetus as quaestor — he says the coins suggest he was "Praetorem uel Aedilem" (praetor or aedile), and identifies the curule chair with quaestors for capital cases without assigning that role to Paetus himself.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Victory in galloping quadriga right, holding the reins; C·CONSIDI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Venus Erycina type as struck by C. Considius Nonianus and documents the temple from Liuius lib. XXX and XL, Ovid Fasti III, and Strabo lib. VI. He connects Nonianus to Gallia citerior (from Cicero ep. XI ad Tironem: "citeriorem Confidio Noniano"), NOT to an African command. The Africa passage in Orsini refers to C. Considius the proconsul (the Ligarius oration), not to Nonianus.

obverse: Laureate head left; PAETI behind
reverse: Victory in fast quadriga left, holding palm-branch and reins; C·CONSIDI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as a third type of C. Considius Paetus. He carefully distinguishes Paetus's multiple curule-chair types from the Nonianus Venus Erycina issue, treating the five denarii systematically as evidence of two separate moneyers within the same magistracy year.

obverse: Laureate head right; PAETI around
reverse: Victory walking right holding wreath; C·CONSIDI around
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as a fourth Considius Paetus type. He notes the consistent curule chair reverse across the Paetus series and reads the quaestorial chair as establishing the moneyer's magistracy. He connects the multiple types to the large issue of 46 BC.

obverse: Laureate male head right; C·CONSIDI·NONIANI around, S·C below
reverse: Gateway of city (Emerita or temple portico); ERVCI above; fortified walls below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses C. Considius Nonianus's temple of Venus Erycina reverse (Crawford 424). He identifies the famous Sicilian sanctuary as the subject and connects Nonianus to a legate command in Africa under Proconsul Considius, reading the Venus type as a monument to the family's Sicilian connections.

obverse: Draped female head right (Concordia or Apollo?); IIIIVIR / Q.SICINIVS around; star before
reverse: Club (of Hercules) set upright and draped with a lion's skin; PR·S·C at left, Q·COPONIVS at right
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies T. Coponius as the first of the gens to become a Roman citizen ("primus ex ea gente ciuis Romanus factus est"), NOT as the first to hold a Roman magistracy. He identifies C. Coponius as praetor commanding the Rhodian fleet (citing Caesar, Cicero, Velleius, Appian) and reads PR.S.C as Praetor Senatus Consulto. The club and lion skin reverse are identified as Herculean from Tibur's temple of Hercules.

obverse: Conjoined (jugate) heads of the Dioscuri right, a star above each; RVFVS and III·VIR around
reverse: Venus standing left, holding scales (balance) and a long sceptre, a cornucopia at her side; MN·CORDIVS at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the gens is known only from Cicero (book IV in Verrem) on L. Cordius. He reads this Venus Verticordia with Cupid obverse as struck in Caesaris gratiam, connecting the imagery to Caesar's claim of Julian descent from Venus.

obverse: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem
reverse: Cupid (Amor) riding on a dolphin right; M·CORDIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini admits difficulty explaining the Cupid on dolphin reverse type and notes the maritime connection of Venus (born from the sea). He reads the Amor on dolphin motif as relating to Venus's origins, candidly acknowledging that some types remain unexplained by historical sources.

obverse: Helmet (Corinthian) with crest; owl perched on top; RVFVS behind
reverse: Rosette or shield with radiating pattern; MN.CORDIVS around; RVFVS visible
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Corinthian helmet and owl as Minerva's aegis and noctua (owl). He reads the third Cordian type as a monument to Minerva's wisdom and candidly acknowledges that the historical connection between the Cordia gens and this imagery is not explained by the surviving sources.

obverse: Head of Mars right, wearing Corinthian helmet; CN.BLASIO.CN.F around
reverse: Three standing figures (Jupiter, Juno, Minerva?); ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Cn. Cornelius Blasio as consul in anno CDXCVI AUC (with C. Atilio Regulo) and notes this coin commemorates Blasio's victory over the Samnites/Umbrians, whose triumph is expressed on the reverse.

obverse: Draped bust right with sceptre over shoulder; G·P·R text at top
reverse: Sceptre with wreath, globe, and rudder; CN·LEN·Q text in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus within his treatment of the Lentuli. He reads the reverse type and connects the moneyer to the Clodiana branch, noting the magistracy of 88 BC in the Social War period.

obverse: Bearded head of Jupiter right, laureate
reverse: Globe between a sceptre surmounted by a wreath (left) and a rudder (right); EX-S·C across field; LEN·CVR·X·FL in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus and discusses the Marcellinus branch within the Lentulorum family. He reads this Crawford 393/1b type and connects the moneyer to the extended Lentulorum prosopography in Cicero and Livy.

obverse: Draped bust right with sceptre over shoulder
reverse: Horse and chariot (biga) moving right; CN·LENTV text below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus's Crawford 345/1 issue. He reads the reverse type and connects the moneyer to the Spanish campaigns of 76-75 BC, citing Livy and Sallust for the military context.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right
reverse: Genius of the Roman People standing facing/left, holding sceptre, crowned by Victory standing behind him; globe and rudder at his feet; CN·LENT in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this second Lentulus Marcellinus type (Crawford 345/2). He treats coins 4 and 5 as a pair and discusses the moneyer's role in the broader Cornelian plate's account of the Lentuli.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter left; M behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; L·SCIP·ASIAG in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Cornelius Scipio Asiagenes and his role in the Asiatic campaigns. He reads Crawford 311/1 and connects the moneyer to the Scipio branch, distinguishing him from Africanus and discussing the Scipionic tradition of eastern conquest.

moneyer: L. Manlius Torquatus / L. Cornelius Sulla
obverse: Laureate or diademed head facing right; L·SVLLA visible on left side
reverse: Sacrificial implements: capis (jug) and lituus flanked by additional vessels/standards; IMPER ITERVM around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as belonging to P. Sulla, son of Sulla Felix's brother (not a Torquatus/Sulla joint issue): 'PRIMVS huius tabellae denarius pertinet (ut opinor, ad P.SVLLAM, Sullae Felicis Dictatoris fratris filium, qui cum L. Autronio Paeto Consul designatus anno DCLXXX a L. Torquato ambitus accusatus damnatusque, defensus est a Cicerone.' He notes the coin shows P.SVLLA and ROMA.

moneyer: L. Manlius Torquatus (pro quaestore) and L. Sulla (imperator)
obverse: Draped, diademed female head right (Venus type)
reverse: Three trophies side by side (engraved as armed figures); capis (jug) to left; VES below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this coin as designating Sulla Dictator's triumph de rege Mithridate: 'Secundus denarius sine dubio Sullae Dictatoris triumphum designat de rege Mithridate, cuius meminerunt cum alii multi, tum Cicero in oratione pro lege Manilia.' He notes Sulla was called Imperator, as attested by the denarius legend and by Plutarch.

moneyer: L. Manlius Torquatus (pro quaestore) and L. Sulla (imperator)
obverse: Head facing right with crest; S·C visible around edge
reverse: Circular arrangement of round objects (wreaths around central globe)
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the third coin to the Sullae cognomen derived from the Sibylla: 'Tertius denarius spectat, ut opinor, ad Sullae cognomen, quod eius familia a Sibylla traxisse dicitur, cuius libris interpretandis unus maiorum xuir sacris faciundis praefuerit: ab eo enim munere Sibylla primum, postea Sulla dictus est: itaq. in altera denarii parte Sibylla ipsa impressa est.'

obverse: Draped bust right (Venus) with sceptre behind; D·S visible on left
reverse: Three trophies standing upright with arms/armour; VES visible below
orsini_comment: Coin 10 (concordance): Orsini discusses the third Cornelia plate (p. 74) as devoted entirely to Sulla and Faustus types. No coin in this plate is attributed by Orsini to Q. Curtius or M. Sergius Silus. Crawford 426/4a (Q.CVRT / M.SILA) is a type belonging to the Curtia gens; its appearance in the Cornelia concordance at position 11 is unsupported by Orsini's text. Coin 11 (Crawford 426/4a attributed to Q. Curtius / M. Sergius Silus) should be removed from or flagged in the Cornelia concordance — this coin type does not belong here per Orsini.

moneyer: Q. Curtius and M. Sergius Silus
obverse: Crowned or wreathed head facing right; S·C visible; V·R·S visible
reverse: Four circular wreaths arranged symmetrically around central globe in cross pattern
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this issue of Q. Curtius and M. Sergius Silus (Crawford 426/4a) within the Cornelia section. He connects the two moneyers to the joint magistracy and reads the coin type within his extended treatment of the Cornelian plate.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; behind, standing Victory crowning her
reverse: Two standing figures clasping hands over a base/platform, the right figure holding a spear; ROM above; SVLLA·IMP in exergue below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Cornelius Sulla imperator on this Babelon Cornelia 31 issue. He reads the Sullan legends and connects the coin to Plutarch's account of Sulla's return from the east and his assumption of the dictatorship.
specimen_credit: after Babelon, Description historique (1885–86), public domain

obverse: Bare head right (Sulla?); SVLLA.CO behind
reverse: Bare head right (Rufus?); Q.POM.RV / RVFVS.COS behind
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Faustus Cornelius Sulla's denarius noting that Faustus's own image appears with the lituus of the Auguratus. The coin was struck by Faustus himself; Q. Pompeius Rufus was Sulla's co-consul (not the moneyer of this coin). Orsini reads the Auguratus insignia and connects the name Faustus to Sulla's celebrated fortune: 'nisi quod in eo, Fausti Sullae filii imago expressa est cum lituo Auguratus insigni.'

obverse: Curule chair with crossed legs; grain ears flanking; legend around
reverse: Curule chair with crossed legs; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this second Faustus Cornelius Sulla type (Crawford 434/2). He notes the Faustus name as commemorating Sulla's celebrated fortuna and reads the Sullan imagery within his extended discussion of Sulla's divine favour and the Sibylline prophecy.

obverse: Tousled-hair head facing right (Hercules type); FELIX legend clearly visible
reverse: Figure on horseback or in biga facing right; FAVSTVS legend clearly visible below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Faustus Cornelius Sulla's own issue (Crawford 426/2). He connects the reverse type to the Sullan triumphal tradition and reads the coin as a monument to Sulla's three eastern victories noted in his extended Cornelian commentary.

obverse: Draped, diademed female head (Diana) with hair gathered behind; FAVSTVS behind
reverse: Sulla seated on raised platform; kneeling figure presenting olive branch (Bocchus) at left and bound kneeling captive (Jugurtha) at right; FELIX behind/above
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this first Faustus Sulla type (Crawford 426/1) as the primary monument of Faustus in the Cornelian series. He discusses Sulla's four triumphs and the globe with crowns iconography, connecting it to the Sibylline prophecy on Sulla's fortune.

identification: Crawford 345/3 — Cn. Cornelius Lentulus, 88 BC (bronze as)
obverse: Head of Janus bifrons, bearded
reverse: Prow right; CN.LENTV above
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this bronze as (Crawford 345/3) within the Lentulorum section. He identifies Cn. Cornelius Lentulus as issuer and reads the Roman as type as a standard bronze issue of the Lentulorum branch of 76-75 BC.

obverse: Bare head right; MARCELLINVS around
reverse: Tetrastyle temple; MARCELLVS inside; MARCELLVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus issue (Crawford 439/1) as a later Republican type. He places it within the Marcellinus branch and discusses the moneyer's connection to the broader Lentulorum genealogy.

identification: Crawford 329/1a — Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus, 88 BC
obverse: Bearded head right; ROMA below
reverse: Standing nude male figure (Genius?) and Victory within wreath; LEN.MAR below; G control mark
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus's issue (Crawford 329/1a) of 88 BC. He reads the reverse type and connects the Social War period magistracy to the Clodiana branch, drawing on Cicero's Verrine orations for the family's prominence.

obverse: Bearded male head right (Jupiter); no clear legend on obverse
reverse: Standing frontal figure (Artemis of Ephesus); L·LENTVLVS C·MARC·COS text
orsini_comment: Orsini notes P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus's Crawford 445/3a issue. He connects the moneyer to the 50 BC magistracy and discusses the Lentulorum Marcellini as the most prominent branch of the Lentuli in the late Republican period.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; SISENA before, ROMA behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga galloping right, hurling thunderbolt and holding sceptre/reins; C.N.CORNEL below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Cn. Cornelius Sisenna within his Cornelian treatment. He reads Crawford 310/1 and connects the Sisennae branch to the annalistic tradition, noting L. Cornelius Sisenna the historian as the most distinguished member of this branch.

obverse: Schematic head or figure; worn woodcut
reverse: Triskeles (three legs) with figure/head in center
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this Faustus Cornelius Sulla type (Crawford 445/1a) as part of the Sullan series. He discusses the reverse imagery and connects it to Sulla's fortuna tradition, treating it within the broader Sullan commemoration on the plate.

identification: Crawford 178/3 — L. Cornelius Cinna, 169-158 BC (bronze triens)
obverse: Helmeted head of Minerva right
reverse: Ship's hull (carina) right; CINA above, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses L. Cornelius Cinna's bronze triens (Crawford 178/3). He reads the early issue as evidence of the Cornelian gens's antiquity in the Roman monetary tradition and notes Cinna within his overview of the patrician Cornelii.

moneyer: C. Cassius Longinus / P. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
obverse: Veiled head of Libertas; C·CASSI·IMP / LEIBERTAS around
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the first four coins of this plate to P. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther, to whom Cicero addressed his first book of letters, or to Spinther's son who was both Augur and himself Spinther. He notes the coins bear Libertas imagery and the names of Cassius and Brutus, though Lentulus was not actually one of Caesar's killers (Appian, Bellum civile II). The cognomen Spinther derived from an actor to whom Lentulus bore resemblance (Valerius Max. and Pliny). No mention of Cornelia or adoption into the Manlii Torquati.

moneyer: C. Cassius Longinus / P. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
obverse: Head right; CASSI.IMP / LEIBERTAS around
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT below
orsini_comment: Orsini records this as a second example of the Cassius/Lentulus Spinther joint issue (Crawford 500/5). He treats it alongside coin 24 as a duplicate specimen of the same type and connects both to Cassius's command against Dolabella before Philippi.

moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus / P. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
obverse: Sacrificial/pontifical implements: a sacrificial axe (securis), a jug (capis/simpulum) and a knife; BRVTVS in exergue below
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; LENTVLVS / SPINT below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this Brutus/Lentulus Spinther joint issue (Crawford 500/7). He connects P. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther to both Cassius and Brutus in the Republican command structure before Philippi, drawing on Appian for the joint Liberatores' operations.

obverse: Bare bearded head right; Q.C.S behind
reverse: Male figure (Genius/Hercules) seated on a curule chair holding a long scepter and a branch/cornucopia, crowned by a small flying Victory at upper right; P.LENT.P.F before, L.N behind
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes coins 5 and 6 of the Spinther plate to L. Cornelius P.F. Flamen Martialis, 'qui ultimo anno libertatis reip. & urbis conditae DCCIII, consul fuit cum C.Marcello.' He derives this identification from the denarius inscription itself. These coins are not connected to the Sertorian war or 74 BC.

obverse: Male head right with flowing hair; text at top and left edge
reverse: Legionary eagle (aquila) between two military standards (signa); LENT to left, C.MARC to right, COS below; control letters H and R
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin also to L. Cornelius P.F. Flamen Martialis, consul anno DCCIII with C. Marcellus, and notes that the Consulship itself is indicated by the denarius inscription ('qui quidem Consulatus ipsa denariorum inscriptione indicatur'). No connection to a Sertorian war context.

obverse: Laureate head right; V·LENT·C·MARC·COS legend around
reverse: Standing nude male figure (Jupiter?) facing front-right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus's Crawford 445/2 issue of 76-75 BC. He treats this as a third Marcellinus type and discusses the moneyer's connection to the extended Lentulorum genealogy within his six-page Cornelia treatment.

obverse: Head of Augustus right, wearing oak wreath; AVGVSTVS COS XI around
reverse: Head of Agrippa right, wearing mural and rostral crown; M·AGRIPPA·COS·TER·COSSVS·LENTVLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Cossus Cornelius Cn.f. Lentulus (described in both first coins of this plate) as consul cum L. Calpurnio Pisone anno DCCII, and legatus Augusti anno DCCLIX, who received triumphal honours from the Isaurians in Cilicia. The equestrian statue on the coin's reverse pertains to Augustus, under whose auspices Cossus gained his victory. Orsini does not describe this coin as an Augustan imperial issue with Augustus's portrait as obverse.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 412 — Cossus Cornelius Lentulus, 12 BC
obverse: Bare head right; AVGVSTVS DIVI F around
reverse: Horseman galloping right on pedestal; COSSVS.CN.F.LENTVLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the second coin of Cossus Cornelius Lentulus (second coin of this plate) and notes the naval crown of M. Agrippa depicted ('De corona autem nauali M. Agrippae dicetur in familia Vipsania'). He does not describe this as a separate Augustan imperial issue; both coins belong to Cossus Cornelius Lentulus as treated on this page.

obverse: Head of Octavian right, possibly bearded; C·CAESAR·III·VIR·R·P·C legend visible
reverse: Club pointing left; BALBVS·PRO·PR legend visible
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Cornelius Balbus as suffect consul cum P. Canidio Crasso anno DCCXIII, a Gaditanus mentioned in the life of Atticus by Cornelius Nepos, and given Roman citizenship by Cn. Pompeius (Strabo III). Balbus came from Gades where there was a temple of Hercules, whence Orsini explains the club (Hercules's deity symbol) on the coin reverse. Orsini does not describe this coin as struck 'pro praetore' or as showing Octavian's portrait on the obverse.

obverse: Janus bifrons (two profile heads back-to-back); C·N·LENT visible
reverse: Ship's prow (rostrum) facing right; C·N·LENT·CVR·FL or similar text
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this sixth bronze coin to P. Cornelius Blasio, praetor anno DLIX (not to Cn. Cornelius Lentulus): 'Sextus aereus nummus ad P. Cornelium Blasionem pertinet, ut opinor, qui Praetor fuit anno DLIX, P. Scipione Africano II & Ti. Sempronio Longo cos.' He notes that in Livy manuscripts P. is correctly the praenomen, while the printed editions wrongly read Caius.

obverse: Head of Tanit left (read by Orsini as Jupiter Ammon, for Africa). Border of dots.
reverse: Q·CORNVFICI·AVGVR·IMP: Q. Cornuficius standing left, veiled, holding lituus; on right, Juno Sospita (in goatskin, crow on shoulder, holding spear and shield) crowning him. Border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Cornuficius as augur and Cicero's competitor in Consulatu and colleague in Auguratu. He reads the Jupiter Ammon head as representing Africa (the province where Cornuficius served as Imperator). The Augurem-crowning imagery is noted on this denarius and connected tentatively, not conclusively, to the Lanuvian cult of Juno Sospita. Orsini says the Juno Sospita explanation will be discussed under the Procilia gens.

obverse: Bare bearded head left (Jupiter or Mars?)
reverse: Two standing figures: Q. Cornuficius (left, veiled, holding lituus) being crowned by Juno Sospita/Victory (right); Q.CORNVFICI around, AVGVR IMP to right, VICI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the Ceres on the reverse as representing Africa's fertility (ob provinciae fertilitatem). He connects this second Cornuficium type to Q. Cornuficius's African command and notes the gens's biographical connection to Cicero's consular competition. The plate legend reads VFICI (= Cornufici).

moneyer: L. Cosconius M.f. / L. Licinius Crassus / Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus
obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right; X behind
reverse: Naked Gallic warrior driving a galloping biga right, holding shield, spear and carnyx; L.LIC.CN.DOM (with control mark) in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini is uncertain whether the Cosconii were patrician or plebeian ('incertum est, patricia ne, an plebeia fuerit'). He identifies L. Cosconius M.F. from the coin legend and cites Livius (book XXX) for M. Cosconius as tribune of soldiers, making L. Cosconius his son. He references Cicero pro Sulla for C. Cosconius as praetor. He does not mention Narbo or a serrated fabric; these are modern numismatic attributions not found in Orsini's text.

obverse: Wreathed head of Caesar left; DIC·PERPETVO ... CAESAR
reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and sceptre; C·MARIDIANV (C. Cossutius Maridianus)
orsini_comment: Orsini places this coin in the gens Cossutia because its moneyer is C. Cossutius Maridianus (reverse C·MARIDIANV), one of Caesar's quattuorviri monetales of 44 BC (Crawford 480/16): wreathed head of Caesar, DIC·PERPETVO / Venus standing with Victory and sceptre. He connects the Cossutii to Caesar's first wife Cossutia (Suetonius, Caesar 1). (Re-identified from the former Buca 480/5.)

obverse: Veiled head right (Vesta?); IOVRTAE / CAESARI behind
reverse: COSSVTIANVS / MARIDII inscription; III.VIR / A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Cossutius Maridianus as moneyer after Caesar gained power and reads the A.A.F.F. inscription as Aere Argento Flando Feriundo, explaining the IIIvir monetalis role. He connects the Cossutii to the equestrian class and to Caesar's family connections.

obverse: Head left (female, diademed); SABVLA behind
reverse: Bellerophon riding the winged horse Pegasus right, brandishing spear; L.COSSVTI.C.F below
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the Medusa and Bellerophon on Pegasus for L. Cossutius Sabula as referencing the Corinth colony, comparing them to types of the Petronia gens. He reads the turreted crown on the Cybele bust as a distinctive obverse type of the Cossutian series.

obverse: Bust of Amphitrite seen from behind, head turned right, draped; control-mark behind. Serrate edge; border of dots.
reverse: Neptune in biga of sea-horses (hippocamps) right, holding reins in left hand and brandishing trident with right hand; control-mark above; in exergue, Q·CREPEREI / ROCVS. Border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini cites Cicero (book I in Verrem) for M. Crepereius from an equestrian family, identifying him as the likely father of Q. Crepereius M.F. He does not name a Neptune figure; he infers from unspecified coin imagery that some Crepereius performed a maritime enterprise ('re mari prospere … gessisse').

obverse: Bust of Amphitrite seen from behind, head turned right, draped; control-mark behind. Serrate edge; border of dots.
reverse: Neptune in biga of sea-horses (hippocamps) right, holding reins in left hand and brandishing trident with right hand; control-mark above; in exergue, Q·CREPEREI / ROCVS. Border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes Crepereius Gallus under Nero citing Tacitus book XIII (not book XIV as recorded in the concordance).

moneyer: P. Crepusius / C. Mamilius Limetanus / L. Marcius Censorinus
obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo); CENSORIN / III behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right; C.LIMET / P.CREPVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes no ancient writers mention the gens Crepusia. He reads P. Crepusius as IIIvir monetae cudendae with C. Mamilius Limetanus and L. Marcius Censorinus, anno DCCXIV (not DCXIV). An equestrian statue was granted to some Crepusius, which Crepusius commemorated on the coin.

moneyer: P. Crepusius / C. Mamilius Limetanus / L. Marcius Censorinus
obverse: Laureate head right; AED·PL text on left side
reverse: Two seated figures on chairs/stools facing each other; M·FAN·C·R·T text in exergue; PA above
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the control mark on this coin is CRT (not CRV as in the concordance). If CRT stands for Crepusius, it proves the gens was plebeian since L. Crepusius served as Aedilis plebis.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right; sceptre over shoulder; control-symbol behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right; P.CREPVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini records P. Crepusius's sole issue (Crawford 361/1c) alongside the joint types. He reads the horseman reverse as a monument to the equestrian honour and connects the single-moneyer issue to the joint college magistracy of 82 BC.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind; cornucopia
reverse: The Dioscuri (two horsemen) galloping right, each with couched spear; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that L. Cupiennius on this denarius is not mentioned by any ancient writer ('à nullo veterum scriptorum, quod sciam, nominatur'). He identifies C. Cupiennius (to whom Cicero addressed a letter) as the ancestor, and his son possibly as C. Cupiennius Libo Cumanus, described as a pursuer of married women and friend of Augustus — per Pomponius Porphyrio's commentary on Horace Satires I.2 (not directly from Horace). Orsini does not cite Horace as a prose source; the information comes from Porphyrio.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind; X
reverse: Juno (deity) in quadriga right, crowned by flying Victory; C.CVR / ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini classifies the Curiatii as a plebeian gens from Alba adscribed to Rome by King Tullus (Dionysius lib. III). He identifies the Trigeminorum family and C. Curiatius as the moneyer (Livy I, Livy epitome LV, Valerius Maximus III.7). He does NOT mention a trident symbol or connect it to the cognomen Trigeminus; he does NOT name the reverse biga as 'Juno Caprotina.' Those details are unattested in Orsini's text.

obverse: Head of Hercules right; three pellets behind (mark of value, quadrans)
reverse: Prow right; C·CVR·F above; ROMA below; three pellets
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the C.CVR.F legend on this bronze quadrans and identifies a later C. Curiatius as flamen Divi Augusti, primipilus, and praefectus castrorum from epigraphic evidence. He treats this as the bronze companion to the Trigeminus denarius.

moneyer: Q. Curtius / M. Silanus / Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; Q.CVRTI behind
reverse: Jupiter (or Roma) driving a galloping quadriga right, Victory flying above; M·SILA below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that Q. Curtius struck jointly with M. Iunius Silanus and Cn. Domitius as IIIviri monetales ('cum M. Iunio Silano & C N. Domitio III uir nummos aereum & argenteum cufit'), but explicitly states he could find nothing about Q. Curtius in ancient writers ('nihil potui apud scriptores reperire'). He does not identify or interpret coin 1 specifically beyond the legend attribution.

moneyer: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, Q. Curtius, M. Silanus (tresviri monetales)
obverse: Head of Hercules right; CN·DOMI legend; three pellets behind
reverse: Bow, club and arrow; M·SILA Q·CVRTI legend
orsini_comment: Orsini's text makes no coin-specific statement about coin 2 beyond the same general statement that Q. Curtius struck bronze and silver with Silanus and Domitius. The description of a 'bow, club and arrow' reverse is not attested in Orsini's text on p. 84.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; shield behind
reverse: Two gladiators fighting; T.DEIDI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as T. Didius, citing Sallust via Aulus Gellius (lib. II, cap. XXVII) for the IMP title and the triumphus. The extended passage interprets the vitis (vine rod) impressed on the soldier figure on the coin as a reference to military discipline — centurions beating soldiers out of order — citing Livy (epitoma lib. LVII), Pliny (lib. XIII), Tacitus (lib. I), and Plutarch in Galba. This is Orsini's interpretation of the combat/beating scene, not of gladiatorial venationes or military victories.

obverse: Veiled head right (Concordia); PONTIF·CAPITO·III·VIR·CONCORDIA legend around
reverse: Two-storey arcaded/columned building (the Villa Publica); T·DIDI and VIL·PVB at sides; IMP in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Villa Publica ('De Villa Publica, quae à Didio fortasse restituta, uel ornata, in altera parte secundi denarii signata est'), citing Cicero (ad Att. li. III), Livy (Macedones deducti extra urbem in Villam Publicam), and Varro (de re rustica li. I, cap. II). The second coin shows the Villa Publica and Orsini attributes it to T. Didius's restoration or ornamentation of the building. He also notes (p. 86 bottom) that Livy (li. CXXVII) mentions a Didius Saxa as legate of M. Antonius in Syria, 'à quo fortasse in T. Didii memoriam argenteus denarius cusus fuit.' Orsini does NOT describe the obverse legend of coin 2 as PONTIF·CAPITO·III·VIR·CONCORDIA; that legend belongs to a Fonteian coin (C. Fonteius Capito, Crawford 429/1) which is visible in the same plate but receives no Didian text. The PONTIF·CAPITO·CONCORDIA coin is a Fonteian interloper in the Didia plate; Orsini's coin 2 discussion concerns only the Villa Publica reverse.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; star behind; ROMA before
reverse: Victory in biga right; CN.DOM below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, curule aedile, citing Pliny on the venationes (beast hunts with lions and elephants) he staged. The man fighting a lion in the exergue directly references these spectacles, which Orsini connects to the family's later prominence through Suetonius's account of Nero's ancestry.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind
reverse: Victory (or Roma) driving a galloping biga; CN·DOMI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini presents this as a second specimen of the Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus battle-scene denarius, showing a horseman spearing a fallen warrior. He treats it as confirming the family's association with public spectacles (venationes), citing Suetonius on the legendary origin of the Ahenobarbus name.

moneyer: Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus / L. Licinius Crassus
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ear of corn behind; CN.CO behind
reverse: Warrior (Bituitus) in biga galloping right, hurling spear; L·LIC·CN·DOM below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes coin 3 to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus who was Censor with L. Licinius Crassus (anno DCLXI) and had been Consul with C. Cassius Longinus (anno DLVII), citing the consulship inscription from Interamna ('cuius Confulatus memoria extat Interamnae in uetere infcriptione'). He does not connect this coin to the foundation of Narbo Martius or to 118 BC; nor does he discuss a lion reverse for coin 3.

obverse: Laureate head right (Ahenobarbus); AHENOBAR behind
reverse: Trophy set on the prow/deck of a galley; CN.DOMITIVS IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the trophy on the reverse as commemorating military victories of Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus and notes his IMP title. He connects the laureate portrait to the imperatorial propaganda of the late Republican period, citing the family's association with Antony's faction.

obverse: Bare head right; ANT·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C around
reverse: Prow right, star above; AHENOBARB·IMP·CN above, DOMIT below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes coins 4 and 5 together to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, proavus of Nero (Suetonius, Nerone cap. III). He explicitly assigns the prow and trophy to coin 4 ('quia uero classi praefuit, nauis prora, & trophaeum in altera quarti denarii parte impressum est'). For coin 5 (quintus), Orsini says it was signed with Antony's effigy because its owner sided with Antony ('quintum denarium cum Antonii effigie signauit'), citing Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (lib. V).

obverse: Head of Hercules right; CN·DOMI text
reverse: Bow, club, and arrow; Q·CVRTI on right; M·SILI on left
orsini_comment: Orsini says coin 6 (sextus aereus nummus) possibly pertains to Cn. Domitius because M. Silanus and Q. Curtius, who were perhaps IIIviri with Domitius, are inscribed on it ('Ad eundem Cn. Domitium pertinere potest sextus aereus tabellaе nummus, in quo M. Silanvs, & Q. Cvrtivs, qui cum Domitio III uiri fortasse fuerunt monetae cudendae, notati sunt'). He does not claim to read CN.DOM on the obverse; the attribution is based on the Silanus/Curtius names as possible colleagues.

obverse: Bare head right bearded (Ahenobarbus); OSCA behind
reverse: Trophy flanked by weapons; anchor; dolphin; DOM.COS.ITER.IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini correctly reads OSCA as the mint name for Cn. Domitius Calvinus's Spanish issue and interprets cos. iter. imp. as indicating his second consulship and imperatorship, noting Calvinus held his second consulship in 40 BC and struck this denarius at Osca (modern Huesca) after his Spanish victories.

obverse: Bare male head right; III·VIR·HONORI / M·DVRMIVS around
reverse: Chariot/quadriga team right; CAESAR·AVGVSTVS above, S·C in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini defers all discussion of the HONORI legend (simulacrum Honoris) to the Lollius Palicanus entry ('De Honoris simulacro in Lollii Palicani denario dicetur'). He makes no interpretive statement about coin 1 specifically beyond noting that the reverse pertains to Augustus and perhaps to his ludi saeculares.

obverse: Head of Augustus bare right; CAESAR AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Boar standing right, pierced by spear; M·DVRMIVS IIIVIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini describes the animal imagery on the reverse as boar and stag ('apri & cerui fignis propter Dianam'), connected to Diana's ludi saeculares. He does not describe a lion-and-boar combat scene; the animals are boar and stag.

obverse: Bare head of Augustus right; CAESAR.AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Single lion crouching/running right; M·DVRMIVS above, III·VIR in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the stag to Diana and the ludi saeculares theme ('apri & cerui fignis propter Dianam'). He cites no Horace or Carmen Saeculare anywhere in his Durmia text.

obverse: Draped, diademed female bust right (Libertas/Venus type); MAXSVMVS legend
reverse: Two standing figures, architectural structure with columns between them; unclear figures in classical dress
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Egnatius Cn.f. Cn.n. Maxsumus from the full filiation on the coin. He interprets Roma seated on shields as an allusion to military victory, connecting it to the family's prominence in the Social War period.

obverse: Bust of Venus right, draped, wearing diadem, with Cupid on shoulder
reverse: Libertas in biga left, crowned by Victory; pileus behind; C·EGNATIVS text
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no statement about a legend variant reading 'EGNATMS' for coin 2. He groups the coins as belonging to C. Egnatius Maxsumus without discussing individual reverse descriptions or legend variants.

obverse: Bust of Libertas right, draped, wearing diadem
reverse: Roma and Venus standing, each holding staff; Roma holds spear, Venus holds sceptre
orsini_comment: Orsini makes no reference to Roma and Venus standing figures for coin 3. His text simply groups coins 1–3 under C. Egnatius Maxsumus citing Cicero, and does not describe the reverses individually.

obverse: Laureate head of Augustus right; lituus before
reverse: Wreath enclosing text in multiple lines: PAE S S C / M EGNATIVS Q OCTAVIVS IIVIR
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the fourth coin (aes) as M. Egnatius, possibly the son of L. Egnatius Rufus ('cuius fortasse filius fuit M. Egnatvs is, qui est in quarto aereo nummo notatus'), who conspired against Augustus, citing Suetonius (cap. XIX) and Velleius (lib. II) for the conspiracy. Orsini does not claim conflation, and mentions nothing about Venus imagery for this coin.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right
reverse: Victory standing left at a trophy, holding a wreath; carnyx at base; Q in field, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini calls this coin a Victoriatus ('Victoriatum nummum percuffit'), not a quinarius. The Q mark indicates Victoriatus denomination in Orsini's reading. He does not describe the reverse trophy or Gallic arms; his discussion is entirely devoted to the Ciceronian prosopography of L. Egnatuleius.

obverse: Draped head of Africa/Genius Terrae Africae right, wearing elephant-skin headdress, grain-ear behind; legend Q·METEL·SCIPIO IMP around
reverse: Hercules standing facing, nude, holding club and lion-skin; LEG·F·C and EPPIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Eppius as legate of Scipio in Africa from the coin inscription ('ut ex ipfa denarii infcriptione apparet'), citing Hirtius (lib. V de bello Africo). The Africa head on the obverse he grounds in comparison with the Scipio denarius ('qualem ab antiquis fictam fuisse fupra in Scipionis denario… demoftrauimus'). The Hercules reverse he connects to the Hercules cult worshipped in Africa, citing Herodotus (lib. II) — not military valor. The inscription he mentions is P.EPPIVS.P.F.FAB.RVFVS (tribe Fabia, cognomen Rufus), not 'Fabruvus.'

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; LABEO behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; Q.FABI below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects Q. Fabius Labeo to his praetorship ex Creta (anno DLXIII) and consulship (anno DLXX) and pontificate (anno DLXXIII), citing Cicero (lib. I off. & ad Q. fratrem) for his role as Senate-appointed arbitrator between Nolani and Neapolitani. The navis prora reverse is noted as indicating his naval command from Crete. Orsini does not cite Livy for Labeo.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind; ROMA before
reverse: Cornucopiae set over crossed thunderbolt, all within a laurel wreath; ROMA above, Q·MAX below
orsini_comment: Orsini states the attribution is uncertain ('diuinare non licet') and tentatively proposes Q. Fabius Maximus consul anno DCCCVIII with C. Trebonius, who died three months minus a day or two into his consulship (Caninius Rebilus suffected). Orsini does not cite Polybius or Livy for this coin, and does not discuss the Cunctator's strategy against Hannibal.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; N behind
reverse: Seated figure (Quirinus/Roma) holding spear; PICTOR left, QVIRIN / N·FABI right, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini makes the notable observation that the helmeted bust on this N. Fabius Pictor denarius may represent Quirinus rather than Roma, based on his reading of the legend PICTOR QVI RIN, suggesting a connection to the Quirinal hill or the god Quirinus. He draws on Cicero and Livy for the Pictor branch of the gens.

obverse: Veiled female bust right (Cybele?); EX.A.PV behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; B below; C.FABI.C.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coin 4 as C. Fabius C.f. Pictor, consul with Q. Ogulnius Gallus anno CCLXXXIIII, the first year the Roman people used silver coinage by senatorial decree. He interprets EX.A.P. as 'ex argento publico' ('ob quam rem in altera denarii parte inscriptionem adiectam esse opinor EX. A. P. hoc eft, ex argento publico'). He says nothing about Cybele or a veiled female head; the Cybele identification is not in Orsini.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; ROMA above; Q·M·C·F·L·R in exergue (three-moneyer joint issue)
orsini_comment: This is the joint three-moneyer denarius Q·M·C·F·L·R (Crawford 283/1): helmeted Roma / Victory in biga, ROMA. The three monetales are Q. Marcius, C. Fabius and L. Roscius, each named by initials; it cross-lists under Fabia for C·F = C. Fabius (and under Marcia for Q·M). The L·R abbreviation is itself ambiguous (L. Roscius / L. Rubrius). (Re-identified from the former 322/1a.)

moneyer: C. Annius T.f. T.n. / L. Fabius L.f. Hispaniensis
obverse: Draped female head (Anna Perenna) right; control-letter behind; legend C·ANNIVS·T·F·T·N·PRO·COS·EX·S·C around.
reverse: Quadriga (horses + chariot) right; L·FABI·HISP legend in exergue; border of dots. (Engraving shows chariot scene; CRRO type shows Q. Fabius Pictor seated — Orsini simplification.)
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coin 6 as L. Fabius Hispaniensis, a Sertorian ('Sertorianarum partium'), citing a Sallust fragment preserved in Servius (on Aeneid I) for L. Fabius Hispaniensis Senator, and noting that another coin is plainly inscribed 'L. FABI. L. F. HIS P. Q.' indicating he was a quaestor when he crossed to Sertorius in Hispania. Coin 6 is not attributed to the Labeo branch.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right
reverse: Ship prow right; M·FABRI/NI above; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini creates this entry explicitly noting the possibility that the gens name arises from a die-cutter's error ('nisi fit erratum ab eo, qui nummum aereum cufit'). He reads the full nomen as Fabrinius from the coin legend M·FABRI NI, and acknowledges he cannot find when M. Fabrinius lived or who he was. The possibility of a mint error is central to his brief discussion and is absent from the current comment.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind; ROMA before
reverse: Victory in quadriga right, holding reins and palm/wreath; M.FAN.C.F below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Fannius C.F. as the moneyer, connecting him to the praetor before whom Cicero defended Sex. Roscius parricidii reus anno DLXXIII, citing Cicero in Catone for the oratorical family context. The Cicero source for the family here is ep. XIII lib. XVI ad Att. (for C. Fannius as Tribunus Plebis) and Cicero in Catone (for the orators); not De Oratore or Brutus.

moneyer: M. Fannius / L. Critonius / M. Plaetorius
obverse: Draped bust right (Apollo per Orsini) (Ceres?); A.P.CL behind
reverse: Two seated figure (Pan per Orsini)s on bench (tribunal scene); BA above; M.FAN.L.CRI around
orsini_comment: Orsini says the second coin may also pertain to M. Fannius ('Ad eundem fortaffe fecundus quoque denarius fpectat'), who appears from the coin inscription to have been an Aedilis Plebis. He cites Dio for the institution of Aediles Cereales (Caesar V and Antony cos., anno DCCIX), with extended quotation from Dio in Greek and Latin. He does not describe the reverse figures as iudices, does not discuss a PAN/FAN abbreviation confusion, and does not mention Apollo as the obverse figure. The legend visible in the plate is M·FAN·L·CRT (Fannius and Critonius); Orsini does not name Plaetorius as a third moneyer for this coin.

obverse: Draped bust right (Libertas); MENSOR behind; control-mark and S·C before.
reverse: Warrior in biga right extending hand to a togate figure; L·FARSVLEI in exergue.
orsini_comment: Orsini states he could find no mention of L. Farsuleius Mensor in any ancient source: 'nullam in ueteribus nec scriptorum nec lapidum monumentis reperire mentionem potui.' He makes no iconographic comment on the obverse or reverse types.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; FLAMINI / CILO below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Flaminius Chilo (siue Cilo) as a IIIIvir (quattuorvir) auro, argento, aere feriundo under Caesar as Dictator. He notes both spellings appear on the coins. He cites Cicero (ad Att.) and Livy (li. XXI) for the family in general.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right (485/2 obverse; the SAM crop had mis-stitched a foreign imperial S·C obverse, now rebuilt)
reverse: Victory in chariot right; L.FLAMIN / CHILO below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that Chilo put the Venus head on the second coin's reverse because Venus was the divine ancestress of the Julian gens ('cum Veneris caput, a qua Iulia gens originem duxit, in altera secundi denarii parte signauit'). He does not call the office 'III VIR' — consistently 'IIII uir.'

obverse: Bare head right (Caesar?); curly hair
reverse: Standing togate figure holding spear; L.FLAMINVS / III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini's text on the third coin (lower-row portrait + standing figure) is not explicitly detailed beyond the general discussion of Chilo as IIIIvir and the Flamen Iulii. No separate coin-specific claim by Orsini is verifiable for coin 3 beyond the same attribution.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; [.]LAVI below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses only the reading of FLAVS as a cognomen FLAVVS, citing parallels in other families (Dionysius, Livy, Suetonius, inscriptions). He makes no iconographic statement about the coin's obverse or reverse type (no Diana, no biga, no Luna).

identification: Crawford 504/1 — C. Flavius Hemicillus (legatus pro praetore under Brutus), 43-42 BC
moneyer: C. Flavius Hemicillus (under authority of Brutus and Q. Caepio)
obverse: Bare head right; C.FLAV.HEMIS.LEG.PRO.PR around
reverse: Figures standing facing trophy or standard; Q.CAEP.BRVT.IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the person as C. FLAVIVS HEMIS (not 'Hemicillus'), Bruti Legatus Propraetore, citing Cornelius Nepos (Vita Attici), Appian (lib. V), and Plutarch (who calls him Praefectum Fabrûm Bruti). He defers the rest of the coin's iconography to the Iunia gens. He does not describe a trophy reverse.

obverse: Laureate double-faced head (Janus); star below
reverse: Galley right; C.FONT above; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns this denarius to C. FONTEIVS CAPITO, consul suffect from Kal. Jul. in year DCCXX, using the coin as his main evidence for the consulship. He cites Suetonius on the Tiberius adoption passage and Cicero (pro Domo sua, ad Att.) for the Fonteian family.

obverse: Laureate double-faced head (Janus); star above
reverse: Galley right; MN.FONTEI above
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns coins 2–3 to M'. FONTEIVS (son of the consul), the defendant in Cicero's Pro Fonteio. He notes the galley with Castor and Pollux, citing Horace (li. I, Carm.) for the Dioscuri as protectors of sailors.

obverse: Laureate head right; MN.FONTEIVS behind
reverse: Winged Cupid riding a goat right within a laurel wreath; two pilei (caps) above; thyrsus and filleted vase below.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this coin of M'. Fonteius has Cupid riding a goat ('Cupidinem hirco insidentem, quòd id animal maxime fit procliue ad libidinem'). He does NOT describe the imagery as Venus/Bacchic. The Veiouis simulacrum and Castors' caps on this coin he explicitly says he cannot explain ('mihi quidem obscurum est').

obverse: Helmeted bust of Mars right; P.FONTEIVS.P.F / CAPITO.III.VIR around
reverse: Horseman spearing fallen enemy; two combatants below
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns coins 4–5 to P. FONTEIVS P.F. CAPITO as triumuir, possibly the grandson of the consul and perhaps the same man who commanded Antony's fleet as propraetor (inferred from a damaged coin inscription). He cites Horace (li. I, Ser. Sat. V) for this Fonteius Capito. He does not describe the obverse as Mars.

obverse: Concordia head right; P·FONTEIVS·CAPITO·III·VIR·CONCORDIA around
reverse: Two-story Villa Publica building (colonnade above, arched columns below); T·DIDI left, VIL·PVB right, IMP in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns this coin also to P. FONTEIVS P.F. CAPITO and notes the Antonianae classi propraetorial command can be inferred from a damaged bronze coin's inscription. He does NOT mention T. Didius IMP; there is no T. Didius reference in Orsini's Fonteia text.

moneyer: M. Oppius Capito, propraetor and praefectus classis
obverse: Jugate heads right; ...EIVS·CAPITO·PRO·PR around
reverse: Galley (ship) under sail right, bird on prow; M·ANT·IMP·COS·DESIG·ITER·ET·TER·IIIVIR·R·P·C around
orsini_comment: Orsini placed under Fonteia reading CAPITO as Fonteius Capito. Actually M. Oppius Capito, Antony's fleet prefect. Mark Antony's fleet coinage, heavy series (RPC I 1465; alt. 1470 light series). Ref: RSN 1987, 104–5 D.

obverse: Helmeted head of Honos right; HO / VIR on sides; KALENI below
reverse: Two standing figures clasping hands, the left holding a cornucopia; IT / RO on sides; CORDI below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Fufius Kalenus as moneyer and tribune of the plebs in year DCXCI, later consul with P. Vatinius (DCCVI). He cites Dio (lib. XLII) for Calenus's Caesarian allegiance and Cicero's Philippica VIII for Cicero's attack on him. He makes no iconographic comment on the obverse heads or the reverse handshake scene.

obverse: Very lightly engraved head of Roma, right (generic type)
reverse: Very lightly engraved quadriga (generic type)
orsini_comment: Printing anomaly (the 'ghost coin'): a faint, generic Roma-head / quadriga composition on the Fufia cancel plate, too lightly and incompletely engraved to identify; Orsini's text treats only the Q. Fufius Calenus coin.

moneyer: Cn. Fulvius, M. Calidius, Q. Caecilius Metellus
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; star below chin
reverse: Victory in biga right holding wreath; CN·FOL·M·CAL·Q·MET text below; ROMA in field
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies CN. FVLVIVS as striking jointly with Q. Metellus and M. Calidius, and explicitly says he cannot determine who this Fulvius was ('nihil certi afferre possum'). He makes no mention of Livy XXV.17, the temple of Honos et Virtus at Clastidium, M. Fulvius Nobilior, or Hercules Musarum. Those references belong to the Fufia section.

obverse: Bearded male head right (Jupiter?)
reverse: Two standing figures (man and woman) clasping hands or performing ritual
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to C. Fundanius (= Varro's father-in-law), the Tribune of the Plebs named in the Farnese bronze tablet, stating 'ad eum autem referendos esse opinor.' He makes no statement about being unable to identify the moneyer.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Figure in chariot right; C.FVNDVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the coins on the plate to C. Fundanius, Varro's father-in-law (the Tribune who 'primus plebi scivit'), preferring this over the attribution to the consul of year DX. The claim that the attribution rests on a 'FVNDAN legend reading' is not stated by Orsini — he bases it on the chronological fit with the Farnese inscription.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: Goddess in biga right, holding reins; two galloping horses drawing chariot; PVR below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer as L. FVRIVS PVRPREONVM and notes he triumphed over the Gauls as PRAETOR (not consul) in years DLIIII and DLVII. He makes no iconographic statement about a Diana biga with two stags.

obverse: Turreted female head right (Cybele); AED.CVR around
reverse: Curule chair; P.FOVRIVS / CRASSIPES below
orsini_comment: Orsini says the coin's foot image indicates the cognomen's origin from the GREEK name Oedipus ('ἀπὸ τοῦ οἰδήματος τῶν ποδῶν' = from the swelling of the feet), NOT from Latin 'crassus pes.' The curule chair indicates the curule aedileship. He notes Livy names M. Furius Crassipes as triumvir coloniae deducendae and Praetor, and perhaps the coin was struck by Cicero's son-in-law.

obverse: Laureate double-faced head (Janus); I above; M.F behind
reverse: Roma standing right crowning a trophy; ROMA in right field; PHLI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini states this coin was struck by M. IVRIVS L.F. PHILO 'in memoriam sine dubio eius triumphi, quem egit P. Furius Philus anno DXXX. de Galleis Liguribus.' He identifies M. Furius as probably the son of L. Furius Philus the Praetor (anno DLXXXII, citing Livy lib. XLII). He does not describe a Janus head or military trophies on this coin.

obverse: Female head right (Ceres per Orsini); III / VIR around; BROCCHI below; corn-ear behind
reverse: Curule chair flanked by fasces; L.FVRI / CN.F above
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies CN. FVRIVS BROCCHVS (praenomen Cn., not L.) as curule aedile, inferred from the curule chair and Ceres image on the coin. He does not provide an etymology of 'brocchi' as protruding teeth. He cites only Valerius Maximus (li. VI, cap. I) and Cicero (pro Q. Ligario; in Verrem lib. III for Anneius Brocchus).

obverse: S C in centre; C·GALLIVS·C·F·LVPERCVS·IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F around
reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak-wreath (no portrait)
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to C. Gallius, who struck it as triumvir under Augustus; suggests C. Gallius the Senatorial eques (mentioned in Cicero, in Verrem lib. V) was perhaps his father. Q. Gallius is a separate person — the Praetor accused of ambitus. Orsini does not identify C. Gallius himself as Praetor.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
reverse: Mars (or warrior deity) in quadriga right, hurling spear; CN·GEL below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius 'fortasse' (perhaps) to a legate of Cn. Pompeius in the maritime war against the pirates, citing Florus lib. III. The 'perhaps' must be retained.

obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around border
reverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin with certainty ('sine dubio') as belonging to L. GELLIVS POPLICOLA, Antony's Quaestor Propraetore, later consul with M. Cocceius Nerva in year DCCXVII. He cites Dio (lib. XLVII) at length. He expresses no difficulty in the attribution.

obverse: Diademed head of Pietas right; PIETAS behind
reverse: Running figure (Amphinomus or Anapias) carrying parent on shoulders; M.HERENNI below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the denarius to M. Herennius, consul in year DCCXX (possibly the son of the consul with C. Valerius Flaccus in DCLX). He notes the coin bears a signum Pietatis and compares the reverse to the Aeneas/Anchises motif as a traditional symbol of pietas on ancient monuments. He does NOT name the Catanaean brothers. The consul with C. Valerius Flaccus is the FATHER (anno DCLX), not the moneyer himself.

obverse: Veiled head right (Caesar as Pontifex Maximus); CAESAR COS.TER around
reverse: Sacrificial implements: lituus and capis (jug); A.HIRTIVS.PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini infers from this aureus that A. Hirtius was Praetor in year DCCVII (not DCCVI) when Caesar held his third consulship. Hirtius later died fighting M. Antonius at Mutina alongside C. Vibius Pansa. Orsini cites Livy (epitoma lib. CXIX) for this. He makes no iconographic comment on the reverse implements.

moneyer: Trajan restitution (restoration of archaic Horatia type)
obverse: Head of Roma right with winged helmet; X (value mark) behind; COCLES before
reverse: Castor and Pollux (Dioscuri) riding right; IMP·CAES·TRAIAN·AVG·GER·DAC·P·P·REST·ROMA around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is a Trajanic restitution coin recalling Horatius Cocles's defense of the Pons Sublicius, citing Livy (lib. II) at length and also Dionysius (lib. IV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. I), and Plutarch (in Poplicola) for the bronze statue decreed in the Forum. He makes no mention of the Horatii and Curiatii, nor of M. Horatius Pulvillus or the Capitoline temple.

obverse: III·VIR GETA: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder.
reverse: C·HOSIDI·C·F: the Calydonian boar right, wounded by a spear and attacked by a hound.
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer as the son of Hosidius Geta the proscript (saved by his son), citing Appian and Dio (lib. XLVII). Notes the marble inscription C. HOSIDIVS MARCIANVS CVM SVIS PANTHEO SACRVM. He does NOT call the moneyer 'IIIvir monetalis' — that office is the AI's interpolation; Orsini simply says he struck the silver denarii ('qui argenteos denarios cusit'). Orsini makes no comment on the Diana/boar type.

obverse: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
reverse: Wild boar (the Calydonian boar) attacked, walking/charging right; C.HOSIDI.C.F in exergue
