orsini_comment: Orsini includes this die variant as one of the two denarii he has seen ('duos tantum denarios... nobis uidere licuit'). He makes no separate iconographic comment on this coin beyond attributing it to the same moneyer, and does NOT discuss Diana devotion or a Calydonian boar myth. C. Hosidius Geta (Dio lib. LX) is the Claudian general who received triumphal honours — he is the moneyer's probable brother or cousin, not the moneyer himself described as 'tresvir monetalis.'

obverse: Head of bearded male right, hair flowing
reverse: Naked warrior in fast biga (chariot) galloping right, holding spear and shield, driven by a charioteer; SASERN below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to the Sasernae (father and son) who wrote on agriculture. The obverse shows images of the gods that the Sasernae wished to illustrate on their denarii, relating to Gallic monuments.

obverse: Draped female head, unhelmeted
reverse: Diana standing facing/front, holding a stag by the antlers in one hand and a spear in the other; SASERNA at left, L.HOSTILIVS at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Diana of Ephesus on the reverse may reference Saserna's praetorship in the province of Asia. The obverse female head relates to Gallia or Victory.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted with plume
reverse: Victory advancing, holding a caduceus and a trophy over the shoulder; SASERNA at left, L.HOSTILIVS at right
orsini_comment: Orsini suggests the Victory on the reverse may refer to King Tullus Hostilius's triumphs over the Albans, from whom the Hostilii traced their descent.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this single coin to L. Iccium (the coin reads L.ITIO, but Orsini argues 'ut opinor' that ITIUM is an error for ICCIUM in the manuscripts of Hirtius — 'sic enim in uetuftiffimis codicibus pro ICCIUM, scriptum reperiri'). He identifies this L. Iccium as the addressee of Horace, Odes 1.29, and notes that Cicero in Philippics 3 also mentions a M. Iccium. Orsini says nothing about a turreted head, Cybele, or poor condition of the coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right, wearing winged helmet; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Two horsemen (Dioscuri) galloping right, each holding spear; L.IVLI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this first denarius to L. Iulius Caesar, consul with P. Rutilius Lupus. Notes the XVI numeral refers to the value (denarius = 16 asses after the reduction).

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right, wearing winged helmet; corn-ear (spica) behind
reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins; L·IVLI below
orsini_comment: Orsini presents this as the second denarius, attributable to a son of the L. Iulius of coin 1, who was Consul with L. Marcius Figulus ('Secundus denarius ad L.IVLIVM huius filium potest pertinere, qui Consul fuit cum L. Marcio Figulo anno DCLXXXIX'). He infers this moneyer was an Aedile from the spica (grain ear) symbol ('ex symbolo spicae, quo Aediles utebantur, intelligere possumus'). The reverse bears a Cupid chariot ('Cupidinis currus'), used to indicate the Iulian family's origin from Iulus, son of Aeneas, who was born of Venus ('ad indicandam Iuliae gentis originem, quae a Iulo Aeneae, qui Venere genitus est, filio principium habuisse dicitur').

obverse: Helmeted head of Mars left (Mars or Roma); D to left and right of head; CAESAR behind
reverse: Venus in biga of Cupids left, holding sceptre and reins; L·IVLI·L·F below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to L. Iulius, son of the preceding, who served in Africa under Cato as Pro Quaestor during the civil war. The Venus with Cupid references the Iulian family's divine descent.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right, wearing winged helmet; mark behind
reverse: Cupid driving biga right; SEX.IVLI / CAESAR in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 113-114) identifies the fourth coin as Sex. Iulius Caesar, noting many of the Caesarum family used this praenomen ('difficile est, quis fuerit affirmare'), and suggests he may be the consul with L. Marcius Philippus anno DCXLII. Orsini makes no specific statement about the reverse type of this coin (the plate shows ROMA/biga). The Venus/Cupid framing belongs to coins 2-3 in the same table; it is not applied by Orsini to coin 4.

obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right, wreathed; CAESAR.DICT behind, PERPETVO before
reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and sceptre; L.BVCA in field
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius was struck by L. Aemilius Buca as IIIIvir monetalis, with Caesar as Dictator in perpetuum. The Venus Genetrix or Victrix on the reverse is described by Orsini as **standing** ('Veneris Genetricis siue Victricis simulacrum **stans**'), not seated. The standing Venus Genetrix relates to Caesar's claim of divine Iulian ancestry from Venus through Aeneas.

obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.DICT.PERPETVO around
reverse: Globe, crossed fasces and caduceus, axe, and clasped hands; L.BVCA.L below
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the reverse symbols: the globe represents Caesar's world dominion; fasces signify justice; the caduceus peace; clasped hands concordia; and the securis religion. These were virtues Caesar promised the Roman people.

obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.IM around
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Venus Genetrix) holding sceptre; BVCA / COSSERTIVS (or CREMITIVS) around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Venus Genetrix on the reverse, standing with trophy, references the Iulian family's divine origin from Venus through Aeneas.

obverse: Wreathed head right; CAESAR·IMP text on left side
reverse: Text arrangement: L·AEMI at top right, then LI·VS below, then BVCA at bottom; small objects visible between text (clasped hands, fasces)
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the clasped hands as symbolizing concordia. Notes the Augural lituus is added to indicate Caesar's sacerdotal office.

obverse: Laureate and veiled head of Julius Caesar right; DICT.PERPETVO.CAESAR around
reverse: Standing female figure (Venus) holding sceptre and Victory on globe; L.BVCA at right
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Caesar's golden laurel wreath decreed by the Senate on this L. Aemilius Buca issue showing Caesar as DICT PERPETVO, and notes the golden chair (sella aurea) placed in the theatre as another of Caesar's unprecedented honors. He cites Suetonius and Dio Cassius on these extraordinary distinctions.

obverse: Bare head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.III.VIR.R.P.C around
reverse: Inscribed tablet/plaque reading CAES.DIC.PER, surmounted by a small wreath, resting on supports above two crossed cornucopiae
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the two Cossutius Maridianus coins together: one bears CAESAR PARENS PATRIAE and the other CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO ('in eorum altero CAESAR PARENS PATRIAE, in altero CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO inscriptum est'). The PARENS PATRIAE coin prompts his extended discussion citing Cicero, Suetonius, and Livy on when this honor was conferred. He does not mention a curule chair for these coins, and does not connect them to Octavian as IIIvir.

obverse: Diademed bust of Venus right; C·CAESAR IMP COS ITER
reverse: Trinacrus standing facing, holding triskeles, right foot on prow; A·ALLIENVS PRO COS
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Allienus, Praetor governing Sicily with proconsular authority, struck in Caesar's second consulship with P. Servilius Isauricus, year 705 AUC ('Quintus denarius ab ALLIENO Praetore, qui Siciliam proconsu lari potestate obtinebat, signatus est Caesare II Consule cum P. Seruilio Isaurico anno DCCV'). On the reverse, Orsini sees Minerva's image ('Simulacrum Mineruae in altera nummi parte'), holding Victory alongside a snake, which he connects to the tradition that Minerva was called παρεδρον of Victory, citing Phurnutus. He notes the coin was struck the same year Caesar went to Africa.

obverse: Bust of Victory right, draped; CAESAR·DIC·TER legend; border of dots.
reverse: Minerva standing left, holding trophy over shoulder, spear and shield with gorgoneion, snake before; C·CLOVI PRAEF legend; border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Victory image and African trophy reference Caesar's victory over Juba in Africa. The bronze likely a colonial or praefectural issue.

obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; COS.TERT / DICT.ITER around
reverse: Augural implements: lituus, capis (jug), and axe; AVGVR / PONT.MAX around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Caesar's Pontificatus Maximus and augural implements. Notes the lituus and capis indicate Caesar's priestly offices as both Pontifex Maximus and Augur.

obverse: Elephant walking right, trampling serpent or dragon; CAESAR below
reverse: Priestly implements: simpulum, aspergillum, axe (securis), and apex (priest's cap)
orsini_comment: Orsini says the elephant in this coin's reverse may relate to a beast-hunt spectacle Caesar put on in the arena ('licet ad elephantum quoque spectaculum in harena a Caesare editum referri possit; de quo meminit Plinius lib.viii.cap.vii'). The priestly implements (Augurat and Pontificat insignia) are discussed separately in connection with the adjacent coin (coin 13), not this one: 'De Caesaris Auguratu & Pontificatu Maximo, quorum insignia in primo denario notata sunt.' Orsini does not describe the elephant as symbolizing 'triumph over evil or the barbarian world,' nor does he connect this type to the outbreak of the civil war.

obverse: Female head right (Venus), with hair tied back
reverse: Aeneas walking left, carrying Anchises on shoulder and holding palladium; CAESAR at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Venus head indicates the Iulian family's origin, and Aeneas carrying Anchises with the palladium is the central symbol of Iulian pietas and Trojan descent.

obverse: Female head right (Venus), wearing diadem, hair in knot at back
reverse: Trophy of Gallic arms with oval shield and carnyx; two seated captives at base; CAESAR below
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the trophy with captives as referencing Caesar's victories over the Gauls and Germans. The trophies and bound captives symbolize his military triumphs.

obverse: Female head left (Venus or Pietas), hair in bun
reverse: Trophy of arms with shields; seated captive at base; CAESAR at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Gallic trophy type and connects the trophies erected by Caesar after defeating Pharnaces, citing Dio. He treats the female head on the obverse as Venus or Pietas and discusses the seated captive at the base of the trophy as a representation of Caesar's eastern victories.

obverse: Female head right wearing oak-wreath and diadem
reverse: Gallic trophy: standing armored figure with horned helmet, oval shield (with trident device), and axe; CAESAR text below
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 117) identifies coins 4-6 of this table (coins 16-18 in the concordance) as referencing Caesar's victories and trophies over the Gauls, Germans, and other peoples: 'Quartus, quintus, & sextus huius tabellae denarii referunt, ut opinor, victorias ac trophaea de Galleis, & Germaneis, aliisque gentibus à Caesare deuictis.' No carnyx or specific Gallic shields are mentioned by Orsini. The Venus image in these coins references the Iulian family's divine origin.

obverse: Bare head of Julius Caesar right
reverse: Cult/sacrificial implements (cornucopia, caduceus, apex, rudder) above a globe; L·MVSSIDIVS·LONGVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Mussidius Longus as IIIIvir monetae cudendae. On the reverse, he says, are the symbols of goddesses ('Dearum symbola') in whose honor the Senate had dedicated temples to Caesar: CLEMENTIA, AEQVITAS, LIBERTAS PVBLICA, CONCORDIA NOVA, and FELICITAS ('eae uero sunt: CLEMENTIA, AEQVITAS, LIBERTAS PVBLICA, CONCORDIA NOVA; & FELICITAS'). Concordia and Felicitas are symbolized by cornucopia and caduceus; a ship's rudder and globe refer to imperial rule; an apex (priest's cap) is added for Caesar's priestly office ('ad indicandum Caesaris sacerdotium... Flamen Dialis'). Orsini cites Plutarch (in Caesare) and Dio lib.xliii.

obverse: Bust of Victory, right, draped. C.CAES / DIC.TER around
reverse: Praefericulum (sacrificial jug) with handle; L.PLANC / PRAEF.VR around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to L. Munatius Plancus as Praefectus Urbi under Caesar. Notes the Maximi Pontificatus insignia and Victory image on the reverse.

obverse: Veiled head right; C·CAESAR COS·TER around
reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus (augural staff); A·HIRTIVS·PR around
orsini_comment: Orsini does not describe a coin struck by A. Hirtius as moneyer in his Iulia section. Hirtius appears in Orsini only as a cited author (Hirtius lib.v de bello Africo, Hirtius lib.v de bello Gallico). No coin of A. Hirtius as moneyer is discussed in any of Orsini's Iulia tables (pp. 113–124).

obverse: Laureate head right, no visible legend
reverse: Legionary eagle (aquila) between two military standards; legend Q DESIG around, TI SEMPRONIVS above / GRACCVS in exergue, S C in field
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to Ti. Sempronius Graccus as Quaestor designatus. The denarius pertains to the colony of Cassilinum, deduced anno DCXCIII by Caesar and Bibulus. The reverse shows the four colonial deduction symbols Orsini explicitly names: **signum cohortis** (cohort standard), **aquila Legionis** (legionary eagle), **aratrum** (plow), and **sceptrum** (sceptre). The aratrum is a key colonial deduction symbol; its omission from the previous comment was an error.

obverse: Laureate head right; legend CAESAR IMP around
reverse: Venus (Venus Victrix) standing holding Victory and sceptre; legend MACER and P SEPVLLIVS around, K in field
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 118) discusses the fifth and sixth coins of this table as both struck by P. Sepullius Macer: the fifth (quintus) with a comet added = struck after Caesar's death ('mortuo iam Caesare'); the sixth (sextum), in which Caesar's image appears in Pontifical dress = struck while Caesar was still alive ('uiuente adhuc Caesare'). Of the two Sepullius coins: one has Venus Genetrix **standing** ('stans'), the other has Venus **seated** ('sedens'). Orsini's coin 23 (sixth of the table) = ante mortem, Venus sedens with standard inscriptions.

obverse: Wreathed head of Caesar right; CAESAR·DICT·PERPETVO text
reverse: Venus seated right holding Victory in right hand and sceptre in left; L·BVCA text
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the title PARENS PATRIAE granted to Caesar. Cites Cicero and Suetonius on Caesar being called Father of the Country, and the statue placed in the Forum with the inscription PARENTI OPTIME MERITO.

obverse: Veiled and wreathed head right; legend PARENTIS PATRIAE CAESAR around
reverse: Legend in field: C COSSVTIVS / MARIDIANVS / A A A F F arranged in lines
orsini_comment: This coin is part of Orsini's extended discussion of the PARENS PATRIAE title (same as coin 24), drawing on Cicero, Suetonius, and Livy. Orsini does not discuss the A·A·A·F·F abbreviation or any moneyer's authority to strike gold, silver, and bronze in this context.

obverse: Wreathed head right; legend DICT PERPETVO CAESAR around
reverse: Standing female figure (Venus Genetrix) holding Victory and sceptre, shield at feet; C MARIDIANVS in field
orsini_comment: This is the second Cossutius Maridianus coin. Orsini says it bears CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO as inscription ('in altero CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO inscriptum est'), while coin 25 bears CAESAR PARENS PATRIAE. Orsini does not describe a Venus Genetrix reverse for the Cossutius coins.

obverse: Single laureate head; legend around
reverse: Single standing figure holding a small object and a long scepter; IIII·VIR and L·FLAMINIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini says the L. Flaminius Quartumuiro coin has nothing particularly noteworthy except the Pacis signum on the reverse ('nihil est magnopere notandum, nisi quod in altera eius parte Pacis signum expressum est'). He does not describe the standing figure or any other iconographic detail.

obverse: Head right with diadem, lituus behind
reverse: Bull charging right; legend L LIVINIVS above, REGVLVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini argues this coin was struck after Caesar's death for two reasons: first, a laurel branch is added behind the head ('quia lauri ramus imaginis occipitio adiectus est'), which Pliny (lib.xv, cap.ultimo) records was sent to Augustus from heaven (though Dio attributes it to Livia); second, because L. Livineius also served as head of the mint under Caesar as Triumvir R.P.C. ('hic idem Liuineius sub C.Caesare Triumuiro R.P.C. cudendae monetae praefuit'). For the bull on the reverse, Orsini interprets it as referring to a bull-hunt spectacle given by Caesar as Dictator in year 708 AUC, citing Pliny lib.viii.cap.xlv on the Thessalian practice of killing bulls on horseback.

obverse: Laureate head right; CAESAR·IMP around
reverse: Standing figure (Venus) holding Victory and long scepter; M·METIVS to right, A in field
orsini_comment: Orsini mentions M. Mettius as one of the IIIIviri monetales who struck coins for Caesar, but does not provide specific commentary on the reverse type of this coin in the surviving text of his Iulia section. The prior comment contained a self-contradictory description (attributing a 'Gallic trophy with captive' then correcting it to 'Venus Victrix'). Orsini's general statement for this group of Buca-table coins is that Venus Genetrix or Victrix 'stans' (standing) appears on some reverses ('Veneris Genetricis siue Victricis simulacrum stans').

obverse: Laureate head right; legend CAESAR DICT QVART around
reverse: Figure driving biga right; M METTIVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the coin inscribed DICT QVART as an aureus ('Tertius huius tabellae aureus nummus'), attributing to it the Senate's grant to Caesar, when he was Dictator for the fourth time, of the right to wear the laurel wreath in perpetuity. He cites Appianus lib.ii, Dio lib.xliii, and Suetonius cap.xlv: 'Ex omnibus decretis sibi a Senatu, populoq. honoribus, non aliud aut recepit, aut usurpauit libentius, quam ius laureae coronae perpetuo gestandae.' Orsini does not describe a Victory in biga for the reverse of this coin.

obverse: Head right within wreath; legend DIVI IVLI around
reverse: Bull (calf) standing left; legend Q VOCONIVS above, VITVLVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this Q. Voconius Vitulus coin as a characteristic Roman practice of expressing the family name through imagery, with the vitulus (calf) on the reverse as a direct visual pun on the moneyer's cognomen Vitulus. He places it in the Iulia section because of the DIVI IVLI portrait on the obverse.

obverse: Bearded head right with wild flowing hair
reverse: Bull or calf standing right; legend Q VOCON above, VITVLVS DESIG in exergue, S in field
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the comet (stella crinita) that appeared after Caesar's death, which Suetonius says shone for seven continuous days. The calf is a punning type on the cognomen Vitulus.

obverse: Bare head right; legend CAESAR IMP around
reverse: Bare head right (M. Antonius); legend M ANTONIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini does not describe a confronted Octavian/Mark Antony type under the Iulia gens in the plates examined (pp. 113–124). No coin showing both Octavian and Antony is discussed in this section.

obverse: Laureate head right; DIVOS IVLIVS text around
reverse: Laureate head right; DIVI·F text around
orsini_comment: Orsini does not discuss a colonial AE issue with DIVOS IVLIVS legend in the Iulia plates (pp. 113–124), nor does he argue that Octavian used DIVI F status as a basis for succession in this section. The 'western provinces' framing does not appear.

obverse: Head of Venus right (mirrored), diademed
reverse: Cornucopia; S·C to left, EX to right
orsini_comment: Orsini does not discuss a coin of Crawford 376/1 type (cornucopia in laurel wreath) in his Iulia section, nor does he make any attribution based on EX S C for a coin of this type. No such entry appears in pp. 113–124.

obverse: Draped winged bust, a trident behind the shoulder
reverse: Victory in a biga at speed; legend L·IVLI·BVRSIO below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not discuss a Jupiter quadriga type (Crawford 352/1) or an IVLI legend coin in his Iulia section. No such early Republican type is attributed to the Iulia gens in pp. 113–124.

obverse: Bare head right; legend CAESAR AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Eight-pointed star (comet); legend DIVVS IVLIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the sidus Iulium (Julian star/comet) that appeared after Caesar's assassination on this Augustus/Divus Iulius type, treating it as evidence of Caesar's apotheosis. He cites Suetonius and Pliny for the comet's appearance and its interpretation as a divine sign marking Caesar's elevation to godhood.

obverse: Bare head of Octavian right; legend IMP·CAESAR·DIVI·F·III·VIR·ITER·R·P·C around
reverse: Distyle temple/shrine enclosing a figure, DIVO IVL within; legend COS ITER ET TER DESIG around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the second coin of the last Iulia table as showing the Temple of Venus ('Veneris templum'), with Caesar's statue in augural dress and the inscription DIVO IVL, and an altar at which the Roman people swore oaths by Caesar, citing Suetonius ('plebs Romana, ut Suetonius inquit, sacrificare, uota suscipere & controuersias quasdam interposito per Caesarem iureiurando distrahare, longo tempore consueuit'). He also cites Pliny lib.ii.cap.xxv on the star in the temple's pediment.

obverse: Laureate head right; CAES·DIC·Q·VAR text around
reverse: Wreath encircling empty field (no text inside)
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this as an aureus ('Tertius huius tabellae aureus nummus'), connected to the Senate's grant of the perpetual laurel wreath to Caesar when Dictator for the fourth time. He cites Appianus lib.ii, Dio lib.xliii, and Suetonius cap.xlv on this honor ('ius laureae perpetuo gestandae concessum fuisse'), quoting Suetonius directly.

obverse: Bearded male head right (Brutus ancestor); BRVTVS behind
reverse: Bearded male head right (Ahala); AHALA behind
orsini_comment: Orsini notes L. Brutus and C. Servilius Ahala were both tyrannicides: Brutus expelled the kings, Ahala killed Sp. Maelius. M. Brutus struck this denarius to advertise his descent from both lines of liberators.

obverse: Female head right (Libertas) with diadem; LIBERTAS behind
reverse: Four standing figures (the consul Brutus walking between lictors); BRVTVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the consul L. Brutus with lictors as the first consul of the Republic; for this coin he cites Virgil (Aen. VI): 'Consulis imperium hic primus saeuasq. secures / Accipiet &c.' Suetonius ('Subscripsere, inquit, quidam L. Bruti statuae, utinam uiueres') is cited in connection with M. Brutus's coin 1 context (statue inscriptions), not for coin 2 (lictors). The consular fasces and secures are discussed via the Virgil citation only for this coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; M·IVNI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to M. Iunius Silanus, Augustus's colleague in the consulship ('qui Augusti collega in nono Consulatu fuit anno DCCXXVIII'). He says nothing about the coin type (no mention of Roma head or Dioscuri).

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; C·IVNI·C·F below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to C. Iunius C.F. Silanus ('C.IVNIVM C. F. SILANVM'), Consul with C. Furnius in year DCCXXXVI. He places this coin in the Silani branch, not the Bruti branch.

obverse: Bearded male head right (laureate); long flowing hair
reverse: Victory in biga right; D.SILANVS.L below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to D. Iunius Silanus L.f. and notes the Silani branch's connection to the Manlii Torquati through adoption, citing ancient sanctimony of the Torquatae virgines.

obverse: Female head right (Salus); SALVS behind
reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins and whip; D.SILANVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini states the Salus image in the sixth coin pertains to C. Iunium Bubulcum Brutum, who vowed a temple to Salus as Consul, contracted it out as Censor, and dedicated it as Dictator, citing Livy lib. IX and X.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; control letter A behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; XIII (control numeral) above; D·SILANVS·L·F below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the first two denarii of D. Silanus as belonging to the same moneyer; the third denarius may belong to his brother M. Silanus L.f.

identification: Crawford 337/5 — D. Junius Silanus L.f., AE as, c. 91 BC
obverse: Head of Janus left and right, laureate
reverse: Prow of galley right; D·SILANVS above
orsini_comment: Orsini states that M. Silanus appears on a bronze (aes) coin that belongs to the Domitia gens plate, not the Iunia plate: 'In nummo etiam aereo Cn. Domitii, M. hic SILANVS notatus est in ea tabella, in qua gentis Domitiae denarii incisi sunt.' He does not discuss this bronze further under Iunia.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, holding sceptre and hurling thunderbolt; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the fourth coin of the second Iunia plate to M. Brutus, Caesar's assassin ('Quartus denarius pertinet ad M.BRVTVM Caesaris interfectorem, qui fuit filius M. Bruti eius, qui (ut scribit Plutarchus) Mutinae a Pompeio Magno occisus est'). There is no mention of Q. Curtius or any colleague moneyer.

moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus / L. Plaetorius Cestianus
obverse: Head right, laureate; legend around border
reverse: Cap (pileus) between two daggers; EID·MR below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the pileus (cap of liberty) and the two daggers as the most explicit numismatic commemoration of the tyrannicide on the Ides of March 44 BC. For the EID MAR coin specifically, he cites Suetonius ('Suetonius & alii'), Cicero (Philippics lib. II: 'Caesare statim interfecto cruentum altè extollens M. Brutus pugionem'), and Appianus (lib. II: 'pileum aliis hastae fixum ferebat symbolum libertatis'). Plutarch is cited later (p. 128) for Brutus's Imperator title on related coins, not specifically for the EID MAR daggers.

moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus / L. Plaetorius Cestianus
obverse: Veiled female head right (Libertas); LEIBERTAT[IS] around
reverse: Lituus (augural staff) on left and capis (jug) on right; BRVT·IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini states the fifth and sixth coins of the second Iunia plate were struck by L. Plaetorius with the BRVT.IMP inscription, and infers Brutus held some sacerdotal office (Pontifex or XVvir sacris faciundis), supported by Plutarch's mention of the Imperator title in the Brutus. He says nothing about LEIBERTAS legends, a veiled Libertas obverse, a lituus, or a capis on the reverse.

moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus / L. Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
obverse: Jug (capis) and lituus (augural staff); LENTVLVS / SPINT below
reverse: Sacrificial implements: axe (securis), simpulum/sprinkler, jug; BRVT.IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini infers from the sacerdotal implements on these coins (huius & sequentis tabellae denariis ad rem sacram faciendam instrumenta impressa sunt) that Brutus himself held a priestly office — Pontifex or XVvir sacris faciundis. He does not mention Lentulus Spinther in this context; Lentulus Spinther appears as a separate coin type on the same plate.

obverse: Bearded male head right (portrait); CASCA / LONGVS around
reverse: Victory standing right, holding wreath; BRVTVS / IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to Brutus's military mint, noting C. Cassius Longus and M. Servilius Casca were among the conspirators. The Victory with wreath celebrates Brutus's initial military successes.

obverse: Female head right (bust of Artemis/Diana); LEG. / COSTA around
reverse: Standing male figure (trophy/warrior) with military standards; IMP / BRVTVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 128) attributes this coin to Pedanius Costa as Brutus's legate. He notes it 'nihil habet aliud notatu dignum, praeter eandem de subactis Bessis, Imperatoris appellatione' — nothing beyond the Imperator title and the conquest of the Bessii. No trophy is mentioned by Orsini for this coin.

obverse: Draped female bust right (Libertas); LIBERTAS around
reverse: Lyre flanked by a branch/plectrum (not enclosed in a wreath); Q·CAEPIO·BRVTVS·PRO·COS around
orsini_comment: Orsini uses the third denarius of the third Iunia plate to demonstrate the adoption formula by which M. Brutus was called Q. CAEPIONEM BRVTVM, citing Cicero (Philippics lib. X), Plutarch (in Catone Vticense), and Dio (lib. XLVI and XLVII). The discussion of the Ludi Apollinares, lyre, and laurel branch belongs to a different coin (the laurus/cithara reverse, discussed separately at pp. 129–130) and does not belong to this adoption-formula coin.

identification: Crawford 504/1 — M. Iunius Brutus with C. Flavius Hemicillus, 43-42 BC
moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus (imperator) with C. Flavius Hemicillus (legatus pro praetore)
obverse: Head right; C.FLAV.HEMIS LEG.PRO.PR around
reverse: Two standing figures: a military/togate figure on left crowned by Victory (winged) on right; IMP and Q·CAE / BRVT legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this coin (Victory on ship's prow) 'nihil habet aliud, quod ad Brutum pertineat, praeter IMP. inscriptionem'; the Victory on a ship's prow can relate to Brutus because of the fleet he assembled and with which he controlled the Mediterranean. He does not say Cassius appears as joint imperator on this coin.

moneyer: M. Iunius Brutus / L. Plaetorius Cestianus
obverse: Veiled female bust right; legend around including PRO
reverse: Sacrificial implements: tripod, axe, patera; Q.CAEPIO.BRVTVS.PRO.COS around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the sacrificial instruments on the reverse indicate Brutus's role as Pontifex and sacerdotal authority. Struck by L. Plaetorius Cestianus.

moneyer: L. Sestius (pro quaestor) and Q. Caepio Brutus (pro cos.)
obverse: Priestly implements: axe (securis), simpulum (jug), knife (secespita); BRVTVS·PRO·COS and Q·CAEPIO text
reverse: Tripod on three legs; L·SESTI text below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes L. Sestius as ProQuaestor under Brutus and says that details about him will be given under the Seftia gens ('De L. autem SESTIO item ProQuaestore, dicetur in Seftia'). He cites Cicero Philippics lib. II on the Quaestors and legates appointed to Brutus and Cassius. Orsini does not specify Macedonia as the location for this coin.

obverse: Bearded male portrait head right; POSTVMVS / COS around
reverse: Wreath enclosing legend; ALBINVS / BRVT.F inside wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 131) states that D. Iunius Brutus was adopted by 'A. POSTVMIO BRVTII F.' (A. Postumius, son of Brutus) and thereby called ALPINVS ('ALPINVS dictus est'). The adopter is Postumius son of Brutus, not 'A. Postumius Albinus.' The adopted cognomen is ALPINVS (not Albinus). Orsini cites Plutarchus (in Caesare) for D. Brutus Albinus's character and closeness to Caesar.

obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right (crested helmet)
reverse: Sacrificial implements: capis (jug) above, crossed securis (axe), knife and aspergillum (sprinkler) below; ALBINVS and BRVTI around
orsini_comment: Orsini cites Plutarch (Caesar) describing D. Brutus Albinus as one who kept a gladiatorial troop ('gladiatorum manu, quos ad exhibendos Romanis ludos alebat, munitum') and whom Caesar trusted. He says nothing about Gallic shields or carnyces on this coin.

obverse: Female head right (Pietas); PIETAS behind
reverse: Two joined hands holding caduceus; ALBINVS.BRV.T.F below
orsini_comment: Orsini says the caduceus and joined hands (manus iunctae) are the symbol of Concordia ('Concordiae symbolum') and were placed on the second and third coins of this group to indicate the conspiracy among Caesar's assassins. He says nothing about a 'Pietas head' on the obverse.

moneyer: D. Iunius Brutus Albinus / C. Vibius Pansa
obverse: Head of Pan right with goat horns; C.PANSA behind
reverse: Two clasped right hands holding a winged caduceus; ALBINVS·BRVTI·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini mentions C. Vibius Pansa only in the context of his consulship year ('Brutus & C. Cassius Praetores erant, D.Brutus Cos.designatus'), cited from Velleius. He says nothing about a Pan or Faunus head or pastoral imagery on this coin.

identification: Renaissance fantasy / pasticcio bearing BRVTVS·IMP — no genuine ancient prototype (Caesarian globe-reverse of L. Mussidius Longus, Crawford 494/39 = Babelon Mussidia 58)
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right (generic Republican obverse)
reverse: Globe, caduceus, and ship’s rudder; legend BRVTVS·IMP
orsini_comment: Orsini (Familiae Romanae, p. 132, “Quintus denarius”) attributes this denarius to M. Brutus, reading the globe, caduceus and ship’s rudder as “orbis terrarum pace.” No genuine coin of M. Brutus bears this type. The globe-rudder-caduceus reverse belongs to L. Mussidius Longus (Crawford 494/39 = Babelon, Mussidia 58: head of Caesar / rudder, globe, cornucopia, winged caduceus, apex), where the globe is a Caesarian symbol of the calendar reform; the coinage of Brutus contains no globe or comparable motif (verified against Babelon, gens Iunia). The engraving therefore records a Renaissance fantasy or pasticcio — the Caesarian/Mussidian globe-reverse (minus its cornucopia) paired with a generic Roma head and relabelled BRVTVS·IMP, internally incoherent in its symbolism and unrecorded in any catalogue. It is the one entry in the corpus with no genuine ancient prototype. Moreover, genuine BRVTVS·IMP issues always name the magistrate who struck them — Brutus’s lieutenants in the East before Philippi (Babelon: Lentulus Spinther, Flavius Hemicillus, Pedanius Costa, L. Plaetorius Cestianus, M. Servilius, C. Servilius Casca), all represented in this corpus under their own gentes (Cornelia 26, Flavia 2, Pedania 1, Plaetoria 7–8, Servilia 1/9) and among the genuine Brutus coins of this very plate (Iunia 11–22). The present piece names no magistrate at all — a further mark of fabrication. The mistake here is the forger’s, not Orsini’s: he recorded in good faith a fabrication already circulating in a sixteenth-century cabinet — so this piece stands apart from his own identification errors.
orsini_error: Orsini accepts and records as M. Brutus’s a coin he could have recognised as spurious: a generic Roma head with BRVTVS·IMP and Caesar’s globe-emblem, a combination foreign to all genuine Brutus coinage. The fabrication is the forger’s, but recording it uncritically is Orsini’s lapse.

obverse: Bare male head right (portrait); DESE[RT] ANTO[NIVS].AVGVR.COS around
reverse: Inscription in field (no wreath): M.SILANVS.AVG / Q.PRO.COS
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the sixth coin of the last Iunia plate to M. Iunius Silanus, who served as Antony's Quaestor ('M.IVNIO SILANO Antonii Quaestore percussus est'). He infers from the coin inscription that Silanus was an Augur and administered a province with proconsular power. Orsini does not connect this coin to the Manlii Torquati adoption discussion, which appears much earlier (p. 126).

obverse: Male portrait head right; PARTHICVS around or similar legend
reverse: Horse standing right; A below or in field
orsini_comment: Orsini notes Q. Labienus was son of T. Labienus, Caesar's legate. He was sent to Orodes (the Parthian king) before the battle of Philippi; after the Republican defeat he remained with the Parthians, invaded Syria and Asia Minor with Parthian support, and took the cognomen Parthicus in a manner entirely contrary to Roman custom ('ratione a more Romano diuersissima'). Orsini cites Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (in Parthico) for this account. He does not state that Q. Labienus was defeated and killed in this section.

obverse: Janus bifrons (two-faced head back-to-back); I denomination mark
reverse: Prow right; L·MENA text; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this first (aereus) coin to L. Muraena (Murena): 'primus tabellae aereus numus cusus est, ut opinor, à L. MVRENA co, qui Consul fuit cum D. Iunio Silano anno DCXCI.' He derives the cognomen Muraena from the fish the Greeks call μύραινα, noting Varro lib. II cap. III de re rustica for the derivation.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; C·MALLE·C·F; X (value mark)
reverse: Naked bearded warrior (Bituitus) in biga right, hurling spear, holding shield and carnyx; L·LIC·CN·DOM below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to the Licinia gens, identifying this as an early denarius of P. Licinius Crassus. Notes the family had multiple branches: Murenae, Crassi, Nervae, and Stolones.

obverse: Bare male head right (portrait, bald)
reverse: Warrior standing right holding a spear, a horse beside him; P·CRASSVS·M·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to P. Licinius Crassus M.f. (son of the triumvir M. Crassus), who served as Caesar's legate in Gaul with cavalry and later perished with his father at Carrhae.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; star or dot behind
reverse: Three-arch voting scene (citizens voting); P.NERVA around, with figures on platform
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Roman voting process illustrated on this coin in great detail, identifying the Septa (voting enclosures), Pontes (voting bridges made narrower by C. Marius, Tr.Pl. anno DCXXXIII, per Cicero lib. III de leg. and Plutarch in Mario), Cista (ballot box), and Diribitor (ballot distributor). He connects the legislation on the reverse to C. Marius, not to C. Licinius Macer. He also cites Nicolaus Grucchius on the Comitia, Plinius lib. XXXIII cap. II for the nine hundred ballot custodians, and Cicero post reditum in senatu for the Diribitor's function.

obverse: Laureate head of Fides right; ·LICINI legend (no NERVA shown)
reverse: Horseman galloping right, dragging naked warrior by hair; A·LICINIVS III VIR
orsini_comment: Orsini places this A·LICINI issue under the Licinia gens based on the legend reading, treating the Fides head and horseman reverse as typical of the Augustan period's moral imagery. His identification of the specific Licinius moneyer remains uncertain.

obverse: Laureate head right (Salus per Orsini); SANCT[ITAS] above left, A·LICINI above, FIDES before
reverse: Horseman galloping right wielding spear; III·VIR above, NERVA below
orsini_comment: Orsini places this A·LICINI issue alongside coin 5 as the fifth and sixth denarii of the plate, stating both 'potest ad A. LICINIVM NERVAM eum pertinere, qui anno DL XXXII. in Cretam primò, deinde triennio pòst in Macedoniam ad exercitus uisendos Legatus missus est,' but immediately adds: 'Alii ad A. LICINIVM NERVAM SILIANVM referunt, qui Cos. fuit cum Q. Caecilio Metello Cretico Silano anno DCCLIX.' Orsini leaves the identification between A. Licinius Nerva and A. Licinius Nerva Silianus explicitly open. He discusses the Apollo head and Fides/Salus imagery in the context of Apollinares ludi, and describes De Fidei simulacro with reference to Horace Odes I.35.

obverse: Bare male head right (imperial portrait); legend around including CAESAR.AVGVSTVS
reverse: Large S C (Senatus Consulto) in center; legend around including LICINIVS
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies A. Licinius Nerva Silianus as 'qui triumuir sub Augusto primum huius tabellae nummum aereum cufit,' noting he was adopted by P. Silius ('à P. Silio adoptatum') and served as consul anno DCCLIX (not DCLIX).

obverse: Oak wreath (between laurel branches) enclosing OB / CIVIS / SERVATOS
reverse: Large S C; P·LICINIVS·STOLO·IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: P. Licinius Stolo, triumvir monetalis 17 BC (RIC I² Augustus 345): sestertius with the civic oak-wreath OB CIVIS SERVATOS / large S C, P·LICINIVS·STOLO·IIIVIR·A·A·A·F·F. (Distinct from RIC 346, the AVGVSTVS·TRIBVNIC·POTEST dupondius of the same moneyer.)

obverse: Horseman right (equestrian figure); AVGVSTVS.DIVI.F around
reverse: Conical object (meta or cippus) between two arches/shields; P.STOLO / III.VIR below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that from the impressions on the reverse of the third and fifth denarii of this plate (the ancilia and apex), one may conjecture — his word is 'coniicere' — that P. Licinius Stolo was one of the twelve Salii, or that one of his ancestors was ('unum ex duodecim Saliis eum fuisse, uel maiorum suorum aliquem'). He reasons from the fact that the ancilia are Salian shields. He then cites Lucanus lib. I ('Et Salius laeto portans ancylia collo') and Sex. Pompeius on the ancilia's form, and quotes Lucanus lib. IX on the patrician Salii. The Salian connection is explicitly conjectural, not asserted.

obverse: Female head right
reverse: Charioteer (Minerva) in fast quadriga right; C·LICINIVS·L·F / MACER below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to C. Licinius Macer, noting Plutarchus calls him an orator accused de pecuniis repetundis. When convicted, he committed suicide rather than face exile. Valerius Maximus gives a variant account.

obverse: Single bare male head right; AVGVSTVS / TR·POT legend around
reverse: Conical object (meta) between two shields or arches; P.STOLO / III.VIR below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the ancilia (Salii shields) reference the sacred shields of the Salii priesthood. The apex and ancilia signify priestly office connected to Numa Pompilius's institution of the Salii.

obverse: Lion-headed Genius terrae Africae standing, holding ankh; G·T·A Q·METEL·PIVS SCIPIO·IMP text
reverse: Victory standing left, holding caduceus and patera; P·CRASSVS·IVN LEG·PRO·PR text
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this African campaign issue in the context of the Pompeian faction's political messaging, treating the Concordia and Pax imagery as reflecting the Republican cause's claims to constitutional harmony. He identifies P. Licinius Crassus's role as Scipio's legate propraetor and discusses his adoption from the Iunia family.

moneyer: P. Licinius Crassus Iunior / Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio
obverse: METEL·PIVS / SCIP·IMP: Bust of Jupiter right, hair tied with band; below, eagle's head and sceptre. Border of dots.
reverse: CRASS·IVN / LEG·PRO·PR: Curule chair; above, scales balanced on a cornucopia; on left, corn-ear; on right, dragon's head. Border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this coin with the others of the African campaign series ('HVIVS tabellae denarii, non est dubium quin à P. LICINIO CRASSO IVNIANO signati in Africa sint'). The SCIPIO·IMP / METELP legend connects to Scipio Metellus commanding in Africa. Orsini makes no mention of an elephant on this coin.

moneyer: P. Licinius Crassus Iunior / Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio
obverse: Turreted head of Genius Terrae Africae (Africa) right, corn-ear before; CRASS·IVN / LEG·PRO·PR around.
reverse: Trophy of arms; on left, lituus; on right, jug (praefericulum); METEL·PIVS / SCIP·IMP around.
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to P. Licinius Crassus Iunior as Scipio's legate Pro Praetore in Africa. Notes Crassus was born into the Iunia family but adopted by P. Licinius, and was called Crassus Iunianus after the adoption formula.

obverse: Head right, bare
reverse: Modius with wheat ears; REGVLVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Livineius Regulus as IIIvir monetalis and son of L. Regulus. Notes he was also Aedilis Curulis, as indicated by the curule chair and modius types on several of his coins.

obverse: Head of man right, bare
reverse: Hunt/venatio scene: animals and figures in combat (no single standing Diana, no bow); REGVLVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini infers from the animal-combat scene that Regulus staged venationes during his aedileship ('quem Aedilem Curulem fuisse, ex iis quae in altera parte... expressa sunt, intelligere possumus'). He does not cite Pliny, and does not connect the scene to spectacles given by Caesar.

obverse: Head of male figure right, bare; legend around
reverse: Two curule chairs (bisellium) between standards/columns under a triangular roof element; REGVLVS·F above, PRAEF·VR below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the PRAEF·VR inscription indicates Regulus also served as Praefectus Urbi. The curule chair and fasces denote his magistracy.

obverse: Bare male head right; REGVLVS above, PR below
reverse: Ceremonial curule seats with two upright torches; L·LIVINEIVS above, REGVLVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as another die variant of the L. Livineius Regulus aedilician series. He does not cite Pliny for the spectacle scenes; Pliny does not appear in the Livineia section.

obverse: Bare male head right (portrait)
reverse: Bisellium on platform; L.LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the PRAEF·VR inscription as confirming the Praefectura Urbi ('Eundem autem Regulum Vrbis etiam Praefectum aliquando fuisse, ex tertii denarii inscriptione apparet'). The seat shown is a Curuli sella (curule chair), not a bisellium.

obverse: Male head right with attributes (possibly laureate); caduceus behind
reverse: Bull charging right; L.LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the bull as referencing venationes (beast hunts) staged during L. Livineius Regulus's aedileship under Caesar.

obverse: Bare head of Octavian (Caesar) right; C·CAESAR·III·VIR·R·P·C (IIII·VIR / CAESAR) around.
reverse: Victory standing right, holding wreath and palm-branch; L·LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS around.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius pertains to L. Livineius Regulus, son of L. Regulus, whom he considers the same person described by Cornelius Tacitus and Dio.

moneyer: L. Livineius Regulus / P. Sulpicius Plautius Hericlianus / C. Plotius Rufus
obverse: Clasped right hands holding a caduceus; REGVLVS PVLCHER around
reverse: Large S C; III·VIR·A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to L. Livineius Regulus, noting the animal (lion or panther) may also commemorate arena spectacles. Tacitus lib. III mentions Livineium Regulum as accused in Germanicus's death.

moneyer: L. Cassius and L. Livius Salinator
obverse: Head of Janus left and right, bearded
reverse: Prow of galley right; C·CASSI above, C·SALIN below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes only one coin of the Salinator family appears in this tabella, as a bronze (aereus nummus). The coin legend reads C·CASSI / L·SALIN (visible in plate). Livy lib. XXXIX mentions a Livius who invented the cognomen Salinator by imposing a salt tax during a censorship. Orsini cannot identify which L. Salinator struck this coin.

obverse: Male head right (portrait); HONORIS behind
reverse: Bisellium or sella curulis on platform; PALIKanvs around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to M. Lollius Palicanus, tribune of the plebs whom Valerius Maximus calls a seditious man. The Rostra on the reverse reference the speaker's platform in the Forum where Palicanus agitated for restoration of tribunician power.

obverse: Female head right (Libertas); LIBERTAS around
reverse: Rostra (speaker's platform) with ship prow; PALIKANUS below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Libertas head and Rostra celebrate the restoration of tribunician power under Pompey. Livy and Varro describe the Rostra as a platform adorned with ship prows captured from enemies.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Victory in biga right; M.LVCILI below
orsini_comment: Orsini tentatively identifies M. Lucilius Rufus as possibly the tribune of the plebs who proposed making Pompey dictator (Plutarch in Pompeio). He separately notes a different Lucilius ('alterius Lucilii') who at Philippi offered himself to the enemy in place of Brutus (Plutarch in Bruto and Antonio) — Orsini does not assert these are the same person. The marks A.PV. signify argento publico ('significant argento publico').

obverse: Head of Roma left, helmeted
reverse: The Dioscuri on horseback right; CN LVCR in exergue, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to Cn. Lucretius Trio and suggests the cognomen Trio derives from the Triones (the seven stars of Ursa Major/the Plough), which appear on the later coins of this family.

obverse: Radiate head of Sol right
reverse: Crescent moon with stars around; TRIO above, L·LVCRETI below
orsini_comment: Orsini explains the seven stars represent the Triones (Septentriones/Ursa Major), a punning reference to the cognomen Trio. Varro in De Lingua Latina explains the etymology of Triones from ploughing oxen.

obverse: Laureate male head right
reverse: Crescent moon above; stars around; TRIO in center
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Triones (the seven stars of Ursa Major) imagery on this L. Lucretius Trio coin, citing Varro's De Lingua Latina for the etymology of Triones from ploughing oxen (tri + ones), and referencing Homer and Agellius (Aulus Gellius) for descriptions of the seven stars near the celestial pole. He derives the moneyer's cognomen Trio from this constellation.

obverse: Laureate head of Neptune right; trident behind; control numeral above
reverse: Infant Genius (Cupid) seated on dolphin right; L·LVCRETI / TRIO
orsini_comment: Orsini notes Neptune with trident and Cupid on dolphin on this coin but explicitly states he is uncertain what they signify ('mihi quidem incertum quò spectent'). He tentatively suggests, since the same types appear on M. Cordius Rufus's denarius and others, that they may indicate the Julian family's origin ('in Caesaris gratiam, ad indicandam Iuliae gentis originem'). He does not say 'from Venus through the sea.'

obverse: Bare male head right (imperial portrait); CAESAR.AVGVSTVS.PONT.MAX around
reverse: Large S C in center; MVNIFICAG[...].III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Lurius as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus; Dio lib. XLVIII records him as governor of Sardinia. Tacitus lib. XII also mentions the gens. Marble inscriptions record M. LVRIVS TRIARIVS and M. LVRIVS TREPTVS.

obverse: Helmeted head right (Roma); ROMA behind; CERCO below
reverse: Ship or galley; Q.LVTATI / Q below
orsini_comment: Orsini's friend ('amicus meus') proposed that the two sides of this coin refer to two brothers: Q. Lutatius Cerco (consul who triumphed at Falisceis anno DXII) and C. Lutatius Catulus (Procos. naval victory over the Carthaginians from Sicily, same year). Orsini presents this as his friend's view ('amicus meus existimabat'), not his own settled interpretation. He suggests the coin may have been struck by C. Lutatius Cerco (legatus to Alexandria anno DLXXX, Livy lib. XLII) to celebrate Caius's naval and Quintus's terrestrial victories at Falisceis.

obverse: Bare head left; AVGVST PONT MAX TRIBVN around
reverse: Large SC in centre; legend around including M MAECILI... IIII VIR
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze coin to M. MAECILIVS TVL LVS, noting uncertainty whether this Maecilius traces origin from the patrician branch of the gens (admitted under Tullus Hostilius per Dionysius lib. III) or from the plebeian branch numbered by Livy.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory driving quadriga right; P.MAEN below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini is uncertain whether this silver denarius belongs to the Maecilia gens or should be read as MAENIVS and referred to the Maenia gens; he notes the reading of the monogram is ambiguous.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
reverse: Victory (or charioteer) driving biga of two horses right; C·MINI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this silver denarius as belonging to the Maiania gens, which he equates with the Maenia found in the Capitoline Fasti; he cites an ancient Caeretan inscription as evidence for the family name.

obverse: Janiform head (double head) facing left and right, bare
reverse: Prow of ship right; C M INI above
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze coin to C. Maianius and tentatively connects him to C. Mainium P.f.P.n., who triumphed as consul in year CDXV over the Antiatians, Lavinians ('Lauinieis'), and Veliternaeans, and was later recorded as Dictator II in year CDXXXIX in the Capitoline monuments.

obverse: Helmeted head of Mars or Mercury right; caduceus behind
reverse: Standing figure (Ulysses?) with staff beside column; C.MAMIL / LIMETA(N) around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to C. Mamilius Limetanus, explaining the Mamilia gens traced its origin from Mamilia, daughter of Telegonus (son of Ulysses and Circe), and identifies the reverse figure as Ulysses recognized by his dog after twenty years, following Homer.

moneyer: P. Crepusius, C. Mamilius Limetanus, L. Marcius Censorinus
obverse: Wreathed/draped head right; ...CENSORIN behind
reverse: Venus in biga right, holding reins and goad; XXVIII above, C·LIMETA / P·CREPVSI below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius shows Ulysses with a pileus (cap), citing Nicomachus as the first to add the pileus to Ulysses; he also mentions C. Mamilius as Tribune of the Plebs from Sallust's Jugurthine War, and corrects the moneyer's name to C. Mamilius Limetanus from older readings.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right (plume each side); SER, ROMA
reverse: Sol in quadriga facing; star on either side, crescent at right, waves below; reverse legend A·MANLI·Q·F (NO TORQ); X (value mark)
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to A. Manlius, identifying him as the son ('filius') of Q. Manlii Thurini (Livy lib. XXVIII; Quintilian lib. II), who was Praetor Peregrinus in year DXLV and Aedilis plebis in year DXLVI. He notes the SER mark on the reverse may indicate SERRATVS (serrated coinage), citing Tacitus on the Germans' esteem for serrate coins.

moneyer: T. Manlius Mancinus, Ap. Claudius Pulcher, Q. Urbinius
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Victory in triga right; T·MAL·AP·CL·Q·VR in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the legend as T. MANLIVS and suggests this moneyer may be a contemporary and relative of Cicero, possibly identifiable with the T. Manlius mentioned by Cicero in Brutus as consul.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA and L.MANLI (PRO Q) legend
reverse: Figure in quadriga right; L.SVLLA.IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Manlius as Sulla's ProQuaestor ('Sullae ProQuaestore'), citing Livy in epitome lib. XL, and discusses the episode of Q. Sertorius's proscription in further Spain. He does not discuss the SER inscription in connection with this coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind, X below
reverse: Warrior on horseback galloping right; torque device above; L·TORQVA above, EX·S·C below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the fourth and fifth denarii both belong to L. TORQVATVS, consul in year DCLXXXVIII with L. Cotta. He discusses the Torquatus cognomen's origin from T. Manlius, who took the golden torque from a Gaul in single combat at the River Anio in year CCCXCII (citing Livy, Plutarch in Mario, Cicero de officiis lib. III and de finibus). He notes that on both denarii the torque device refers to this cognomen.

obverse: Head of Sibyl right; SIBVLLI below
reverse: Tripod with stars above; L.TORQVAT / III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the Sibyl's image on one side and a tripod on the other of this fifth denarius allow the conjecture ('possumus suspicari') that L. Torquatus was an XVuir sacris faciundis, since the Sibylline books were guarded by the XVuiri and could not be consulted without senatorial decree, as attested by Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Lactantius, Suetonius in Caesare, and others. He also notes that Sibyls were accustomed to prophesy from a tripod sacred to Apollo.

obverse: Diademed head of Ancus Marcius right; lituus/symbol behind; PHILIPPVS legend
reverse: Horseman galloping right with spear; L.PHILIPPVS below, flower/star symbols
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Philippus, identifying the obverse head as King Ancus Marcius and the reverse as the Aqua Marcia aqueduct, which he says the family claimed Ancus had built; he cites Frontinus and Pliny on the aqueduct's history.
orsini_error: Orsini identifies obverse as Apollo; actually Ancus Marcius (diademed), per Crawford 425/1.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted with plume
reverse: Horseman galloping right; L·PHILIPPVS on tablet below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this second denarius to the same L. Philippus as coin 1. One side shows the same equestrian honor voted to Q. Marcius; the other side shows the image of L. Marcius Censorinus, from whose head a flame shone while he harangued troops in Spain (Livy lib. XXV, Valerius Maximus lib. I cap. VI, Pliny lib. II cap. CX).

obverse: Head of Hercules right; three pellets (quadrans mark) behind; L·PHILIPPVS
reverse: Prow right; rooster above; three pellets before; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this bronze coin ('tertius aereus nummus') as belonging to the same Philippus who was Augustus's stepfather ('Augustui uitricus fuit') and consul with Cn. Lentulus Marcellinus in year DCXCVII, noting also that the coin may refer to his father L. Philippus Q.f., who was first a legate of Sulla, occupied Sardinia after expelling Q. Antonius, and was later consul in year DCLXII (Livy lib. LXXXVI; Cicero pro P. Quintio, pro L. Murena, in Philipp. lib. XI).

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted with wing decoration; X behind
reverse: Single horseman galloping right; Q·PILIPPVS above, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to Q. Philippus, who was consul twice: first with Sp. Postumius Albinus in year DLXVII, then with Cn. Servilius Caepio in year DLXXXIIII, and was later Censor with L. Aemilius Paullus. The reverse shows Castor on horseback ('Castor equo insidens'), with Orsini citing Horace ('Castor gaudet equis') and Homer (Iliad lib. III; Odyssey lib. II) on Castor's association with horses.

obverse: Head of Apollo right, laureate
reverse: Nude male figure (Marsyas) standing with right arm raised beside a tall column surmounted by a small statue; L·CENSOR around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this fifth denarius to L. Marcius Censorinus, consul in year DCCXIIII with C. Calvisius Sabinus, who triumphed from Macedonia on the Kalends of January. Orsini connects 'CONGIARVM populo ab Anco datum' (a grain distribution Ancus gave the people, Pliny lib. XXXI cap. VII) and the 'ACROSTIRIVM nauis' (a ship's ram) to L. Censorinus, who commanded the fleet against Carthage (Appian in Libyco). He also discusses the moneyer's role in publicizing Marcian family monuments.

moneyer: P. Crepusius, C. Mamilius Limetanus, L. Marcius Censorinus
obverse: Female head right (veiled or diademed); L.CENS behind
reverse: Biga galloping right; XXIIII above; C.LIMET / P.CREPVSI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the reverse of this sixth denarius shows a VICTORIA placed on a column ('VICTORIA columnae imposita'), representing Marcian family monuments, but he explicitly leaves open to which Marcius it pertains — whether to King Ancus or to another member of the gens ('quae ignoratur ad quem pertineat Marciorum, ad Ancum ne regem, an ad alium eius gentis'). Orsini attributes coins 5 and 6 together to L. Marcius Censorinus, consul DCCXIIII.

obverse: Two male heads jugate right (Numa Pompilius and Ancus Marcius); NVMA.POMPILI / ANCVS.MARCI around
reverse: Prow or galley right with stern ornament; C.CENSO / ROMA around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the two jugate heads as Kings Numa Pompilius and Ancus Marcius, from whom the Marcia gens claimed descent; the Marcii traced their lineage through Popilia, Numa's daughter, whose son was King Ancus.

obverse: Two male heads jugate right (Numa and Ancus); NVMA.POMPILI / ANCVS.MARCI around
reverse: Prow right; C.MRCI / CENSO around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to C. Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto), noting it shows the jugate heads of Kings Numa and Ancus. He explains that the first two bronze coins and sixth coin of the second plate also show the Ostia colony monument ('Ostiae quoque coloniae, quam anno CXXVII Ancus deduxit, monumentum expressit'), citing Livy lib. I and Strabo lib. V.

obverse: Single bearded male head right
reverse: Single horseman (desultor) galloping right; C·CENSOR below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this silver denarius to C. Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto), noting that the third and fourth coins of this plate show circus victory types: equestrian ('equo singulari') and biga racing victories, which C. Censorinus placed on these coins to celebrate his progenitors' monuments. Orsini is uncertain which ancestor's victories are depicted and notes the Victoria column's referent is also unclear ('Victoriae columnae impositae... ignoratur ad quem pertineat'). Documented Orsini misattribution: these circus-victory reverses have no certain ancient source identifying the specific Marcius honored.

obverse: Female head right (Apollo per Orsini) (diademed or laureate); fillet behind
reverse: Horse galloping; above, two apices each surmounted by a star; C·CENSOR in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this coin (the fourth of the second Marcia plate) together with coin 9 as circus-victory types: 'Tertio quoque & quarto denario Marcii alicuius de ludicris Circensibus equo singulari & bigis partas uictorias designari arbitror, quas C. Cenforinus triumuir sub Augusto, ut progenitoris sui monumenta illustraret, in his nummis signauit.' Orsini does not describe the obverse type of this coin separately or name it as 'laureate Apollo.' The attribution is to C. Marcius Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto) celebrating an ancestor's circus victories.

obverse: OB / CIVIS (within oak wreath); two laurel branches flank
reverse: Large SC in centre; L.ARRV(N)TIVS... around; legend with M.MARC.CENSOR around border
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to C. Marcius Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto, consul DCCXLV with C. Asinius Gallus). Orsini confirms he was an Augur from the coin's own title and from a votive inscription found at Aquinum: 'C. MARCIO L.F. / CENSORINO. COS / AVGVRI. PATRONO. D.D.' He does not say Censorinus 'triumphed under Augustus'; no triumph is mentioned by Orsini for this Censorinus. Engraver metal note: Orsini's plate shows this coin in the bronze (AE) series consistent with an Augustan S.C. bronze.

obverse: Single bearded head right; NVMA·POMPILI legend around
reverse: Two arches: spiral column with Victory under left, prow under right; C·CENSO / ROMA
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this sixth bronze ('sexto item aereo') of the second plate to C. Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto), noting it shows the heads of Kings Numa and Ancus together with the Ostia colony monument, as he established that Ancus founded the Ostia colony in year CXXVII. The reverse does not show a prow; the Ostia colony monument is the distinguishing feature.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri on horseback right; Q.MRC below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Q. Marcius Libo, who struck as triumvir monetalis with C. Fabius and L. Rubrius (or L. Roscius); he notes the pileated Castores (Dioscuri) and victory quadriga on the reverse as standard Marcian types.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma (winged helmet); X behind
reverse: Victory driving a quadriga right; ROMA above, Q·M·C·F·L·R in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the legend as Q. Marcius with filiation C.f. L.n. and notes the LIBO cognomen also belongs to the Marcia gens as well as the Julia family; he finds no memorable mention of this moneyer in ancient writers.

obverse: Single laureate/bearded head left (the engraving renders Janus as a single profile head, not janiform)
reverse: Ship/galley right; Q·MARC above, LIBO below

obverse: Bust of Ceres right, draped; legend CAPIT
reverse: Ploughman with yoke of oxen left; legend C·MARI·C·F / S·C
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to C. Marius C.f. Capito, who served as Pro Triumuir apparently ('ut uidetur') under Augustus. He notes that the colony scene on the reverse may represent either one of the colonies Augustus founded or Eporedia, which C. Marius founded as consul (Pliny lib. III cap. VI; Velleius lib. I), Eporedia having been founded 23 years after Marius's sixth consulship ('Post tres & uiginti annos in Vagiennis Eporedia...'). Orsini leaves the identification open ('uel... uel').

obverse: Bust of Ceres right, draped; CAPIT text visible
reverse: Ploughman with yoke of oxen left; LVIII number visible; C·MARI·C·F / S·C in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the ploughing scene as a colonial foundation, attributing it to C. Marius C.f. Capito; he interprets the PRO III VIR inscription as Pro Triumvir rather than Pro Quaestor, correcting earlier misreadings.

obverse: Head of Augustus left, laureate
reverse: Two standing figures facing each other; Marcus and Agrippa

obverse: Head of Caesar left, laureate
reverse: Eagle standing with wings spread, head turned; C·MARIVS·C·F above, TRO·IIIVIR below

obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around
reverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around

obverse: Head of Augustus bare right within oak-wreath; legend AVGVSTVS DIVI F
reverse: Three heads right (Julia, Gaius Caesar, Lucius Caesar) with wreath above; legend C·MARIVS·TRO·IIIVIR

obverse: Laureate male head right (Saturn or Quirinus); QVIRINVS or SATVRNS around
reverse: Ceres seated right on throne, holding torch and sceptre; C.MEMMI.C.F around; A.P.D.CERIA.MARVLLI.F behind
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as C. Memmius C.f.'s denarius, noting that Memmius as Aedile was the first to celebrate the Cerealia games with horse races in the Circus; he cites Dio lib. XLVII on the games and identifies the bearded head as Quirinus.

obverse: Laureate head right; C·MEMMI·C·F around
reverse: Trophy with captive at base; IMPERATOR on left, C·MEMMIVS on right
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this second denarius to C. Memmius C.F. (Consul suffectus year DCCXIX), son of C. Memmius L.F. The Imperator title in the inscription belongs to the father (L. Memmius's son C. Memmius L.F.), who obtained the Imperator title from Bithynia after serving as Praetor with L. Domitius. Orsini discusses at length whether this C. Memmius or a different one was the patron of Lucretius who sent him De Rerum Natura.

obverse: Laureate head of Saturn right; S denomination mark behind
reverse: Prow right; L·MEMMI above; ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze semis to L. Memmius and considers the remaining denarii of the plate to belong to L. Memmius, whom he identifies as a son of C. or L. Memmius based on the filiation in the legends.

obverse: Male head right, bare
reverse: The Dioscuri standing facing with horses; C.MEMMI around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to L. Memmius with the Dioscuri standing, and notes L. Memmius was among the noble orators listed by Cicero in Brutus; he discusses the Gemellus cognomen found in Cicero as possibly belonging to this branch.

obverse: Laureate bearded head of Saturn left; ROMA below
reverse: Venus in biga right, holding sceptre and reins; Cupid above; L·MEMMI·GAL / ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads GAL in coins 5–6 as L. Memmii cognomen, noting it differs maximally from GEM ('nota à GEM, diuerfissima notetur') and suspects a copyist transposed letters in Cicero's text so that GALLVS (or something similar) became GEMELLVS. He does not read GAL as the tribe Galeria.

obverse: Laureate head of Saturn left; text around
reverse: Jupiter holding sceptre and reins in galloping quadriga right; L·MEMMI below; GAL in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as C. Memmius with the cognomen abbreviation, noting the inscription L.C. MEMMISI could refer to the two brothers C. and L. Memmius; he discusses whether the C. Memmius of this denarius is an otherwise unknown member of the gens.

obverse: Inscription in rectangular frame: IMP / CAES / AVG / S.COMM / CONS; AVGVSTVS.TRIBVNIC around
reverse: Inscription on cippus within laurel wreath: IOM / S.P.Q.R.V.S / PR.S.IMP.CAE / QVOD.PER.EV / R.P.IN.AMP / ATQ.TRAN / S.E
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to L. Mescinius Rufus and notes its reverse inscription 'IMP. CAE. AVGV. COMM. CONS.' ('Imperatori Caesari Augusto communi consensu'), recording the vows of the Senate and People to Iuppiter Optimus Maximus for the safety of Emperor Caesar Augustus.

obverse: Bare male head right
reverse: Mars standing facing, head turned, holding spear and resting hand on parazonium/sword; small inscribed tablet at base; L.MESCINIVS RVFVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that coin 2 records only the vows for Augustus's return ('ea tantum nota notata sunt, quae pro reditu Augusti suscepta fuerunt'), with inscription 'S.P.Q.R. V.PR. R.ED. CAES.' Orsini does not describe a simpulum or FORTVNA REDVCI legend on this coin.

obverse: Statue of Mars standing facing on a pedestal, holding spear and parazonium; L·MESCINIVS·RVFVS around
reverse: Bare male bust (Augustus) on a round shield within a laurel wreath; S·C·OB·R·P·CONS around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that coin 3 shows a signum Martis ('signi Martis') at its base, dedicated with the vow inscription 'S.P.Q.R. V.S.PRO. S. LT. R.ED. AVG.' (Senatus Populusque Romanus votum solvit pro salute et reditu Augusti), and that the column or base records a statue decreed by the Senate and People in common accord ('communi consensu Senatusque consulto statuam decretam fuisse intelligimus').

obverse: Laureate head of Augustus left; LA(?)...IVS / AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Inscription in frame: IMP / CAE / AVG / LVD.S.E / SAEC around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Mescinius Rufus and identifies the SAECVLARE inscription as commemorating the Ludi Saeculares celebrated by Augustus; he cites Dio and Suetonius on the Secular Games and connects the columnar inscription to Politianus' observations.

obverse: Head right, bare; legend around
reverse: Victory driving a galloping biga (two-horse chariot); M·METTIVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the first of Mettius's denarii; he notes the obverse as Juno Sospita of Lanuvium ('Iunonem Sospitam, quae Lanuuii cum hasta, scutulo, calceolis repandis, & pelle caprina colebatur, signauit'). The Lanuvian serpent is not attributed to this coin but to the third.

obverse: Wreathed head of Caesar right; CAESAR IMPER
reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and sceptre, elbow on shield on globe; M·METTIVS
orsini_comment: Orsini presents this as the second of Mettius's denarii ('in secundo'). He does not describe specific types for this coin beyond its being struck under Caesar as Dictator ('sub quo Dictatore quarto M. METTIVS hic (ut apparet) cudendae monetae praefuit'). No citation of Propertius is attached to this coin; the Propertius verses are cited for the third coin.

obverse: Head of male figure right, bare
reverse: Standing draped figure facing/turned, holding object (simpulum/patera); M·METTI in field at right
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to M. Mettius and notes Caesar mentions a Mettius in two places in De Bello Gallico lib. I, though the vulgate texts erroneously print M. Tittius; he corrects this from Vatican manuscript evidence.

obverse: Laureate head right (portrait); legend around
reverse: Three standing figures (central figure flanked by two); PR.Q above, M·MINAT / SABIN below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to M. Minatius Sabinus, whom he identifies as Cn. Pompey's pro-quaestor in Hispania ('M. MINATI I huius, qui Cn. Pompeii, ut ego arbitror in Hispania Pro-Quaestore fuit'). He cites Valerius Maximus lib. III cap. IV on Minatius Rufus (M. Cato's companion in the Cypriaca expeditione) and an inscription from Bisenti (Etruria) mentioning the Sabatina tribe.

obverse: Bare/laureate male head right; IMP before, CN·MAGN(VS) behind/below
reverse: Standing figures, three figures in robes with one central figure between two others
orsini_comment: Orsini notes he finds no mention of this moneyer in ancient writers ('nullam apud ueteres scriptores reperio mentionem'); his libertus may be the M. Minatius recorded in an ancient inscription using the archaic spelling FLVIVM for FLVVIVM. Orsini does not describe this as a 'veteran inscription.'

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Column (Columna Minucia) flanked by two standing figures holding grain ears; RVF.MINVC.AVGVR / ROMA around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Ti. Minucius C.f. Augurinus and identifies the lituus symbol as indicating the moneyer is to be identified with M. Minucius Festum, who became the first Augur from the plebs out of this family in year CDLIII AUC ('anno CDLIII, ut scribit [Liuius] plebi lib. XI'). He does not say this dates to 'around 454 AUC' but to year CDLIII = 453 AUC.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA below; X behind
reverse: Column flanked by two standing figures; C.AVG around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to C. Augurinus, identifying the column as the Columna Minucia erected outside the Porta Trigemina for L. Minucius' grain distribution; he cites Livy and Pliny on the statue and column set up by popular subscription.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri (two horsemen) galloping right; Q.MINV below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini tentatively identifies this as Q. Minucius Rufus, noting he may be the consul who triumphed over the Ligurians and Boii, or possibly Q. Minucius who was dux in Asia against Mithridates, citing Appian.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; ROMA / C·MINVCI below
orsini_comment: Orsini is uncertain whether this is a separate moneyer or the same C. Augurinus as coin 2; he notes it lacks the Lucius cognomen and may represent a different family member who struck both the silver and the bronze (coin 6 of the Augurinus column type).

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma(?) left
reverse: Two warriors fighting; Q.THERM.M.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini states without doubt ('sine dubio') that this coin pertains to Q. Minucius M. Thermi filius, under whose praetorship in Asia C. Iulius Caesar (later Dictator) served his first military service and was awarded the civic crown at the siege of Mytilene ('in expugnatione Mytilenarum ciuica donatus est'). He cites Suetonius in Caesare cap. II. Orsini does NOT identify this coin's moneyer as the legatus of A. Manlius Vulsonis — that reference belongs to coin 4.

moneyer: Q. Fufius Calenus & P. Mucius Scaevola Cordus
obverse: Two heads jugate right (one with beard); HO...VIR / KALENI around
reverse: Two standing figures (Italia and Roma clasping hands); CORDI below; RO(MA) behind
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the joint issue of Calenus (KALENVS) and Mucius Cordus, noting Cordus had 'monetam cum Honoris signo & Virtutis, ad illustranda gentilis sui monumenta signauit.' He cites Dionysius lib. IIII and Quintilian lib. I cap. VII on the Cordus cognomen, and Vitruvius lib. VII on C. Mucius who designed the aedes Honoris et Virtutis Marianae. He also notes (following Vitruvius) that any Mucia gens member 'ex Mucia gente ufi sint' might be connected to this Cordus. He cross-references to the Fufia gens (cognomen KALENVS) for the temple of Honos and Virtus.

obverse: Bust of Victory, right, draped. C.CAES / DIC.TER around
reverse: Oenochoe (jug/capis); L·PLANC / PR·VRB around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as struck by L. Munatius Plancus. He thinks the urceus (jug) on the reverse may indicate Plancus's role as VIIIvir Epulonum, but notes it could equally refer to Caesar as Pontifex Maximus ('quamuis ad C. quoque Caesarem, qui Pontifex Maximus fuit, referri urceolus possit'). He identifies Plancus as consul designatus with D. Brutus for year DCCXI AUC, and as Vrbis praefectus in the coin's inscription context.

identification: Crawford 522/2 — L. Munatius Plancus (under Mark Antony), 32 BC
obverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; III.VIR.R.P.C.M.ANTON around
reverse: Three implements: winged thunderbolt/sceptre at left, oenochoe (jug) at center, winged caduceus at right; C·PLANCVS·IMP·ITER around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Munatius Plancus, citing Velleius lib. II ('Plancus, inquit, Antonianarum adiutor partium, spem magis ostendens auxilii, quam opem ferens Antonio') and Appian lib. III bell. ciuil. ('Plancus cum tribus legionibus transiuit ad Antonium'). The Greek passage from Appian shows Lepidus, Asinius Pollio, and Plancus as those who joined Antonius; Orsini does not say Plancus 'joined Lepidus' — Plancus joined Antonius.

obverse: Head of Ceres right, wearing corn-ear wreath
reverse: L.MVSSIDIVS / LONGVS within corn-ear wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Mussidius Longus, noting the aureus (gold) type with a spiked corona on one side and Ceres' image on the other; he suggests this coin may relate to the Mussidii's frumentary administration under Caesar as Dictator.

obverse: Veiled head of Concordia right; CONCORDIA before
reverse: Shrine of Venus Cloacina: raised circular platform bearing two statues; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS above, CLOACIN on the platform
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the reverse as the shrine of Venus Cloacina, which stood in the Forum near the Cloaca Maxima; he cites Pliny, Plutarch, and Livy on the shrine's origin from the Sabine-Roman peace under Titus Tatius and Romulus, where arms were purified at the site.

obverse: Radiate bust right (Roma/Venus/Concordia per Orsini) (Sol); sun rays around head
reverse: Shrine or altar on platform; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS / CLOACIN around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is a second Cloacina type with the radiate Sol head on the obverse; he discusses the Concordia symbolism connecting the Roman-Sabine reconciliation to the shrine of Venus Cloacina, citing Ovid's Fasti.

obverse: Female head right (Concordia); CONCORDIA around
reverse: Clasped hands holding caduceus; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Concordia head and clasped hands as symbolizing the Roman-Sabine peace; he connects the Concordia imagery across Mussidius' series to the coitio (union) of Romans and Sabines at the Comitium.

obverse: Bust right (portrait); draped
reverse: Biga or chariot right; L.MVSSIDIVS / LONGVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this coin's spectacle types to C. Caesar's Dictatorial victories and cites Suetonius cap. XXXIX specifically ('Circensibus, inquit, spacio Circi ab utraque parte producto, & in gyrum euripo addito, quadrigas, bigasque & equos desultorios agitauerunt nobilissimi iuuenes').

obverse: Head right; crescent behind
reverse: Pontifical/sacrificial implements; L·MVSSIDIVS LONGVS around
orsini_comment: Coinage of L. Mussidius Longus (Crawford 494/39). The obverse shows a head right with a crescent behind; the reverse displays pontifical and sacrificial implements with the legend L·MVSSIDIVS LONGVS around. The cult/sacrificial implements point to the moneyer's religious associations rather than to any games or spectacle.

obverse: Bare male head left; M.LEPIDVS.III.VIR.R.P.C around
reverse: Mars standing right, wearing Corinthian helmet, holding sword in left hand and spear in right hand and resting left foot on shield. Legend L·MVSSIDIVS·T·F·LONGVS·IIII·VIR·A·P·F
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as showing the head of C. Caesar (later Augustus) with the triumviral title, noting the portrait of M. Antonius on the reverse; he considers it part of the concordia series indicating M. Antonii concordiam and connects it to Mussidius as IIIIvir A.P.F. Same type as Aemilia #13 (Crawford 494/7a) but with a different engraving: the coin appears under both gentes because it bears names from both families.

obverse: Head of Octavian, right
