reverse: Mars standing right, wearing Corinthian helmet, holding sword in left hand and spear in right hand and resting left foot on shield
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Mussidius Longus as IIIIvir A.P.F. (quattuorvir for striking gold or silver by public authority); he notes the triumviral portrait of C. Caesar and reads the T.F. inscription as confirming the Quattuorviral monetary authority first instituted by Caesar.

obverse: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem
reverse: Victory driving a triga (three-horse chariot) right; C.NAE.BALB in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the gens as plebeian and notes the S.C. behind the head indicates senatorial authorization on this C. Naevius Balbus denarius with Victory in triga. He connects the moneyer to the Balbus cognomen found in several gentes and discusses the family's limited literary attestation.

obverse: Bare male head right (Augustus); legend around including CAESAR
reverse: S C large in centre; L.SVRDNINVS III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as an Augustan bronze by L. Naevius Surdinus. He has no literary attestation for Surdinus ('nulla, quod sciam, extat mentio apud scriptores') and does not call him 'IIIvir A.A.A.F.F.' — this title is not in Orsini's text. He notes only that Surdinus 'sub Augusto nummum aereum signauit' and points to a Forum inscription about L. Naevius... Praetoris inter ciuis et peregrinos.

obverse: Wreath enclosing legend AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST; oak wreath border
reverse: S C large in centre; L.NAEVIVS SVRDNINVS III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini presents no specific textual discussion of this second Surdinus bronze on the Naevia page. He offers no description of the obverse legend (AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST) and no dating formula discussion. The coin is visible in the plate but Orsini's text does not describe it separately.

obverse: Partially visible; handwritten annotations over engraving; CLXV(?) and C.NAE.BA visible
reverse: Partially visible with handwritten notes overlaid; details obscured
orsini_comment: Later collector's note (French) on a C. Naevius Balbus denarius: a control-number reading («CLXV»?) with «C·NAE·BA», and a diagnostic «S·C derrière la tête» (S·C behind the head).

obverse: Bare head of Neptune right, trident behind; NEPTVNI legend
reverse: Galley (warship) right with sail and ornamental stern; star above; Q.NASIDIV(S) below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the NEPTVNI legend as referring to Sextus Pompey's claim to be Neptune's son ('cuius se filium iactabat') and notes the galley type. He proposes the coin was struck either by Q. Nasidius to commemorate his father L. Nasidius's naval action (Caesar lib. II bell. ciuil.) or because Q. Nasidius himself at some point commanded Sex. Pompey's fleet ('nisi forte... aliquando praefuit'). He cites Dio lib. L and Appian lib. V bell. ciuil. and cross-references under the Pompeia gens.

obverse: Head of Saturn right with harpa; legend NERI·Q·VRB
reverse: Legionary eagle between two military standards (hastati and principes); legend L·LENT·C·MARC·COS
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the coin's moneyer (NERI, Q. VRB.) with Cn. Nerius, mentioned in Cicero ep. III lib. II ad Q. Fratrem as accused by Sestius of electoral bribery in the Pupinia tribe ('Cn. Nerio Pupinia de ambitu est postulatus'). He reads the Q. VRB. as Quaestor Vrbanus. He notes the consular date L. Lentulo C. Marcello Coss. He does not describe the coin types (Saturn head; legionary eagle) — those descriptions are not in his text.

obverse: Bearded head right (Saturnus); S C behind; SVFENAS around
reverse: Seated female figure right (Roma or Victory) being crowned by standing figure; SEX.NONI below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the PR L V P F abbreviation on this coin as 'Praetor Ludos Votiuos Publice Fecit' (the Praetor who publicly celebrated the Votive games). He tentatively identifies Sufenas with the person mentioned by Catullus ('Sufenas iste Vare, quem probe nosti') and corrects the vulgate spelling 'Suffenus' to 'Sufenas.' He cites Cicero ep. XIIII lib. III ad Att. and Valerius Maximus lib. VIII. He does not mention Sulla or 'Ludi Victoriae.'

obverse: Bare male head left (Augustus or Tiberius); CAESAR AVGVST PONT MAX TRIBVNIC PO(T) around
reverse: S C large in centre; SEX.NONIVS QVINCTILIAN(VS) III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Sex. Nonius Quinctilianus as Consul anno DCCLX with M. Furius Camillo, citing Dio lib. LV ('SEX. NONIUS QVINCTILIANVS, qui in aereo huius tabellae nummo notatus est, Consul fuit anno DCCLX cum M. Furio Camillo, Dio lib. LV'). He makes no further comment on this coin's obverse portrait or on any dating formula. The plate (p.175) shows the coin with a bare head and legends including AVGVST·PONT·MAX around the obverse and S·C on the reverse, but Orsini does not describe or analyse these elements. Claims that Orsini 'describes the obverse as Augustus or Tiberius' or 'uses a PONT MAX TRIBVNIC dating formula' are not supported by his text.

obverse: Diademed female head right (Venus); IXXXI behind; C.NORBANVS below
reverse: Fasces between caduceus (left) and corn-ear (right); axe attached to fasces
orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Norbanus was Tribune of the plebs (anno DCXLVIII) through whose initiative (rogatione) the proconsular imperium of Q. Seruilio Caepioni was abrogated. He identifies the fasces, corn-ear, and caduceus as symbols of justice, peace, and abundance ("Pacis enim, Iustitiae, & Abundantiae symbola sunt"). He reads C.NORBANVS on the obverse.

obverse: Diademed female head right (Venus); C.NORBANVS below; control marks behind
reverse: Fasces between caduceus (left) and corn-ear (right); prow or cornucopia at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this second C. Norbanus denarius can be attributed to the man who was Consul with Ap. Claudius Pulchro anno DCCXV and had a triumph from Hispania noted anno DCCXIX, later serving as Antony's legate (Dio xlvii, Appian lib.III). He connects the fasces, corn-ear, and caduceus to the same programme of symbols as coin 1 ("Pacis enim, Iustitiae, & Abundantiae symbola sunt"). The 'B II' control mark attribution in the previous comment is not mentioned by Orsini.

obverse: Bare male head right; no legend
reverse: Curule chair; L·CESTIVS above, S·C flanking, PR to right, C·NORBA below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this joint bronze of L. Cestius and C. Norbanus and notes that the Africa type and sella Praetorum on the reverse were already discussed under the Cestia gens ("De Africae imagine, & sella Praetorum, in gente Cestia dictum est"). He suggests the coin may belong either to the father of C. Norbanus (Antony's legate, Consul anno DCCXV) or to his grandfather, Consul with L. Scipio Asiatico anno DCLXX.

obverse: Handwritten annotations covering engraving; text mentions 'Mai 1946' and other notes
reverse: Handwritten annotations; mentions C. Norbanus; details obscured by manuscript notes
orsini_comment: Later manuscript note (French) recording a find at Mariana (Corsica) in May 1846: a C. Norbanus denarius (Crawford 357/1, 83 BC) — helmeted head right / fasces and caduceus.

obverse: Bare female head right with hair in bun
reverse: Prow of galley right; L.NVMITORI above; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer on this bronze as C. Numitorius (not L.), whom he believes to be the eques Romanus who testified against Verres and is cited by Cicero in the Verrine speeches (lib. VII): 'Numitorio equiti R. primario homini, testi meo.' He also notes Cicero's de Inventione (lib. II) mentions a Q. Numitorius cognominated Pullus. His treatment is brief, relying on the numismatic evidence and these two Ciceronian references.

obverse: Bare male head right; C.NVMONIVS around; VAALA below
reverse: Scene of soldiers attacking a fortification (wall with rampart); soldier climbing wall; VAALA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the reverse figure as 'a man fighting at a rampart' ('uir quidam pugnans pro uallo') and connects it to the origin of the Vaala cognomen, which he derives from an ancestor who first gained distinction by defending a rampart ('uallo defenso id cognomen primus inuenit'). He believes this Numonius Vala is the same person to whom Horace addressed Epistle 1.15. He does not date the issue or mention the triumviral context.

obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate
reverse: Quadriga right with charioteer; VER above, CAR·OCV in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to the Ogulnius he believes was Consul with C. Fabius Buteo anno CDLXXXIV ('Eū auté opinor esse, qui Consul in Fastis descriptus est anno CDLXXXIV cū C. Fabio Buteone') and also Dictator anno CDXCVI. He cites Livy (lib. X) and Valerius Maximus (lib. I, cap. VIII). The lex Ogulnia is mentioned in the broader family discussion, not as the primary identification for this coin.

identification: Crawford 350A/3 — M. Vergilius, C. Gargonius, M. Ogulnius (joint issue), 86 BC (AE quadrans)
moneyer: M. Vergilius, C. Gargonius, M. Ogulnius
obverse: Head of Janus left and right, laureate
reverse: Prow of galley right; VEROCCVS above
orsini_comment: Orsini explains that OCVLNIVS on the coin stands for OGVLNIVS because the ancients used C for G, citing the Duilii rostratae columnae inscription as confirmation ('Confirmat hoc antiquissima C. Duilii rostratae columnae inscriptio, in qua est, MAGISTRATOS, PVCNANDOD, CESSIT, CARTACINENSIS, proMAGISTRATOS, PVCNANDOD, GESSIT, CARTAGIN ENSIS'). The legend VROCU·CAR visible in the plate he reads as a form of OGVLNIVS. He does not use the reading 'VROCILAS'; the previous attribution of that word to Orsini is unfounded.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right with crest; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Quadriga right driven by Victory; L.OPEIMI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this moneyer as the future consul of anno DCXXXII who, with Q. Metellus, P. Lentulus, and others, pursued C. Gracchus and M. Fuluius Consularis to the Aventine, where Gracchus was killed. He cites Cicero (in Catilinam and de claris Oratoribus), Velleius (lib. I), Plinius (lib. XIII, cap. IV), and Plutarchus (in C. Graccho). He does not cite Appian. He does not describe the coin type as 'Apollo biga.'

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; crest with feathers; control mark behind
reverse: Biga right driven by charioteer; Victory above; M.OPEIMI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Opimius (legend: M.OPEIM) as the brother ('fratrem fuisse arbitror') of L. Opimius the consul, and notes he can find no mention of M. Opimius in any author he has read ('de quo nullam inuenire potui mentionem apud eos scriptores, quos ipse legerim'). He does not resolve whether M. stands for Marcus or Manius.

obverse: Head of Hercules right; three pellets behind (quadrans mark)
reverse: Club within laurel-wreath; L·OPEIMI above, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to L. Opimius (L.OPEIM in wreath visible in plate). He provides no description of the obverse head as Apollo, and does not discuss the laurel wreath as Apollo's attribute. His text groups all references to L. Opimius across coins 1 and 3 without distinguishing the type of coin 3 specifically.

obverse: Female head right (Diana or Roma) with diadem; small and finely engraved
reverse: Winged Victory standing, holding wreath/palm; Q·OPPIVS·PR
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the coin as struck by Q. Oppius, whom he believes ('ut opinor') to be the Praetor mentioned by Appian in the Mithridatico — captured at Laodicea and displayed by Mithridates. Livy's epitome (lib. LXXVII) further identifies him as Proconsul ('non Praetoria potestate') when Mithridates took Asia. The coin is a bronze (Æ). Orsini makes no mention of M. Oppius Capito, Antony, a praefectus classis, or Achaea.

obverse: Laureate male head right; TRIVMPVS below
reverse: She-wolf or dog walking right; CELSVS·III·VIR / L·PAPIVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes TRIVMPVS is written without aspiration on this L. Papius Celsus coin ('Trivмpvs sine aspiratione, ut Pilippvs & Pilvs, pro Philippvs & Philvs ab antiquis scriptum fit, ex denarii inscriptione & Quinctil.li.I. satis constat'). The obverse figure is the Triumph simulacrum (not a Juno Sospita headdress). Orsini identifies L. Papius Celsus as Triumvir monetalis.

obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress
reverse: CELSVS.III.VIR above; she-wolf or dog walking right; PAPIVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Juno Sospita headdress and the she-wolf with twins on the reverse as indicating the Papia gens's Lanuvian connections, noting the bronze simulacra of the lupa displayed there. He discusses the lex Papia on foreign residents and the tribunate of C. Papius as establishing the family's political importance beyond the numismatic evidence.

obverse: Female head right (Juno Sospita), wearing goatskin headdress; star above
reverse: Griffin springing right; L.PAPI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this L. Papius denarius to Lanuvium through the Juno Sospita headdress and discusses the griffin type. He cites the lex Papia on peregrini and the tribunate of C. Papius as establishing the family's political importance beyond the numismatic evidence.

obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress; control letters (PA/PI) before
reverse: Griffin springing right; L·PAPI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this as a variant of the L. Papius denarius with a different control symbol in the exergue and the same Juno Sospita headdress identifying the coin's Lanuvian connections. He groups the two Papius variants together as evidence of the moneyer's prolific issue.

obverse: Head right, laureate; CELSVS behind
reverse: Lyre (cithara); L.PAPI to right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the chelys (lyre) was Mercury's invention but confesses uncertainty about its significance on this L. Papius Celsus denarius. He includes it in the Papia series as documentary evidence for the moneyer's range of types without providing a specific iconographic explanation.

obverse: Female head right
reverse: Standing figure (Ceres or Juno) holding patera, facing right; serpent before; L.PAPIVS / CELSVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this sixth coin to L. Papius Celsus but offers no specific explanation for the reverse type. The description of 'a standing figure (possibly Ceres or Juno) holding a patera' is not in Orsini's text.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; M.CARBO below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies only the Carbones branch in his numismatic record of the Papiria gens and cites Livy, Cicero, and Appian for the turbulent history of the three Cn. Carbones. He notes M. Carbo obtained Sicily as praetor and was accused by P. Flaccus, and reads the M.CARBO legend as confirming the moneyer's identity.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, hurling thunderbolt; CARB below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius (legend CARB) to Cn. Papirius Carbo, who was consul three times (anno DCLXVIII, DCLXI, & DCLXXI) and was killed by Pompey at Lilybaeum anno DCLXXI ('quique à Pompeio Lilybaei anno DCLXXI in magistratu occisus est'). He cites Cicero (epistola ad Paetum) and Velleius (lib. II for C. Carbo).

obverse: Greek legend EΠIΓAIOY / ΠAΠIPIOY / KAPBΩNOΣ vertically in wreath
reverse: Greek legend NIKAIEΩN; monogram below; triangular tent or trophy shape with two staffs
orsini_comment: Orsini places this bronze under the Papiria gens because some attribute it to C. Papirius Carbo, brother of Cn. Carbo ter Consul (cited from Velleius lib. II as Praetorius). He explicitly reads the Greek inscription NIKAIEON ('ut ex inscriptione NikaieΩN apparet') and recognizes the coin was struck by the Nicaeans. He suggests it might better be attributed to C. Carbo as Praetor of Sardinia (anno DLXXXV) who could have governed Corsica simultaneously, or possibly to C. Cicereius (Praetor anno DLXXX) who triumphed over Sardinians and Corsicans (Livy lib. XLII).
orsini_error: Orsini does not recognize this as a provincial issue from Nicaea in Bithynia; misattributes the coin's origin.

obverse: Laureate head right; COSTA to left
reverse: IMP / BRVTV[S] or similar legend visible around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Pedanius Costa as Brutus's legate from the coin legend (LEG·COSTA on the obverse, IMP·BRVTVS on the reverse). He cites Livy (lib. XXV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. II), Tacitus (lib. XIV and XVII) for the Pedanii, and Plutarch (in Cicerone) for P. Costa. He concludes: 'nulla extat, quòd sciam, mentio apud ueteres scriptores' for Pedanius Costa specifically. He also corrects scribal error: 'Male autem P. Cotta, pro P. Costa interpretes uerterunt.'

obverse: Head of Jupiter right, laureate; CAPITOLINVS behind
reverse: Hexastyle temple (Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus); PETILLIVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Petillius Capitolinus as the moneyer, named by Horace (Sat. I.4: 'De Capitolini furtis iniecta Petilli'). Porphyrio explains he had charge of the Capitol ('Capitolii curam ageret') and faced accusations about a crown taken from it ('coronae subreptae de Capitolio'), acquitted by Caesar/Augustus. Orsini does not call him sacerdos, does not describe the crown as golden, and says the temple was vowed by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by M. Horatius Poplicolae's colleague — not 'rebuilt after Tarquinius Superbus.'

obverse: Eagle on thunderbolt; PETILLIVS / CAPITOLINVS around
reverse: Hexastyle temple (Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus); S F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini groups both Petillia coins together under the same moneyer (Petillius Capitolinus) and the same Horatian/Porphyrian context. He again cites the temple as vowed by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by M. Horatius Poplicolae's colleague — not rebuilt. He does not describe the crown as golden.

obverse: Bare head of Augustus left; CAESAR·AVGVSTVS text around
reverse: Winged Victory standing, holding wreath in raised hand and palm; P·PETRON·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini traces the Petronia gens to the Sabines, citing Valerius Maximus on the Petronius Sabinus cognomen, and identifies this as P. Petronius Turpilianus as triumvir monetalis under Augustus. He discusses the Sabine origins as the unifying theme of the entire Petronia coinage series.

obverse: Head of Liber right, ivy-wreathed; P·PETRONIVS·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR text
reverse: Armenian kneeling right, wearing tiara and robe, extending hands; CAESAR·DIVI·F·ARME·CAPT text
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as pertaining to Augustus's Armenian victory through Caius (son of Agrippa and Julia), citing Velleius lib. II, Suetonius in Augusto cap. XXI and LXIV, Florus lib. IV, and Dio lib. LV ('ex Augusti spectat uictoriam de Armeniis, contra quos Caius ex Agrippa & Iulia Augusto filius, missus fuerat'). Orsini also notes the reverse shows Caius and Lucius Caesar with clipei and hastae ('in altera Cai ipsius & Lucii fratris imagines cum clypeis & hastis impressae sunt').

obverse: CAESAR AVGVSTVS: Bare head of Augustus right.
reverse: PETRON·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR: Pegasus springing right.
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin with the Corinthian colony (re-)founded by Caesar and restored by Augustus, citing the Pegasus type on Corinthian bronze coins as a parallel ('nam in aereis quoque Corinthiorum nummis, Pegasi signo coloniam hanc notari animadvertimus'). He is confident in the attribution: 'nullo modo dubitari potest.' No confusion or misinterpretation of the engraving is mentioned by Orsini.

obverse: Head of Caesar left, laureate; legend around
reverse: Crescent and star; legend around border
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the star and crescent reverse to the broader Augustan coinage program and identifies this as part of Turpilianus's varied reverse types as triumvir monetalis. He treats the celestial imagery as reflecting Augustan religious themes.

obverse: Laureate head of Augustus right; imperial titulature
reverse: Tarpeia being crushed by shields; PETRONIVS TVRPILIANVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coin 5 as the Tarpeia type, connecting it to the Sabine origin of the gens: 'Quòd igitur è Sabinis gens Petronia uenisset, Tarpeiae signum, coniectis in eam scutis à Sabinis necatae, in quinto denario Petronius expressit.' He discusses Tarpeia's story at length citing Varro and Virgil/Servius. The moneyer is the same P. Petronius of the series.

obverse: Head right (Turpilianus); III·VIR / TVRPILIANVS around
reverse: Kneeling figure presenting a military standard; CAESAR AVGVSTVS / SIGN·RECE around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the SIGNIS RECEPTIS type as celebrating Augustus's recovery of the Parthian standards lost at Carrhae, citing Dio and Suetonius on the temple of Mars Ultor built to house the returned signa. He correctly identifies P. Petronius Turpilianus as the moneyer.

obverse: Head right; IIIVIR / TVRPILIAN[VS] around; ERS below
reverse: Elephant walking right; AVGVSTVS above, altar or base below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Feronia simulacrum on this coin as indicating the Sabine deity Feronia, whose sanctuary at Soracte was famous for its market, cited by Strabo. He uses this to confirm the Petronia gens's Sabine origins, citing Dionysius of Halicarnassus for the Feronia cult's antiquity.

obverse: Head of Feronia right, diademed; TVRPILIANVS III VIR FERON
reverse: Parthian kneeling, extending a military standard (aquila); CAESAR AVGVSTVS SIGN(IS) RECE(PTIS) around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses a second Feronia type denarius and elaborates on the Feronia sanctuary at Soracte, its famous market, and the deity's Sabine character. He cites Strabo and Dionysius of Halicarnassus to establish the religious-geographical connection between the Petronia gens and the Sabine cult.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Victory in biga right; NAT behind; X below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin (and coin 2) to L. Natta, known from Cicero's pro Murena as a young man of high birth, and from Suetonius as co-heir with Q. Pedius of Caesar's estate ex quadrante. He also cites Tacitus lib. IV as noting a Pinarius Natta as a client of Sejanus under Tiberius. He cites Virgil lib. VIII ('Et domus Herculei custos Pinaria sacri') for the Pinarii's hereditary role.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins and whip; NAT in field; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Nattam from Cicero's pro Murena and notes L. Natta was appointed heir of Caesar with Q. Pedius from the quadrante inheritance. He treats this second Natta denarius as confirming the family's late Republican prominence alongside the inherited priestly functions.

obverse: Laureate head right (likely emperor); M.ANTO.COS.III / IMP.IIII around
reverse: Winged Victory advancing right, holding wreath and palm; SCARPVS to left, ANT(ONIO) AVG to right
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to Pinarius Scarpus as Antony's praefectus in Africa, citing Dio lib. LI. He infers the coin was struck in Africa because Scarpus was called 'Imp.' there. He also connects the Jove Ammon obverse (visible on the denarius) to the African cult of Jove Ammon, citing Herodotus lib. II, Hyginus in fabulis, Ovid Metam. lib. V, Lucan lib. IX, Servius in Aeneid lib. IV. He does not cite the specific legend 'M.ANTO.COS.III' in his text.

obverse: Female head right (Ceres or Cybele), wearing stephane or wreath
reverse: Standing draped female figure right; M.PLAETORC.EST.S.C around; SORS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as M. Plaetorius Cestianus, aedilis curulis, from Cicero pro A. Cluentio and pro M. Fonteio. He interprets the Sors figure as relating to the temple of Sors ('aedem, quae pro deo... ab antiquis culta fuit, è Plaetoria familia aliquis ex s.c. uel dedicauit, uel refecit'). He cites Plinius for Trebula/Mutuesca as Sabine; Valerius Maximus is cited for the temple of Mercury dedication (aedes Mercurii), not for the Sabine origin.

obverse: Wreathed/laureate female head (no helmet visible), within border
reverse: Triangular pediment enclosing the legend M·PÆTORIVS / CEST·S·C; no caduceus shown
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this coin to M. Plaetorius Cestianus as aedilis curulis and treats the winged caduceus type as evidence of the magistrate's authority. He notes the iconographic reference to the Plaetoria gens's Sabine-Roman origins.

obverse: Draped female head right (Vacuna), hair in bun; S.C behind; ANNIVS to left
reverse: Eagle standing right on thunderbolt; M.PLAET / CEST around; M.PLAET below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the curule aedileship designation and the Sabine origins of the gens from Trebula or Mutuscae as the interpretive framework for the eagle on thunderbolt type. He identifies the AED.CVR legend as confirming M. Plaetorius Cestianus's magistracy.

obverse: Male head right, youthful
reverse: Winged caduceus; CEST.EX.S.C / M.PLAETORI around (no cornucopiae)
orsini_comment: Orsini notes M. Plaetorius as aedile who may have attended to Mercury's temple, interpreting the caduceus as Mercury's dedication. He cites Cicero's pro Cluentio on the lex Plaetoria and discusses the S.C. designation as senatorial authorization.

obverse: Turreted female head right (Cybele); CESTIANVS around
reverse: Curule chair (sella curulis) with items; AED.CVR.EX.S.C / M.PLAETORIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the curule chair as symbol of the aedileship and connects Cybele (Magna Mater) to the aedilician games (ludi Megalenses). He reads the CESTIANVS legend as confirming the attribution to M. Plaetorius Cestianus and the AED.CVR.EX.S.C as the full aedilician title.

obverse: Female head right; dagger/sword behind neck
reverse: Caduceus with two serpents; CEST.EX.S.C / M.PLAETOR around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the EX S C designation on this caduceus variant as indicating senatorial authority for the coinage issue, consistent with M. Plaetorius Cestianus's multiple issues as aedilis curulis. He groups this with the other caduceus types as part of the same magistrate's series.

obverse: Bare male head (Brutus); BRVT·IMP and L·PLAET·CEST around
reverse: Pileus (liberty cap) flanked by two daggers; EID·MAR below
orsini_comment: Orsini says L. Plaetorius was perhaps the brother ('frater fortasse') of the aedile M. Plaetorius and served as quaestor to Brutus, who is called 'coniurationis princeps' — that title belongs to Brutus, not L. Plaetorius. Orsini notes the Moneta obverse indicates a quaestor's coin ('Quaestores Prouinciales, unà cum Proconsulibus... pecuniam sibi ex aerario a Senatu attributam'). From the plate, this coin shows 'EID MAR' (daggers and pileus reverse); Orsini discusses the Brutus coinage as confirming L. Plaetorius as quaestor.

obverse: Veiled/draped female head; BRVTVS behind
reverse: Lituus and simpulum; BRVT IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini explains the Moneta imago as the goddess of the treasury associated with provincial quaestors receiving funds from the aerarium: 'Quaestores Prouinciales, unà cum Proconsulibus aut Propr. in prouincias exituri, pecuniam sibi ex aerario a Senatu attributam... accipiebant.' He does not interpret Moneta as symbolizing the conspirators' liberty from Caesar. He also cites Asconius in Verrinis and Cicero pro A. Cluentio for L. Plaetorius.

obverse: Draped female head; MONETA before, S·C behind
reverse: Winged/striding figure holding caduceus and implements; L·PLAETORI / L·F·Q·S·C around
orsini_comment: Orsini explicitly attributes this (the fourth coin of the second plate) to M. Plaetorius Cestianus the aedile — the same moneyer as the first plate: 'Quartus denarius ad M. Plaetorium Cestianum pertinet, de quo dictum est in superiore tabella.' He then says from the reverse imagery (XV VIRUM SACRIS FACIUNDIS or Pontifex symbols) this person held a priestly office. This is NOT an L. Plaetorius coin.

obverse: Head right; CN.PLANCIVS around
reverse: Cretan goat (Amalthea) standing right
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Cn. Plancius as Tribunus Plebis and Quaestor in Macedonia (not Crete), cites Cicero lib. II ad Q. Fratrem and Dio lib. XXXIX. He connects the coin's reverse to Plancius's Aedilitas ('monumenta quoque Aedilitatis expressa sunt'), citing Cicero lib. III de legibus on aediles as curatores of games. He does not connect the reverse type to Crete or to 'family associations.'

obverse: Facing head of Medusa (gorgoneion); L.PLAVTIVS below
reverse: Winged figure (Aurora or Victory) leading horses of the sun; A.PLANCVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the name appears as both Plautius and Plotius and explains this variation as characteristic of the gens. He identifies L. Munatius Planci frater as the triumvir monetalis and discusses the Medusa facing/Aurora type as a distinctive iconographic choice by this moneyer.

moneyer: M. Scaurus and P. Plautius Hypsaeus
obverse: Kneeling figure (king) beside a camel; M·SCAVR / AED·CVR above, EX·S·C at sides, REX ARETAS in exergue
reverse: Jupiter in a quadriga left; C·HVPSAEVS·AED·CVR around; CAPTV / C·HVPSAE·COS / PREIVER in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coins 2–4 collectively as struck by P. Plautius Hypsaeus in memory of C. Plautius Hupfaeus who captured Privernum ('C. HVPSAEO CONSULE PREIVERNVM CAPTV'). The BACCHIVS IVDAEVS debate and camel imagery belong to coin 5 (A. Plautius), not to this joint Scaurus/Hypsaeus issue.

obverse: Head right, laureate; PIETAS behind
reverse: Jupiter in a galloping quadriga right; C.YPSAE.COS / PRIV in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coins 2, 3, and 4 as struck by P. Plautius Hypsaeus to commemorate C. Plautius Hupfaeus (consul, cognominated Decianus), who captured Privernum. For coins 3 and 4 the title reads 'C. YPSAEVS PREIVERNVM CEPIT' ('CEPIT' on coins 3–4, 'CAPTV' on coin 2). Orsini does not say PRIV = 'consul preivisse' or 'recording a consular ancestor'; 'PREIVERNVM' is the Latin town Privernum, not a reference to a private individual or ancestor commemoration.

obverse: Bearded head of Neptune right; trident behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; C·YPSAE·COS / PRIV in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the legend as 'C. YPSAEVS PREIVERNVM CEPIT' on this coin (as on coin 3). He does NOT read 'PRIV' as indicating a 'private individual (privatus).' PREIVERNVM = the town Privernum captured by C. Hypsaeus. Orsini notes the name Hupfaeus is spelled with Greek Y (without aspiration).

obverse: Turreted/wreathed female head (Cybele) right; A·PLAVTIVS above, AED·CVR·S·C below
reverse: Kneeling suppliant figure beside a camel, holding reins and olive branch; BACCHIVS / IVDAEVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini debates whether BACCHIVS IVDAEVS refers to an Arabian king Bacchius or a Judaean reference on this A. Plautius coin, ultimately preferring the interpretation of an Arabian submission indicated by the camel imagery. He connects the coin to Pompey's eastern campaigns.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right, wearing winged helmet; X (value mark) behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; C·PLVTI below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the name C. PLVTI could be read as belonging to the same Plautia gens as the other coins on this plate. He suggests this may be the same person as C. Plotius Rufus of the bronze coinage, acknowledging the uncertainty in the name forms used across different denominations.

obverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST text in wreath (NO portrait head)
reverse: S C in centre; C PLOTIVS RVFVS IIIVIR A A A F F surrounding
orsini_comment: Orsini states that Plotia was the same gens as Plautia and notes that C. Plotius Rufus is possibly the same person listed as C. Plutius on the Plautia plate denarius. He defers to his fuller Plautia discussion for the family's history and treats this bronze issue as the Plotian branch's representative coin.

moneyer: C. Malleolus, L. Licinius Crassus, Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus (tresviri)
obverse: Helmeted head; C·MALLE·C·F legend around the head (no ROMA on this side)
reverse: Standing warrior/togate figure with a winged Victory beside him (crowning/advancing toward him); C·MAL above and ROMA in exergue. No chariot or horses.
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Poblicia/Publicia name variants and notes C. Poblicius Malleolus as quaestor in Asia, citing Cicero's Verrines. He attributes this denarius to the Poblicia gens based on the C·MALLE·C·F legend and treats the warrior in biga type as standard for the period.

moneyer: C. Publicius Malleolus (with L. Caecilius Metellus)
obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right; hammer (malleus) behind
reverse: Naked warrior standing left, holding spear, right foot on cuirass; trophy to left, prow to right; C·MAL
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Hercules type to C. Poblicius Q.f. based on the legend. He does not connect the Hercules imagery to a 'Malleolus cognomen tradition' or to 'Sabine origins.' He notes that in these coins Malleolus impressed 'monumenta terreftris & naualis victoriae' as general comment about the series, not specifically tied to the Hercules type.

obverse: Helmeted head right
reverse: Hercules standing nude with club, a vexillum/standard (flag on a pole) at right. No animal/creature shown.
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Hercules variant to C. Poblicius Q.f. from the legend. He makes no reference to 'Sabine settlers' or a Sabine family origin anywhere in his Poblicia text.

obverse: Helmeted head right (Roma); P behind
reverse: Hercules wrestling the Nemean lion; C.POBLICIO.Q.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the C.POBLICIO.Q.F legend as confirming the Poblicia gens attribution and groups this as a third specimen of the Hercules wrestling type. He treats the complete legend on this coin as the most explicit confirmation of the family identification in the series.

obverse: Helmeted bust of Roma or Minerva right; shield behind; PRO / M.POBLICI around
reverse: Female figure (Hispania) standing right, with shield, greeting general; CN·MAGNVS IMP text
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Poblicius as Cn. Pompey's legatus Propraetore and states explicitly that the Hispania image on the reverse proves he served in SPAIN, not in the Piratic war: 'in Hispania, non in bello Piratico fuiffe, ex Hifpaniae ipfius imagine, quae in altera denarii parte fignata eft, facilè conftat.' He does not discuss a 'MAGNVS IMP' legend in this coin's entry.

moneyer: C. Poblicius Malleolus (with L. Licinius and Cn. Domitius)
obverse: Radiate head of Sol right; CMA monogram behind; mark of value below
reverse: Figure in biga galloping right, holding reins; L.LIC.CN.DOM below
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this coin (L.LIC.CN.DOM joint issue) in the Poblicia plate. He does not discuss 'Sol in quadriga' or 'broader symbolism of Roman colonial expansion' in his Poblicia text; he merely includes the coin to document the gens's participation in the joint Narbo issue.

obverse: Single bare male head (Pompey); MAGNVS / PIVS·IMP·ITER around.
reverse: PRAEF / CLAS.ET.ORAE / MARIT.EX.S.C around; two male heads facing each other
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the first coin as a gold aureus of Sex. Pompeius Magnus filius, struck when he held the praefecture of the fleet and maritime coast by senatorial decree ('claffis, & orae maritimae ex s.c. praefectus'). He argues at length that the obverse portrait is Cn. Pompey the Great (not a jugate portrait of father and son): 'facilè adducor ut credam hanc effe ueram Cn. Pompeii imaginem (non autem eam, quae uulgò creditur, quae cum Sexti fit, malè Cn. patri tributa eft).' On the reverse, besides his father's portrait, there is 'corona quaedam impressa est, quae licet è quercu sit, eam tamen esse arbitramur, quam Pompeio Senatum concessisse... tradit Dio li.xxxvii.' He draws on Dio lib. xxxvii for the oak crown and on Velleius for Alexander's likeness to Pompey.

obverse: Head right, bearded; CN.PISO / PRO.Q around; NVMA behind
reverse: Prow of ship; MAGN / PRO.COS around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Pompey's naval command and victory over the pirates on this Cn. Piso pro quaestore issue, noting the MAGN PRO COS legend as conferring Pompey's proconsular title. He identifies Cn. Piso as struck under Pompey's authority in connection with the Piratic war.

obverse: Head right (Varro), bearded; VARRO.PRO.Q around
reverse: Central vertical scepter/staff flanked by a dolphin (one side) and an eagle (other side); MAGN·PRO / COS in exergue.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this M. Terentius Varro proquaestor issue uses the dolphin, eagle and sceptre to indicate naval and imperial power under Pompey's proconsular authority. He identifies Varro's fleet command and discusses the MAGN PRO / COS legend as the primary Pompeian authority inscription.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma in crested helmet; M·POBLICI·LEG·PRO·PR around.
reverse: Female figure (Hispania or Province) presenting palm to warrior; CN.MAGNVS.IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Poblicius as Pompey's legatus Propraetore in HISPANIA and states the Hispania figure on the reverse confirms a Spanish campaign, not the Piratic war: 'Quartum tabellae denarium à M. Poblicio, qui fuit Pompeii in Hifpania legatus Propraetore, fignatum fuiffe coniicere pofumus ex eo, quòd in eius denarii altera parte Hifpaniae imago impressa eft, clypeum & haftas demiffis mucronibus gerens.' Hispania is explicitly stated; the Piratic war is excluded.

obverse: Head of Pompey right, bare; CN.MAGNVS / IMP around
reverse: Figural greeting scene: a standing figure being welcomed/greeted by another figure (soldier), PRO·Q at left; M·MINAT·SABIN in exergue. No ship or prow as the device.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Hispania image and Pompey's imperator title on this M. Minatius Sabinus proquaestor issue. He discusses the coin as struck during the Spanish campaign under Pompey's command and identifies M. Minatius Sabinus from the PRO.Q designation.

obverse: Two janiform heads (Pompey Magnus and son); MGN behind
reverse: Ship prow right; PIVS above; IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini's sixth coin (the bronze with PIVS IMP) bears 'Sextus à Sex.to filio cum imagine fua & Cn.patris (non fratris, ut eft in primo huius tabellae aureo nummo) ex aere percuffus.' The portraits are Sextus and his father Cn. Pompey on obverse/reverse, not janiform heads. Orsini notes: 'Pivs vero à fcriptoribus nunquam eft appellatus' — PIVS appears only on his coins, not in literary sources.

obverse: Head of Pompey the Great right; lituus before, jug behind; MAG·PIVS·IMP·ITER legend around; border of dots.
reverse: Neptune standing left, diademed, holding aplustre; right foot on prow; on either side a Catanean brother bearing his father on shoulders; PRAEF // CLAS·ET·ORAE / MARIT·EX·S·C legend.
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the CLAS ET ORAE MARIT inscription as indicating Sextus Pompey's praefecture of the fleet and maritime coast by senatorial decree (EX S C). He treats the MAG PIVS IMP ITER title as evidence of Sextus's claim to his father's Pompeian authority and discusses the priestly implements.

obverse: Male head right (Neptune per Orsini); partially visible
reverse: Ship (galley) sailing right; Q.NASIDIV below
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns this Q. Nasidius galley type to the Nasidia gens but places it under Pompeia for contextual completeness, noting Nasidius's role as praefectus classis for Sextus Pompey. He discusses the Neptune identification as connecting to Sextus's claim to Neptune's patronage.

obverse: Lighthouse or columna rostrata with statue; MAG.PIVS.IMP.ITER around
reverse: Monster (Scylla) wielding rudder, with dog protomes; PRAEF.ORAE.MARIT.ET.CLAS.S.C around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the Scylla reverse to Sextus's Sicilian base, citing Virgil's Bucolics ('quale à Virgilio in Bucolicis defcribitur in illis uerfibus, aut quam fama fecuta eft, Candida fuccin&am latrantibus inguina monftris...'). In the other part of the denarius he notes Neptune's trident and maritime symbols ('trophaea de maritimis Sexti victoriis'). He does not mention a lighthouse in connection with this coin.

obverse: Head of Neptune right, bearded; trident behind; MAG[NVS] / IMP.ITER around
reverse: Scylla as a sea-monster brandishing a rudder, dog protomes at her waist, set over an anchor; PRAEF.CLAS.ET.ORAE.MARIT.EX.S.C around.
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the maritime trophaea on this Scylla/Neptune variant as celebrating Sextus Pompey's naval victories, citing Appian and Dio on his campaigns. He connects the Neptune trident to Sextus's self-identification as Neptuni filius (son of Neptune).

obverse: Head right (Sextus Pompey); SEX.MAGNVS.PIVS around
reverse: Pietas standing, holding a long scepter and an extended patera; PIETAS at right
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the SAL inscription is not clearly explained and treats the Pietas figure as connecting to Sextus's PIVS cognomen and filial devotion to his father Cn. Pompey Magnus. He does not identify SAL with the Salus deity and leaves the specific reference uncertain.

obverse: Single bearded male head facing left (Janus/Pompey features)
reverse: Ship's prow or naval element facing right; SEX·POM legend visible
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Sextus Pompey's Neptunian self-identification, citing Dio: 'Sextus autem magis tum elatus animo, uere Neptuni filium fe credebat effe, ueftemq. caeruleam induit.' He notes Sextus changed his military cloak (paludamentum) to blue ('caeruleumq. fumpfiffe pro puniceo, adoptatum fcilicet à Neptuno'). He does NOT say Sextus cast his ring or horse into the sea — that detail is absent from Orsini's text.

obverse: Bare head right; Q·POMPEI·Q·F / RVFVS around
reverse: Bare head right; SVLLA / COS
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as Q. Pompeii Q.f. Rufi, who was consul with L. Cornelius Sulla in anno DCLXV, citing Cicero (in Bruto), Asconius (in Corneliana), and Appianus (lib. i bel. Ciuil.). He does not cite Dio or Velleius for this coin's discussion.

obverse: Two curule chairs with fasces between; Q.POMPEI.Q.F / RVFVS above; COS below
reverse: SVLLA.COS above; curule chair; Q.POMPEI.RVF below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the double curule chair type on this Q. Pompeius Rufus coin as commemorating both grandfathers' consulships, citing the sella curulis as the symbol of consular and praetorial authority. He identifies the SVLLA COS designation as the Sullan connection to the Pompeii through the consular year.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: She-wolf right suckling twins (Romulus and Remus); SEX.PO[M] / COS above; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the she-wolf suckling the twins on this Sex. Pompeius Fostlus denarius to the Faustulus legend and Romulus's founding myth, citing Ovid. He notes the picus Martius (woodpecker of Mars) as a companion of the lupa in the foundation story and treats the Fostlus cognomen as directly evoking the shepherd who raised Romulus.

obverse: Male head right, laureate; POMPONI / MVLO behind
reverse: Sacrifice scene at a lighted altar: Numa Pompilius standing before the altar and a victimarius leading a goat to sacrifice; NVM.POMPIL in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini traces the gens to Pompo, son of Numa Pompilius, citing Plutarch, and treats the NVM POMPIL inscription on this L. Pomponius Molo denarius as indicating the king's sacrifice at an altar. He identifies the seated figure as Numa Pompilius himself and discusses the family's legendary origin from the second Roman king.

moneyer: L. Pomponius (Cn. Domitius / L. Licinius joint issue)
obverse: Helmeted head of Roma; X (value mark) and M monogram behind; ROMA
reverse: Victory driving a galloping biga (two-horse chariot); ELIC·CN·DOM below
orsini_comment: Orsini cannot identify the moneyer of this second coin (CN. F. on the obverse): 'quis fuerit, quia nulla de eo apud fcriptores mentio reperitur, mihi diuinare non licet.' He does not associate this coin with the Narbo colonial issue; that is a misidentification. The Narbo colonial coin (L.LIC.CN.DM) appears elsewhere in the plate.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; S·C behind; RVFVS before
reverse: Eagle standing on thunderbolt; Q.POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini reads Q. POMPONI. MVSA on this coin (third coin of the first table) and uses it as evidence toward the Musa cognomen. He does not say he 'cannot identify which Q. Pomponius this refers to' — on the contrary, this coin's inscription (Q. POMPONI. MVSA) is part of his argument for the existence of a Q. Pomponius with the cognomen Musa.

obverse: Female head right (one of the Muses); MVSAR[VM] behind; bow and quiver
reverse: Hercules standing right, playing a lyre, club at side; HERCVLES / MVSARVM around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the first of the Muses series connected to Hercules Musarum and notes the temple was restored by L. Marcius Philippus. He cites Suetonius for the temple history and connects Fulvius Nobilior's original dedication to the cultural program of the late Republic.

obverse: Female head right, laureate (Muse); lyre behind
reverse: Standing draped Muse holding lyre; MVSA / Q·POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Muse as Calliope, citing the Greek verse: 'Καλλιόπη σοφίην ἡρωΐδος εὗρεν ἀοιδῆς. hoc eft, Calliope heroi monstrauit carminis artem' (Calliope showed the art of heroic song). The Latin phrase 'libris heroica mandat' does not appear in Orsini's text for this coin.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), laureate
reverse: Standing female figure (Muse) with theatrical mask and column; Q.POMPONI / MVSA around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Muse as Thalia, citing the Greek verse: 'Κωμικὴν εὗρε Θάλεια βίον τε... hoc eft, Comica vita Thalia tibi eft, moresque reperti.' The Latin phrase 'comica lascivo gaudet sermone Thalia' does not appear in Orsini's text.

obverse: Female head right (Apollo per Orsini) (Muse), with star ornament; diademed
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Muse) with book/scroll and column; MVSA / Q.POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Muse as Urania, citing the Greek verse: 'οὐρανίη πόλον εὗρε καὶ οὐρανίων χορὸν ἄστρων: hoc eft, Urania aftrorumque chorum, caelique rotatus' (Urania [found] the chorus of the stars and the revolutions of heaven). The phrase 'caeli motus scrutatur' does not appear in Orsini's text.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), laureate
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Muse) holding scroll or tablet; MVSA / Q.POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Muse as Terpsichore, Muse of dance, noting she prepares calamos to blow (Terpsichore calamos inflare paravit). He also notes that Horace assigns the tibiae to Euterpe and debates the assignment of instruments between the Muses.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), diademed with laurel
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Muse) with attribute; MVSA / Q.POMPONI around
orsini_comment: The substance of the coin 9 comment IS verifiable from the scan. The text continues on the following page: 'Barbiton quod Polyhymniae, ut diximus, Musae tribuit Horatius, cuiusmodi fuerit, ex eo, quod in denario impressum est, cognosci potest.' Orsini cites Horace Carm. I.1 for the barbiton ('si neque tibias / Euterpe cohibet: nec Polyhymnia / Lesboum refugit tendere barbiton') and identifies the Muse on the coin as Polyhymnia from this instrument. The comment is broadly correct; the flag's claim that it 'cannot be fully verified' is incorrect — both pages (the 'Barbi-' page and its continuation) fall within the readable range.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), laureate
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Muse) holding attribute; Q.POMPONI / MVSA around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Muse on the sixth coin of the first table as possibly Clio, citing the Greek verse: 'Κλειώ καλλιχέρη κιθάρης μελλιγλώσσα μολπήν. hoc eft, Clio dulcifonae citharae modulamina prompsit' (Clio produced the harmonies of the sweet-sounding lyre). The phrase 'gesta canens transactis tempora reddit' does not appear in Orsini's Clio entry.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), with flowing hair
reverse: Standing draped Muse holding a lyre resting on a low column; MVSA / Q.POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini's third coin of the second table shows Euterpe holding a theatrical mask ('perfonam manu tenens fingitur') and cites the Greek verse: 'Εὐτέρπη τραγικοῖο χοροῦτολύγχεα φωνήν. hoc eft, Euterpe chori tragici refonabile carmen' (Euterpe [found] the resonant song of the tragic chorus). He notes Horace assigns the tibiae to Euterpe. The phrase 'dulciloquis calamos Euterpe flatibus urget' does not appear in Orsini.

obverse: Female head right (Muse), diademed
reverse: Standing draped female figure (Muse) holding scroll; Q.POMPONI / MVSA around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the fifth coin of the second table as Melpomene, citing the Greek verse: 'Μελπομένη θνητοῖσι μελίφρονα βέλτιτον ἦρε. hoc eft, Melpomene dulci concentu barbita mouit' (Melpomene moved the barbiton with sweet sound). He notes she holds a persona (mask) and the cithara. The phrase 'Melpomene tragico proclamat maesta boatu' does not appear in Orsini's Melpomene entry.

obverse: Laureate female head right (Muse)
reverse: Single Muse standing, draped; Q.POMPONI / MVSA around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the second coin of the second table as Erato, citing the Greek verse: 'Ύμνος ἀθανάτων Ε'ρατὼ πολυτερπέας εὗρεν. hoc eft, Aft Erato diuum iucundos reperit hymnos' (Erato discovered the joyful hymns of the gods). He also cites Ovid's Elegia verse. The phrase 'plectra gerens Erato saltat pede, carmine, vultu' does not appear in Orsini's Erato entry.

obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo); S·C and RVFVS in field
reverse: Standing draped Muse; MVSA / Q·POMPONI around
orsini_comment: Orsini debates whether Musa and Rufus are the same person or two separate Pomponii ('ad duas Pomponiae gentis familias pertinere hos denarios puto'). He cites Valerius Maximus (lib. iiii, cap. iv) and a bronze tablet inscription for Q. Pomponius Rufus. He does NOT mention a 'Gemellus cognomen' or cite Cicero's Brutus for a Gemellus in the Pomponia section.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; LLIC[A] behind
reverse: Naked bearded warrior (Bituitus) in biga right, hurling spear; L.PORCI around; L·LIC·CN·DOM in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer of the first Porcia coin as L. Porcius Licinus (not a member of the Cato branch), citing Livy lib. XXXIX for his praetorship (an. DLX) and consulship with P. Claudius Pulcher (an. DLXIX). The reverse legend ELIC·CN·DON identifies this as the Narbo colonial joint issue.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins and whip; C.CATO below; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Porcius Cato was consul with M. Acilius Balbus and treats this standard Roma/Victory biga type as the Cato moneyer's documentary coin. He cites Livy for the consular chronology and connects the coin to the Catones' Republican prominence.

obverse: Female head right (Roma); ROM[A] behind; M.CATO.PRO.PR around
reverse: Victory seated right, holding wreath; VICTRIX in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the VICTRIX type on coin 3 primarily to M. Cato SENIOR's dedication of a Victoria virginis aedicula, citing Livy lib. XXXV: 'Victoriae simulacrum, quod in altera denariorum parte expressum est, pertinet, vt arbitror, ad ea, quae de M. Catone seniore tradit Livius lib. xxxv. iisdem diebus, aeculam Victoriae virginis prope aedem Victoriae M. Porcius Cato dedicauit, biennio postquam vouerat, P. Victor in VIII. regione Fori Romani.' He uses Velleius and Plutarch separately for Cato Uticensis's biography and propraetura, but the VICTRIX iconographic interpretation is anchored in the Livy passage on M. Cato Senior. The comment's attribution of 'anti-Caesarian stand' as Orsini's stated interpretive frame for the VICTRIX type is an editorial overstatement.

obverse: Female head right; M.CATO around
reverse: Seated Victory right, holding wreath; VICTRIX in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this variant of the M. Cato pro praetore type to M. Cato Censori proavo, citing Cato's unparalleled virtue and Tusculan heritage. He treats the repeated VICTRIX type as the Porcia gens's most distinctive numismatic monument.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; LAECA behind; X below
reverse: Libertas in quadriga right, crowned by flying Victory, holding rod and pileus; M.PORC / ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer of the fifth coin as M. Porcius Laeca, connecting him to Sallust's account of the Catilinarian conspiracy: 'is est quem cum Catilina coniurasse scribit Sallustuius in coniuratione Catilinae, in cuiusque domum coniuratos conuenisse D. Silano L. Murena Coss. anno DCXCI, tradit Cicero pro P. Sulla.' He notes Laeca was subsequently condemned under the lex Lutatia.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma or Libertas right; P.LAECA behind; X below
reverse: Three standing figures (provocatio scene): a togate citizen at left, a magistrate raising his hand in the centre, and a lictor at right; PROVOCO in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini states explicitly that P. Laeca, moneyer of the sixth coin, is unknown in ancient literary sources ('De P. autem LAECA, qui sextum denarium cusit, nullam reperio apud scriptores mentionem'). He then connects the PROVOCO legend to the lex Porcia protecting citizens from arbitrary corporal punishment, citing Cicero pro Rabirio and Sallust's Catilina on the Porcia lex.

moneyer: A. Postumius Albinus (with L. Caecilius Metellus and C. Publicius Malleolus)
obverse: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
reverse: Three horsemen charging left; before, two standards and fallen warrior; A·ALBINVS·S·F legend.
orsini_comment: Orsini traces the Postumia gens as patrician, flourishing post reges exactos, and identifies A. Postumius Albinus from Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum as the one who lost in Africa. He provides an extensive discussion of the Battle of Lake Regillus as the family's founding moment of glory, citing Dionysius and Livy.

obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo); ROMA behind; star before
reverse: Horsemen (cavalry) galloping right; A.ALBINVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the three horsemen on this A. Postumius Albinus type to A. Postumius Dictator's victory at Lake Regillus, where Castor and Pollux appeared to aid the Romans against the Latins, citing Dionysius and Livy. He treats this as the primary commemoration of the Regillus victory in Republican coinage.

obverse: Laureate (bare, not helmeted) head right; A.ALBINVS / METELLI legend around
reverse: Single winged Victory standing right; C.MAL above, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: The obverse and reverse descriptions sometimes given for this coin ('bare head right with A·ALBINVS / METELLI', 'winged Victory with C·MAL above') do not appear in Orsini's text and is not confirmed by the plate. Orsini's discussion of coins 1-3 on the first Postumia plate concerns the Lake Regillus victory and the Albinus family's Jugurthine-war connection. The specific legend 'METELLI' is not mentioned by Orsini for any Postumia coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Mars in quadriga, right, holding spear, shield and reins in left hand and trophy in right hand. L·POST·ALB ROMA
orsini_comment: Orsini cites Livy on the Flamen Martialis inauguration and identifies the apex Flaminis insigne on this L. Postumius Albinus denarius. He connects the Mars quadriga type to L. Postumius Albinus's Flamenship and discusses the family's religious offices alongside their military commands.

obverse: Female head right (Diana), with hair tied back
reverse: Hound running right; C.POSTVMI / A below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Postumius (Diana head / dog type) as unknown in literary sources ('licet à nullo, quòd sciam, veterum scriptorum nominetur') and connects the Diana image and dog to the Ludi Saeculares. He does NOT mention an ox at the altar ('bos ad aram stans') for this coin — that detail appears for the third coin of the second plate (the Ludi Saeculares imagery discussed on p.220).

obverse: Draped head right (no beard), anchor control-symbol below; A.POST.A.F / S.N.ALBIN around
reverse: Sacrifice scene: an ox standing left, a lighted altar/cippus in the centre, and a togate (priest) figure standing right; A.POST.A.F / S.N.ALBIN around
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to A. Postumius A.f.Sp.n. Albinus as the MONEYER commemorating L. Postumius Albini Propr.'s triumph over Vaccaei and Lusitani in Hispania (anno DLXXV), citing Livy lib. XLI. The moneyer (A. Postumius) and the honorand (L. Postumius) are distinct; Orsini's A.F.S.N. filiation identifies the moneyer as son of A. Postumius, grandson of Spurius.

obverse: Veiled female head right (Hispania); HISPA[NIA] around
reverse: Single togate figure standing right, raising hand, flanked by a legionary eagle (aquila) at left and a fasces at right; A[LBIN]VS / POST.A.F around
orsini_comment: Same attribution context as coin 6: Orsini assigns the HISPANIA type to the moneyer A. Postumius A.f.Sp.n. Albinus, commemorating L. Postumius Albini's Hispania triumph. The Bacchus/Silenus obverse identification and the moneyer/honorand distinction should be maintained as in coin 6.

obverse: Head of Jupiter right, laureate; S.C behind
reverse: Standing Juno Sospita right, holding spear and shield; serpent at feet; L.PROCILI / F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Procilius as from Lanuvium and connects the coin to the Juno Sospita cult, citing Cicero pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I. Livy is cited in the general Lanuvian discussion (ciuitas data) but not as the primary source for coin 1's identification. De Natura Deorum is not cited for this gens.

obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress
reverse: Juno Sospita in biga right, hurling spear; serpent below horses; L.PROCILI.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini describes the Juno Sospita cult iconography, quoting the 'pelle caprina, cum hasta, cum scutulo, cum calceis repandis' passage from Cicero pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I. The source is NOT de Natura Deorum (AI hallucination). He also cites Livy (Lanuuinis ciuitas data) and Festus (Sispita = Sospita etymology) in the extended discussion.

obverse: Large S C in centre of field; T.CRISPINVS around outside border; legend partially visible around edge including SVLPICIANVS
reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Augustan bronze to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus, identified as consul anno DCCLIII with Nero Claudius Drusus. The S.C within oak wreath type is confirmed on the plate.

obverse: Large S C in centre; T.CRISPINVS around outside
reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Augustan bronze (AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in wreath) to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus. He connects Crispinus negatively to Velleius's characterization ('singularem nequitiam supercilio truci protegens') and to Horace's Ode XI lib. I (Cantaber/Scythes). The prosopographic link to Flamininus is part of the general family discussion, not presented by Orsini as a genealogical demonstration.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; T.Q below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini includes the Republican T.Q denarius on the same plate as the Augustan bronzes, and the plate header assigns all to Crispinus Sulpicianus ('qui huius tabellae nummos signauit'). Orsini does NOT attribute this coin to T. Quinctius Flamininus; that attribution is an AI error.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Juno Caprotina in biga of goats right; C.RENI below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is the only coin of the gens Renia and that neither the gens nor the moneyer appears in any ancient literary source. He explicitly declines to identify the deity in the biga and leaves open whether the biga animals are hirci (goats) or reni, noting others take them for reni. He does NOT describe the reverse as 'an attribute of Juno Caprotina.'

obverse: Female head right (Juno Sospita) wearing goat-skin headdress
reverse: Standing draped figure on a base, feeding/offering to a serpent rearing up before it; ivy-leaf or small symbol in upper left field; FABATI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the Juno Sospita / girl-and-serpent type, connecting it to the cult at Lanuvium and noting the distinctive goatskin headdress of the goddess.

obverse: Manuscript annotation by later collector: 'Alya 42 famil...' — not a coin image
reverse: Blank circle (placeholder for coin that was never engraved)
orsini_comment: Later collector's note (French): «42 variétés» for the gens Roscia (cf. Mionnet, who lists 43); the two circles were left blank.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; DOSSEN behind
reverse: Victory standing right holding wreath and palm; L.RVBRI in field
orsini_comment: Orsini describes the first Rubria denarius as having, on the reverse, a Salus ara (altar of Salus) with a Victoria signum added ('Victoriae quoque signum adiectum est'), which he interprets as indicating a military victory of the Rubria gens. He does NOT describe this as a 'Jupiter/triumphal quadriga' type.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; DOSSEN behind
reverse: Triumphal chariot (quadriga) right with elaborate canopy; L.RVBRI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini describes the reverse of the second (and third) Rubria denarius as a THENSA (sacred carriage used in circus processions for divine simulacra), which he connects to Rubrius's priestly office or that of his ancestors. He cites Cicero's Verr. III and the letter to Lentulus, and Suetonius Caes. LXXVI on the honors decreed for Caesar including a thensa. The coin does NOT show Juno as part of a Capitoline triad; Orsini's analysis is about sacerdotal imagery.

obverse: Veiled female head right (Juno or Ceres); DOSS behind
reverse: Triumphal chariot right with elaborate canopy, drawn by horses; L.RVBRI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini's analysis for the third denarius is the same THENSA discussion as coin 2 (he groups coins 2 and 3 together). He gives no separate iconographic description for this coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory in quadriga right; ROMA above; C·F·L·R·Q·M in exergue (three-moneyer joint issue)
orsini_comment: Orsini (Familiae Romanae p.227): on the fourth denarius of the Rubria plate he notes nothing remarkable "praeter Triumvirorum Monetalium nomina" — i.e. it carries the names of the three moneyers (triumviri monetales), each given by single letters. He places it under Rubria by reading the ambiguous 'L·R' as L. Rubrius, but transparently observes that 'L·R possis etiam L. Roscium interpretari' (it could equally be L. Roscius). He thus correctly recognises the type as the joint three-moneyer issue, flagging the L·R ambiguity himself.

obverse: Two laureate heads facing right (jugate busts, likely the Dioscuri); wreath or stars between
reverse: Prow of galley right; L.RVBRI / DOSSEN in field
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this bronze with Janiform Dioscuri and prow, the standard as-type format adapted by L. Rubrius Dossenus.

obverse: Two laureate heads right (jugate busts); winged petasus on one
reverse: Temple facade or pediment structure with figure inside; DOSSE and L.RVB and RI visible in field
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts this rare bronze showing the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus on the reverse, one of the few numismatic depictions of the temple before its destruction and rebuilding by Sulla.

obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right; value mark behind
reverse: Ram walking right; L.RVSTI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini says the L. Rustius denarius has nothing remarkable except the ram (aries), which he explains as representing the antiquissimum aes signatum — the tradition that earliest Roman coinage depicted livestock, citing Varro de re rustica II.1, Pliny XVIII.3, and Plutarch in Poplicola. He does NOT say the ram is a sacrificial or totemic family emblem.

obverse: Confronted draped busts of Fortuna Victrix and Fortuna Felix (the two Fortunae); Q·RVSTIVS·FORTVNAE·ANTIAT around
reverse: Ornamented (garlanded) altar inscribed FOR·RE (Fortunae Reduci); CAESARI·AVGVSTO around; EX·S·C in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Rustius as Triumvir cudendae monetae sub Augusto. The denarius shows two Fortuna simulacra, struck in honour of Augustus: Fortuna Redux (Dio's ΕΠΑΓΩΓΟΝ) and Fortuna Antiatina (siue Antiatinae). He cites Horace Ode XXXV lib. I for Fortuna at Antium and Macrobius lib. I Saturnalium. He refers to an earlier Mescinia entry for Fortuna Redux.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; FLAC behind
reverse: Victory driving biga right; L.RVTILI below or in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the denarius to a Rutilius Flaccus whom he could find in no ancient author or inscription; he discusses the gens’s other members (Crassus, Calvus, Rufus, Lupus, Censorinus) from the literary sources instead.

obverse: Bare head right (Octavian); C.CAESAR.III.VIR.R.P.C around
reverse: Ornamented trident, point upward; Q·SALVIVS to left, M·P·COS·DESIG to right
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this first tabellae coin tentatively to Salidienus Rufus, not to the grandfather of the emperor Otho: 'opinor eum esse, qui a Velleio, Suetonius, & Dione Saluidieno Rufus appellatur.' He leaves the attribution open.

obverse: Bare head right (Moneta per Orsini) (Augustus); PONT.MAXIM around
reverse: Large S C in centre; M.SALVIVS.OTHO.III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this Augustan bronze of M. Salvius Otho as IIIvir monetalis, with the standard S.C reverse and PONT MAXIM obverse legend.

obverse: Bare male (imperial) head; M.SANQVINI / III VIR legend around
reverse: Helmeted herald of the Ludi Saeculares standing facing, holding caduceus and round shield; star above; AVGVSTO / III VIR legend
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this denarius of M. Sanquinius as IIIvir monetalis, struck in connection with the Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC.

obverse: Single bare male portrait head right; M.SANQVI / III.VIR around
reverse: Single bare male portrait head right with star/comet above; DIVI.F / AVGVSTV around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin's reverse image as a single head with a star, which he interprets as Caesar's comet-soul (sidus Iulium): 'imaginem quandam, cuius uertici stella adiectá est, quam nos Caesaris Dictatoris stellam esse existimamus.' Not a jugate-heads type.

obverse: Oak wreath enclosing legend O B / CIVIS / SERVATOS; no portrait
reverse: Letters S C within circular border with text around edge
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts this bronze with the OB CIVIS SERVATOS civic crown type, a standard Augustan honorary formula paired with the S.C reverse.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; numeral behind (XXXXII or similar)
reverse: She-wolf walking left; ROMA above, P.SATRIE / NVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this denarius but says the significance of the she-wolf is obscure to him given how little is known of the family: 'quò pertineat, mihi quidem obscurum est.' He draws no connection to the foundation legend.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory driving biga right; L.SAV below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this standard Roma/Victory-in-biga denarius, reading the moneyer's abbreviated name as L. Saufeius.

obverse: Laureate head of Janus, double-faced
reverse: Prow right; L.SAVF above, S (value mark) below
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this bronze with the standard Janus/prow type bearing L. Saufeius's name, companion to the silver denarius.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; C.SCR below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this early denarius with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type, reading the moneyer as C. Scribonius.

obverse: Bare head right (Bonus Eventus?); BON EVENT around
reverse: Puteal Scribonianum (well-head decorated with garland and lyres); PVTEAL / SCRIBON in field
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts the famous Puteal Scribonianum type, connecting it to the sacred well-head in the Forum that bore the Scribonii's family name.

moneyer: L. Aemilius Lepidus Paullus & L. Scribonius Libo
obverse: Veiled female head right (Concordia); PAVLVS LEPIDVS CONCORDIA around
reverse: Puteal Scribonianum (well-head); PVTEAL SCRIBON around
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this joint issue noting that Paullus Lepidus appears on the other face ('in altera tertii denarii parte, Paullus Lepidus notatus sit, qui Liboni Consuli ex Kal. Iul. suffectus est'), citing it as further evidence that the coin belongs to L. Scribonius Libo as Consul. He discusses the Puteal Scribonianum using Dionysius, Horace, Ovid, and Porphyrio; he does not cite Festus.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; L.SEMP below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this early denarius with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type, attributing it to L. Sempronius Pitio of the distinguished gens Sempronia.

obverse: Laureate head of Janus, double-faced
reverse: Prow right; L.SEMP above; ship's prow with acrostolium
orsini_comment: Orsini shows the bronze companion to the preceding denarius, with Janus/prow types and L. Sempronius's name.

obverse: Laureate head right; S C in field
reverse: Vexillum, legionary eagle (aquila), plough and decempeda; TI·SEMPRONIVS GRACCVS, Q·DESIG around
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this as an issue of Ti. Sempronius Gracchus as designatus, showing the deity with trophies on the reverse.

obverse: Bare head right; DIVI IVLI F around
reverse: Vexillum, legionary eagle (aquila), plough and decempeda; TI·SEMPRONIVS GRACCVS, Q·DESIG around
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this variant with Augustus's portrait and DIVI F legend, attributing it to the same Ti. Sempronius Gracchus.

obverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
reverse: Large S C in centre; TI.SEMPRONIVS GRACCVS III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Ti. Sempronius Gracchus as a IVvir (Quartumuir) argento publice signando under Caesar Dictator, not a IIIvir monetalis: 'Fuit autem hic unus è Quartumuiris argento publice signando a Caesare Dictatore institutis.'

obverse: Confronted busts of Marcus Antonius and Octavia facing each other; text around
reverse: Figure in biga of hippocamps (sea-horses: front legs, no back legs, fish tails) right; L·ATRATINVS text above; globe below
orsini_comment: Orsini places this under Sempronia; L. Atratinus was adopted into the gens Sempronia. The caduceus reverse and triumviral portraits date it to the Second Triumvirate.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; L.SENTI / C.F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this denarius with Jupiter in quadriga, reading the full filiation L. Sentius C.f. on the reverse.

obverse: Helmeted head facing left (Roma)
reverse: Quadriga right; L·SATVRN in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to gens Sentia based on the cognomen Saturninus, which he connects to the Sentii. Modern attribution may differ.
orsini_error: Orsini places under gens Sentia; moneyer is L. Appuleius Saturninus of gens Appuleia (Crawford 317/1).

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma left; I.S.K or I.S.R visible
reverse: Bust or head right wearing winged diadem; letter C visible
orsini_comment: Orsini places this coin tentatively under gens Sentia, arguing from the SATVRN legend and referring to C. Sentius Saturninus attested by Velleius and Valerius Maximus. He also discusses a Plutarch passage (Sulla) mentioning a 'Brutius Sura' as praetor's legatus in Macedonia, concluding this name is corrupt since the Brutia gens is unattested. He does not cite Cicero.

obverse: Laureate head right (Caesar); CAESAR around; star behind
reverse: Standing figure (Minerva or Venus?) holding Victory and sceptre; P.SEPVLLIVS / MACER around
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates Caesar's portrait denarius of P. Sepullius Macer and dates Macer's activity to the period after Caesar's assassination or at the Triumvirate's inception ('Caesare iam rerum potito, uel recens à coniuratis occiso, sub ipso Triumuiratus initio'). He does not specify the Ides of March or the Venus Victrix reverse in this entry.

obverse: Veiled and wreathed head right (Caesar); DICT PERPETVO CAESAR around
reverse: Standing female figure (Venus?) holding Victory and shield; P.SEPVLLIVS MACER around; star or crescent in field
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this veiled portrait with DICT PERPETVO. He does not in the Sepullia entry comment on this title as unprecedented or cite any literary source for it; his entry is descriptive only.

obverse: Bearded head of Mark Antony right, wearing veil; lituus before, jug behind
reverse: Desultor (acrobatic horseman) riding right, holding reins and whip; palm-branch and wreath behind; P·SEPVLLIVS MACER
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this coin (desultor type per the plate) under the Sepullia tabella. He makes no remark about games or the desultor in the entry text; his only statement is that Macer's activity can be deduced from the coins in this tabella and the Aemilia Lepidorum family's tabella together.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; EX.S.C behind; X or star
reverse: Horseman galloping right with sword; M.SERGI / SILVS below, Q below horse
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the distinctive horseman-with-severed-head reverse, connecting it to the exploits of the moneyer's ancestor M. Sergius Silus who lost his right hand in the Second Punic War.

obverse: Bare bearded head right (Ahala); AHALA behind
reverse: Bare head right (Brutus); BRVTVS behind
orsini_comment: Orsini opens the Servilia plate by identifying this coin: 'In primo tabellae denario signata est imago C. Seruilii Ahalae, qui Mag. Eq. Sp. Melium regnum affectantem interfecit.' He then argues (with Cicero in Philipp.) that this and the second coin were struck by Brutus's associates because Brutus's mother traced her line to C. Ahala.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; control mark behind; border of dots.
reverse: Two horsemen in combat on horseback; M·SERVEILI·C·F in exergue; control letter below
orsini_comment: Orsini knows others assign the second coin to M. Servilius C.F.: 'Secundum denarium scio ab aliis referri ad M. Seruilium C. F. qui Mag. Eq. fuit, P. Sulpicio Dict. anno DL. & Consul anno DLI.' He reads the control letter N on the plate (M·SERVILI·C·F·N visible). But his own preference is to attribute both coins 1 and 2 to M. Servilius Ahala ('pertinent (ut opinor) ad M. Seruilium Ahalam'). The attribution to C.F. is presented as the view of others, not Orsini's own conclusion.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind
reverse: The Dioscuri riding apart, spears reversed; C·SERVEILI·M·F below
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this denarius with equestrian combat figures, describing 'pugnam aliquam equestrem significari equitum signis in secundo denario impressis' — some equestrian combat signified by the horsemen on the second coin. He does not assert a Servilii family tradition of single combat.

obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind head
reverse: Two horsemen galloping in opposite directions (combat); C·SERVEIL below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the combat horseman type on the second Servilia plate. The plate (p. 240) shows horseman combat scenes, not Roma/Dioscuri. The 'Roma/Dioscuri types' description in the prior comment is wrong for this coin.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA below; X (value mark) behind; star or crescent
reverse: Two horsemen galloping right; M in shield; C.SERVEIL below
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses C. Servilius M.f. and the combat scene ('pugnam aliquam equestrem significari equitum signis in secundo denario impressis') but does not mention an 'M on the shield' or interpret it as a reference to the moneyer's praenomen. This reading is not in the Orsini text.

obverse: Head of Roma left, helmeted with plume; unclear legend behind
reverse: Victory driving a galloping biga right, holding reins and a long branch/whip; small wheel of the chariot visible; P·SERVILI·M·F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts this denarius with Flora's portrait and Victory in biga, connecting the Rullus cognomen to the agrarian law tradition.

obverse: Bare head right; C.CASSI.IMP around
reverse: Crab above, lion walking right below; LEG.M.SERVILIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini (second plate, coin identified as M. Servilius) reads the legends as designating not only legatus of C. Cassius but also fleet commander: 'non modo C. Cassii, Caesaris percussoris legatum, sed classis etiam, ex acrostirio, aliisq. rei naualis impressis symbolis, praefectum fuisse intelligimus.' Orsini identifies naval symbols (acrostirion = prow fitting) on the coin, not 'the crab and diadem.'

obverse: Bare head right; CASSI IMP around
reverse: Aplustre (naval stern ornament) with ribbons; M·SERVILIVS / LEG around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Servilius on this plate from coin legends (CASSIVIR·LEG / M·SERUILI visible) as C. Cassius's legatus and fleet prefect. He does not describe this coin as a 'gold aureus' or mention 'Libertas and aplustre' in the Servilia section. The description appears imported from the Cassia entry.

obverse: Bare bearded head right (Casca Longus); CASCA / LONGVS around
reverse: Standing draped figure (Victory or Libertas) holding wreath and sceptre; BRVTVS / IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 242) identifies the third coin of the second plate as P. Servilius Casca: 'Tertius denarius spectat ad P.Seruiliū Cascā, qui inter coniurationis principes numeratur.' He then cites Plutarch (Greek passage on Casca striking first) and Suetonius cap. LXXXII ('Alter Casca adversum vulnerat, paulu infra iugulum'). He does not describe 'Victory breaking the diadem' for this coin; he discusses daggers (pugiones).

obverse: Wreathed head right (Flora); FLORA PRIMVS around
reverse: Two warriors flanking trophy with shields; C·SEREIL in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this denarius with Flora and the combat scene, noting FLORAL PRIMVS refers to the moneyer's role as first organizer of the Floralia games.

moneyer: M. Junius Brutus (Q. Servilius Caepio Brutus)
obverse: Bearded head right (portrait); CAEPIO Q and BRVT IMP around
reverse: Two seated figures on tribunal or platform; AD.INV.MV / EX S.C below
orsini_comment: Orsini treats the Caepio coin but explicitly says its identification is uncertain: 'denarius ad quem pertineat Caepionem, mihi quidem obscurum est; illud certè ex iis, quae in eo impressa sunt, satis constat, Caepionem hunc, quicunq. fuerit, Pisonis in Aedilitate collegam ad frumentum emundū ex s.c. fuisse.' He does not identify 'L. Junius Brutus with lictors' on this coin; the plate (p. 242) shows DIONYS·CAEPIO·Q with a seated figure type (AD·FRV·SIAV·EX·S·C).

obverse: Bare or veiled head right; SESITIO or Q.SESTIVS around; PRO Q below
reverse: Priestly implements (simpulum, securis, lituus); Q.CAEPIO BRVTVS PRO.COS around
