orsini_comment: Orsini places this under gens Sestia as a coin of L. Sestius, proquaestor of Brutus in Macedonia. The plate shows priestly implements on the reverse. Orsini does not say the implements reference 'Brutus's role as pontifex'; he discusses L. Sestius's role and cites Appian and Dio on his career.

obverse: Priestly implements on left (simpulum, axe, etc.); Q.CAEPIO BRVTVS PRO COS around
reverse: Military tent or pileus (cap of liberty) between two daggers; L.SESTI / PRO Q below
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this variant with priestly implements on both sides, noting L. Sestius's title PRO Q (proquaestor) and the military context of Brutus's eastern campaign.

obverse: Head of Apollo right, hair tied with band; Q·SICINIVS·III·VIR text
reverse: Club draped with lion skin; arrows and bow flanking; C·COPONIVS·PR·S·C text
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Sicinius as Triumvir monetae cudendae from the coin legend (Q·SICINIUS·III·VIR visible in plate). He notes no ancient author mentions this moneyer: 'nullus, quòd sciam, facit mentionem.' The obverse type he describes as Fortitudinis imago (first coin without inscription). He does not describe Apollo, Hercules, a lion-skin club, or Pompeian allegiance — these are modern identifications not in Orsini's text.

obverse: Female head right (Fortune or Ceres?); P.R behind; FORT below
reverse: Caduceus with wreathed cross; Q.SICINIVS / III.VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the second coin type as FORT.P.R. = Fortitudo Populi Romani: 'in secundo denario cum inscriptione FORT.P.R. impressa est, hoc est, Fortitudo populi Romani.' He connects this to the traditions of Sicinius Dentatus. Orsini does not say 'Roma and caduceus' for this coin.

moneyer: P. Silius (with L. Aelius Lamia and C. Annius)
obverse: Clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio); caduceus above; ANNIVS LAMIA SILIVS around
reverse: Simpulum and patera above S·C; III·VIR / A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the joint coin of Silius and Annius Lamia. The plate shows clasped hands with legend ANNIVS·LAMIA·SILIVS and a vessel with the IIIvir monetalis legend. Orsini identifies both moneyers' names from the coin inscription and situates Silius as probably the Consul of year DCCLXV from Livy and Velleius. He does not describe a caduceus, a simpulum-and-patera reverse, or use the phrase 'dextrarum iunctio' — these are modern type descriptions not in the Orsini text.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Luna in biga, right, holding reins in left hand and goad in right hand. SPVRI ROMA
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to the gens Spurilia, noting A. Spurilius as moneyer with the standard Roma/horseman type.

obverse: Bare bearded head right (portrait)
reverse: Scene with standing figures; MVRCVS IMP in field; trophy or captive between figures
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates Murcus's coin and identifies him as Imperator from the reverse legend MVRCVS·IMP. The plate (p. 248) shows a portrait head obverse and two togated figures on the reverse — not Neptune. Orsini establishes his command from coin legends and Cassius's letter ('In Suriam me profectum esse scito ad L.Murcum...Imperatores'), not from a Neptune type. 'Neptune reflecting his command' is not in Orsini.

moneyer: T. Statilius Taurus (with Claudius Pulcher and Livineius Regulus)
obverse: Clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio); caduceus above; REGVLVS PVLCHER TAVRVS around
reverse: Large S C in centre; III·VIR / A·A·A·F·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini relates the coin to the gens Statilia and takes the bull as an allusion to the Taurus cognomen, leaving open whether the issuing Taurus is the proconsul (triumph 35 BC) or his consular son (AD 11).

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Horseman (Dioscurus) galloping right with lance; P.CALB below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the legend as P CALB (visible in the plate) and notes the coin shows the Dioscuri on horseback on the reverse with ROMA below. He connects it to P. Galba of the patrician Galba branch of the Sulpicia gens ('Patriciorum G A L B A E in antiquis denariis'). He does not comment specifically on the Apollo obverse type or any connection to Apollo's cult.

obverse: Bare head right; S C in field
reverse: Aedile's implements: curule chair with garland above, knife and AE CVR in field; P.GALB below
orsini_comment: Orsini reads AE CVR on this coin and infers 'Eundem Aedilem Curulem fuisse ex secundi denarii inscriptione intelligimus.' The reverse shows sacral implements ('secespita, simpulum, & securis impressa sunt, ut Galbae scilicet Pontificatus, vel aliud simile sacerdotium indicaretur'). He does not say the implements indicate Galba held the curule aedileship when the coin was struck; rather, he infers the aedileship from the AE CVR inscription and the priestly implements indicate a pontifical or priestly office.

obverse: Bearded male head right; L·SERVIVS RVFVS legend visible
reverse: Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux) standing facing, each holding spear, swords at waist
orsini_comment: Orsini says he believes this coin depicts Ser. Sulpicius Rufus the jurist and consul ('effigiem opinor expressam esse Ser. Sulpicii Rufi, qui iurisconsultus fuit, quique Consul in Fastis cum M. Marcello, anno DCCII descriptus est'). He cites Cicero pro L. Murena and discusses Sulpicius's fame at length. He does not say the coin 'may be provincial.'

obverse: Jugate heads of the Dei Penates right, stars above; SER·SVLP / RVFVS (D·P·P)
reverse: The walls/gate of Tusculum with towers; TVSCVLI across the field
orsini_comment: Orsini says he believes this gold coin was struck to illustrate 'aliud familiae suae monumentum, ex qua extiterit Ser. Sulpicius is, qui Tusculum obsidione exemerit' — the Ser. Sulpicius who relieved the siege of Tusculum, citing Livy lib.vi. The TUSCVL inscription on the reverse refers to Tusculum as a place, not a sanctuary. He also notes it was a gold coin ('aureum nummum').

obverse: Single laureate head right; SER before, SVP (SVLP) below
reverse: Three vertical implements: knife on left, simpulum (ladle) in center, decorated axe on right; AED·CVR text
orsini_comment: Orsini says 'Quintus denarius, vt ex inscriptione intelligitur, à Ser. Sulpicio cusus est: sed à quo Sulpicio, mihi quidem incertum est, cum multi in hac gente eo praenomine usi reperiantur.' The attribution is explicitly uncertain.

obverse: Draped bust of Hispania right; HISPANIA before; corn-ears and small round shield behind
reverse: Horseman galloping right; SER·GALBA·IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as belonging to Ser. Sulpicius Galba who became emperor, citing Suetonius lib. vii. cap. iii. He describes the reverse as an equestrian statue: 'Statua vero equestris, quae est in altera denarii parte signata, potest ad Galbae equestrem aliquam statuam pertinere, quae ab Hispanis ei decreta fuerit.' He does not name Hispania Tarraconensis, and describes an equestrian statue (not a personification of Hispania) decreed to Galba by 'the Hispani.'

obverse: Jugate laureate heads of the Dei Penates right; D·P·P before
reverse: Two soldiers standing facing each other, each holding a spear and pointing at a sow lying between them; C·SVLPICI·C·F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes others attribute this coin (first of the second plate) to C. Sulpicius C.F. Galus, consul anno DLXXXVII with M. Claudius Marcellus — a Republican figure, not Augustan or Imperial. He himself prefers to attribute it to C. Sulpicius Platorinus ('Mihi vero magis placeret, si denarius huiusmodi ad C. Sulpicium Platorinum referretur').

obverse: Bare head left (Augustus); AVGVSTVS behind
reverse: Two seated figure (Moneta per Orsini)s on platform or tribunal; C.SVLPICIVS PLATORIN around
orsini_comment: Orsini connects this coin to C. Sulpicius Platorinus and says that, being from Lavinium ('apud Lauinium ut videtur ortus'), Platorinus impressed on the coin 'porcam & Penates deos, qui Lauini colebantur, vt patriam indicaret suam.' The coin shows a sow (porca) and Penates, not two figures seated on a tribunal.

identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 408 — C. Sulpicius Platorinus, 13 BC
obverse: Bare head right; M.AGRIPPA.PLATORINVS.III.VIR around
reverse: Bare head right; CAESAR.AVGVSTVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini says 'In secundi denarii altera parte Rostra quaedam, & duo in eis sedentes uiri, quantum ego coniicio, Augustus, & Agrippa, signati sunt: ac Rostra quidem opinor esse ea, quae Iulia siue Noua appellata sunt.' The two figures are seated on the Rostra Iulia (New Rostra), not jugate or confronted.

moneyer: C. Tarquitius P.f. (with C. Annius T.f. T.n.)
obverse: Bare/diademed head right; legend around C.ANNI.T.F.T.N.PRO COS EX S.C
reverse: Victory driving a galloping biga right, holding reins/palm; C·TARQVITI(·F) in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Tarquitius on this coin as a supporter of Sertorius in Spain, grounding the attribution in Plutarch's Sertorio and a Sallust fragment quoted by Servius Grammaticus. He does not call it a proconsular issue and does not question its authenticity.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
reverse: The Dioscuri: two horsemen galloping right with couched spears; C.E below, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the coin of C. Terentius Lucanus, citing Pliny lib.xxxv cap.vii who records that Lucanus was the first to exhibit gladiatorial paintings publicly ('Pingi autem, inquit, gladiatoria munera, atque in publico exponi coepta à C. Terentio Lucano'). The coin is NOT attributed to M. Terentius Varro.

obverse: Janiform head (bearded and laureate double-faced head)
reverse: Prow right; C.TER.LVC above, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this standard Janus/prow bronze of C. Terentius Lucanus, reading the abbreviated legend C.TER.LVC.

obverse: Bearded male head right; VARRO·PRO·Q
reverse: Upright scepter flanked by a dolphin (left) and an eagle (right); MAGN·PRO / COS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as struck by M. Terentius Varro when Pompey's legate and proquaestor in Spain; the obverse shows Iuppiter Terminalis ('Iouis Terminalis caput impressum est'). The reverse carries sceptrum, aquila, and dolphin. Orsini cites Velleius and Suetonius — not Caesar's Bellum Civile or Varro's own writings.

obverse: Bearded head of Jupiter (Terminus) right; VARRO PRO Q around
reverse: Dolphin (left) and eagle (right) flanking an upright scepter; MAGN.PRO / COS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini treats this as a variant of the Varro proquaestorial issue. The legend visible in the plate reads MAGN·PRO / COS (Magnus Proconsul = Pompey), not 'MAGO PRO / COS.' Orsini cites Plinius lib.vii cap.xi on Varro's rostral crown from Pompey, and Pliny lib.xvi cap.iv on Varro and Agrippa.

obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right wearing goatskin headdress; I.S.M.R around
reverse: Bull charging right; L.THORIVS / BALBVS in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini explains the Juno Sospita reverse as reflecting Balbus's Lanuuine origin ('Lanuuio municipio THORIVS natus fuisset, Iunonis Sospitae simulacrum, quae Lanuuii colebatur, in altera denarii parte signauit'). He expands I.S.M.R. as IVNO SOSPITA MAGNA REGINA. He interprets the bull reverse as referring either to the family name (from animal-based nomina per Varro) or to the lex Thoria on public land.

obverse: Head of Roma right wearing winged helmet; X (value mark) behind
reverse: Victory driving galloping biga right; C·TITINI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this standard Roma/Victory-in-biga denarius, reading the moneyer as C. Titinius and noting the XVI mark of value.

obverse: Bearded head of Mutinus Titinus right
reverse: Pegasus flying right; Q.TITII below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not identify the obverse head as Mutinus Titinus. He attributes this coin to Q. Titius and notes the Pegasus reverse. Some scholars connected the Pegasus to Titius the poet (Horace Epistles 1.3); Orsini himself prefers the Pegasus to reference Corinth as a Caesarian/Augustan colony.

obverse: Ivy-wreathed head of Liber (Bacchus) right
reverse: Pegasus flying right; Q.TITII below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not identify this obverse head as Bacchus or Liber. He shows the coin as a Q. Titius denarius with Pegasus reverse. The identification of the head type is not specified by Orsini.

obverse: Female head right with elaborate hair; laureate or diademed
reverse: Pegasus flying right; Q.TITI below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not identify this obverse head as Ariadne or Libera. He shows the coin as a Q. Titius denarius with Pegasus reverse. The identification of the head type is not specified by Orsini.

obverse: Janiform head (bearded double-faced head); Q.TITI legend
reverse: Prow right; ship's prow with detailed structure
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this as the bronze (Æ) denomination of Q. Titius, noting it as a fourth coin. He does not compare beard details of the faces, does not describe the reverse as a 'prow,' and does not call it a 'companion to the silver series.'

obverse: Bearded head of King Titus Tatius right; SABINVS / A.PV around
reverse: Tarpeia scene: a frontal figure (Tarpeia) standing between two soldiers who raise their shields above/upon her; L.TITVRI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies king Tatius on the obverse and the Rape of the Sabine Women on the reverse, connecting the family's Sabine heritage to Rome's foundation legend.

obverse: Bearded head of King Titus Tatius right; SABINVS / A.PV around
reverse: Two soldiers, each carrying off a Sabine woman; L.TITVRI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini recounts the legend of Tarpeia who betrayed Rome to the Sabines and was crushed under their shields as punishment on this L. Titurius Sabinus coin. He cites Livy and Plutarch for the narrative and connects the A.PV control mark to die identification within the series.

obverse: Bearded head of King Titus Tatius right; SABIN around
reverse: Two soldiers, each carrying off a Sabine woman; L.TITVRI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this die variety carries the TA monogram instead of A.PV as the control mark, commenting on the variation without further explanation. He treats the two soldiers carrying off a woman as depicting the Rape of the Sabine Women and connects the type to the moneyer's cognomen Sabinus.

obverse: Bearded head of King Titus Tatius right; SABIN around
reverse: Victory in biga right; L.TITVRI in exergue; small control symbol below horses
orsini_comment: Orsini shows this Victory/biga variant of the Titurius series, maintaining the Tatius portrait on the obverse but using the standard Victory reverse.

obverse: Bearded head right (Bacchus per Orsini) (Titus Tatius or Jupiter)
reverse: Victory standing, holding a wreath out toward a trophy (pole topped with helmet and shield); P·SABIN in field, Q below, K to side
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this fifth coin (a quinarius) to P. Sabinus ('quintum Quinarium percussit: in cuius altera parte trophaeum & victoriam expressit, ad patris contra Vnellos gesta fortasse respiciens'). The reverse shows a trophy and victory. Orsini cites Caesar lib.iii de bello Gallico for the Veneti campaign. There is no mention of 'Bacchus' on this coin; the obverse continues the Tatius portrait of the series.

obverse: Handwritten note only (text describing a coin that was not engraved); coin image not present in engraving
reverse: Handwritten note only; CAESAR in legend mentioned
orsini_comment: Later marginal note (French) referencing another quinarius and a Faliscan (Falerii) type; reading uncertain.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, hurling thunderbolt; L·TREBANI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini's main point about this coin (a bronze aereus, not a denarius) is that the legend TREBANI may be an engraver's error for TREBATI, making the gens itself doubtful. He does not describe obverse or reverse types and does not read the name from an 'exergue.' The engraving shows a helmeted head obverse and a biga/quadriga reverse with TREBANI / ROMA.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma or Minerva right
reverse: Victory driving a quadriga (four-horse chariot) right; X below; M·TVLLI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini leaves the identity of M. Tullius open between two candidates (Decula or Cicero) and explicitly declines to decide: 'haud facile est... diuinare.' He does not assert that 'the direct link is unproven' as a caveat after connecting to Cicero — rather, both candidates are stated with equal tentativeness. The engraving shows M.TVLLI on the reverse below a Victory-in-biga or similar type.

obverse: Head of Apollo right, hair tied with band; star above; acisculus behind; laurel-wreath border
reverse: Head of Sibyl right; laurel-wreath border; L·VALERIVS ACISCVLVS
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the Apollo/Sibyl type of L. Valerius Acisculus (Crawford 474/3a). The engraving shows the head of Apollo right (L·VALERI, with star and acisculus pick as the moneyer's punning emblem) on the obverse and the head of the Sibyl right (ACISCVLVS) on the reverse.

obverse: Head right with diadem or fillet; ACISCVLVS around
reverse: Eagle standing right on thunderbolt; L.VALERIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the diademed-head/eagle type of L. Valerius Acisculus (Crawford 474/2a). The engraving shows a draped, diademed female head right (ACISCVLVS) on the obverse and an eagle standing right on a thunderbolt (L·VALERIVS) on the reverse, the eagle being a Jovian symbol.

obverse: Head right with diadem; ACISCVLVS around; star
reverse: Europa on bull right; L.VALERIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the diademed-head/Europa type of L. Valerius Acisculus (Crawford 474/1a). The engraving shows a draped, diademed head right (ACISCVLVS, with star) on the obverse and Europa seated on the bull moving right (L·VALERIVS) on the reverse.

obverse: Winged draped bust of Victory right; N behind
reverse: Aquila (legionary eagle) between two military standards; EX.S.C / IMPERAT legend
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates L. Valerius Flaccus's issue as imperator, with Victory and military standards reflecting his command during the Sullan civil war.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Victory in biga right; FLAC / C.VAL.C.F above, ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini shows the earlier Flaccus denarius with Victory/Victory-in-biga types, reading the full filiation C. Valerius C.f. in the exergue.

identification: Crawford 306/1 — L. Valerius Flaccus, AR denarius, 108-107 BC
obverse: Draped female bust right
reverse: Nude male figure (Mars) standing facing, holding spear; apex upper left; corn-ear to right; L·VALERI / FLACCI in field
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the denarius of L. Valerius Flaccus (Crawford 306/1, 108-107 BC). The engraving shows a draped, winged female bust right (Victory) on the obverse and a nude Mars standing left holding a spear, with an apex (priestly cap) to the left and a corn-ear to the right, inscribed L·VALERI / FLACCI.

obverse: Single bare male head right; M·ANT·IMP·AVG·III·VIR·R·P·M·BARBAT around
reverse: Single bare male head right; CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C around
orsini_comment: Orsini explicitly identifies this coin as M. Valerius Barbato, M. Antonii Triumuiri R.P.C. Quaestori Provinciali ('PRIMUS tabellae denarius cusus est à M. VALERIO BARBATO'). He does not treat it as a Barbatia gens coin mis-placed under Valeria — rather, he treats M. Valerius Barbatus as a Valerius. He identifies Barbatus as Antony's quaestor and later discusses M. Valerius Barbatus Cos. (father of Messalina, noted from Suetonius).

obverse: Modius (grain measure) on base; III·VIR·A·A·A·F·F around
reverse: Large S.C in center; L.VALERIVS.CATVLVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this second bronze of the second table as L. Valerius Catullus, 'qui Triumuir auro, argento, aere in secundo aereo nummo notatus est, C. Valerii Catulli poetae filius, uel frater credi potest.' He does not read 'F.V.R.I.A' — he reads L. VALERIVS CATVLLVS from the inscription. He notes that nothing about Catullus survives in the ancient sources.

obverse: Helmeted head or bust right (possibly Neptune); MESSAL.F around
reverse: Curule chair between two fasces; PATRE.COS / S.C in field
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the third coin of the second table as M. Valerius Messalla, consul with Cn. Domitius Calvinus anno DCC. He reads the sella (curule chair) and Bacchic thyrsus on the coin: 'fella in eo impressa, coniicere possumus: cui ad indicandam fortasse Liberalia, quae in eo munere Messallae filius fecit, Bacchi thyrsus suppositus est.' He does NOT read the legend 'PATRE COS' nor discuss the coin as referencing Messalla's father's consulship in those terms.

obverse: Modius (grain measure) on base; IIII·VIR·SISENNA·MESSALLA around
reverse: Large S·C in center; A·A·A·F·F·CALVS·APRONIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini notes the unusual IIIIVIR title (instead of the standard IIIvir) on this quattuorviral issue and identifies Sisenna Messalla and Antonius as joint moneyers alongside Galus. He uses this to illustrate the expansion of the monetary college under Augustus and connects it to the Valeria gens's continued presence in the Augustan administration.

obverse: Head right with diadem; ACISCVLVS around
reverse: Victory driving galloping biga right; L.VALERI in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini says the fifth and sixth coins of the second table are Trajanic restorations of the Acisculus types, and identifies their obverse types as Sol's head and Apollo's head respectively: 'in eorum autem altero Solis caput, in altero Apollinis, qui cum Sole idem est, expressum arbitror.' There is no Hercules or horseman. Orsini connects the Sol/Apollo choice to Valerius Acisculus's link to Heliopolis and the river Acis near Etna.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; value mark behind
reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, hurling thunderbolt; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini's central comment on this coin is the identification of M. Vargunteius as M. Crassus's Parthian-war legate, supported by the Appian text (corrupted but recognizable). He also connects the moneyer to the Catilinarian conspirators (Cicero pro Sulla). He does NOT merely 'read the abbreviated name M.VARG' — the text on p. 272 cites the full inscription M.VARGVNTEIVS / VARGVNTEIA.

obverse: Janiform bearded head (Janus, two faces back-to-back) with wild/curly hair
reverse: Prow of ship; VER·CAR·OGVL above
orsini_comment: The legend Orsini reads on this bronze (Æ) coin corresponds to VER + Carisio + Ogulnio as the three curatores; the engraving shows VER·GA·OG. Orsini does NOT attempt to connect the Vergilius here to the poet Virgil. He says the reading is 'satis constat' (sufficiently clear), not difficult. The difficulty Orsini expresses is about identifying the man, not reading the legend.

obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo or young figure)
reverse: Victory driving galloping biga right, holding reins/wreath; VER / CAR-OCV in field
orsini_comment: Orsini says this silver denarius is attributed to the gens Vergilia ('arbitror'), but he explicitly does not decide the identity of the moneyer or period: the difficulty is about the man, not the legend. He discusses at length the possibility that Ogulnius is the oldest attested colleague (p. 273: 'multo eis antiquior Ogulnius fit, qui Vergilii in cudenda moneta collega in eodem denario notatus est') and declines to assign the coin to either direction definitively.

obverse: Head of Honos or Virtus right, diademed; SABINVS or legend around; T.VETTI behind
reverse: Warrior in biga right with charioteer; IVDEX or similar legend; T.VETTIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse as T. Tatius's image (not a bearded Sabine king generically) and the reverse as a horseman labeled IVDEX / T·VETTIVS with a spica (ear of grain) as an Aedileship emblem. He does not describe a 'Rape of the Sabines' reverse. He does not mention C. Annius. He cites Plutarch, Cicero (Vatinium), Suetonius (lib. I cap. XVII and XX), and Dio (lib. XXXVIII) — not Livy.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
reverse: Oath-taking scene: two figures facing each other, kneeling figure between them holding a pig; ROMA around
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the famous oath-taking scene (foedus), identifying the two warriors swearing over the sacrificial pig as a representation of an ancient Roman treaty ceremony.

obverse: Single young laureate head in profile
reverse: Oath-taking scene: two standing warriors, kneeling figure between holding pig; trophy or standard above; ROMA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini cites Livy lib. I for the Roman-Alban (NOT Roman-Samnite) treaty formula in extenso. He explicitly rejects the Caudine Peace / Roman-Samnite identification: 'Nec enim pacem Caudinam, ut quidam putant, quam T. Veturius Caluinus fecit... significari ea nota credendum est.'

obverse: Head of Mark Antony right, bearded; VARVS text visible
reverse: Fortuna standing left, holding Victory in right hand and cornucopiae in left; C·VIBIVS VARVS
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Primus denarius, in cuius una parte effigies M.Lepidi, in altera signum Concordiae expressum est" — obverse = portrait of M. Lepidus; reverse = image of Concordia. Orsini notes that the Concordia type was also used in Imperial bronze coinage with the added title CONCORDIA. He attributes the striking to C. Vibius Varus as triumvir in the period of the Republic.

obverse: Laureate head of Apollo, right
reverse: C·VIBIVS VARVS — Venus standing left, facing away, looking at herself in mirror held in left hand; on right, column
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Secundus aureus nummus, quòd in eo Veneris imago signata fit, ad Iuliae familiae origine a Venere per Aenean ductam, pertinere potest" — he suggests the Venus image on this aureus may relate to the Julian family's Trojan/Venusian origin via Aeneas, but states this tentatively ("pertinere potest"). He identifies the coin as an aureus ("aureus nummus").

obverse: Helmeted head of Minerva right
reverse: Hercules standing with lion skin; SALVA / C·VIBIVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini: "In tertio & quarto denario praeter Herculis, & Mineruae simulacra, nihil est notatu magnopere dignum. ea verò ad indicandam Vibiorum originem spectant e Vibone oppido, in quo Hercules, & Minerua in primis colebantur" — the Hercules and Minerva types on coins 3 and 4 point to the Vibii's origin from Vibone (Hipponium/Valentia), where Hercules and Minerva were chiefly venerated. Orsini adds no specific legend reading (no 'SALVA' inscription noted).

obverse: Male head right with ivy-wreath and berries in hair (Bacchus/Liber)
reverse: Helmeted figure (Minerva/Roma) standing, holding a long spear and a small Victory; shield at feet; C·VIBIVS / VARVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini treats coin 4 together with coin 3: both Hercules and Minerva types are read as indicators of the Vibii's Vibonese origin. He makes no claim about a 'military context of 42 BC' or about the combination of 'two martial deities.' The sole observation is the topographic/genealogical connection to Vibone.

obverse: Head of Apollo or Liber right, laureate
reverse: Figure on altar or tribunal; panther below; C.VIBIVS / VARVS around
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Quintus denarius non est dubium, quin ad Liberi patris sacra pertineat... in eius enim vna parte Liberi caput impressum est, in altera tigris, tyrsus, & persona arae imposita" — obverse = head of Liber (Bacchus); reverse = tiger, thyrsus, and a figure placed on an altar. He cites Virgil Bucolicis (Daphnis/Armenias curru subiungere tigres) and Georgics II (Non aliam ob culpam Baccho caper) for the Bacchic imagery, and Servius for Caesar's introduction of Liber-sacra to Rome. The coin is attributed to Liberalia or Aedilitian games celebrated by C. Vibius Varus.

obverse: Laureate female head right; PANSA behind
reverse: Genius (possibly Roma or Ceres); C.VIBIVS below; small animal at feet
orsini_comment: Orsini assigns the coins of the second table to C. Vibius Pansa ("AD C. VIBVM PANSAM huius tabellae denarii & sequentis pertinent"), not to C. Vibius Varus. The specific identification of coin 6's type should follow the Pansa sequence. Orsini does not describe a 'Venus/Cupid' type for this coin; the second table's coins relate to Cereales ludi and Sicilian origin. Comment requires re-grounding against the Pansa plate description.

obverse: Male head right with ivy-wreath; PANSA text on left; S below chin
reverse: Minerva in quadriga right, holding spear and trophy; C·VIBIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini does not connect the quadriga type to the cognomen Pansa or to the satyr Pan anywhere in the Vibia section. He connects the Pansa coins to the Cereales ludi and to the Sicilian origin of the gens, not to a Pansa/Pan etymology. The specific iconographic content of this coin as described by Orsini requires direct grounding from the Pansa plate text.

obverse: Minerva in quadriga, holding spear and trophy; C·VIBIVS·C·F in exergue
reverse: Minerva in quadriga, holding spear and trophy; PANSA in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts the Minerva-in-quadriga type, noting that both sides feature galloping quadrigae, an unusual double-action composition.
specimen_credit: after Babelon, Description historique (1885–86), public domain

obverse: Bearded laureate head right (Jupiter); PANSA below
reverse: Jupiter Axur standing left, holding patera and scepter; IOVIS·AXVR / C·VIBIVS·C·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini: "in altera Iouis Axuri simulacrum expressum est, cuius meminit Virgilius in lib.vii" (Aen.vii: 'queis Iuppiter Anxurus aruis Praesidet'). He cites Servius and Porphyrio on Anxurus = Jupiter worshipped at Terracina (then called Anxur), and notes that the ancient coin inscription IOVIS CVSTO[S] supports the ANXURUS reading of Virgil and Horace. The obverse in context shows Libera/Proserpina, not 'a bearded mask as Pan.'

obverse: Single laureate head right; PANSA legend
reverse: Standing draped figure with attributes; C·VIBIVS·C·F·C·N around
orsini_comment: Orsini shows the Bacchus/Ceres type, connecting the Eleusinian pair of Liber and Ceres to the Pansa family's Bacchic iconographic program.

obverse: Laureate head right (Persephone per Orsini) (Apollo); PANSA behind; wreath border
reverse: Figure riding on pair of sea-serpents (or hippocampi) right; C.VIBIVS.C.F.C.N around
orsini_comment: Orsini depicts the variant Ceres-in-serpent-biga reverse, noting the serpent-drawn chariot as Ceres's traditional conveyance in the search for Proserpina.

obverse: Laureate female head right (Bacchus per Orsini) (Ceres or Liber); PANSA behind
reverse: Helmeted warrior/standing armed figure holding a long spear; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this variant with fragmentary reverse inscription, noting the same Bacchus obverse but an uncertain standing figure on the reverse.

moneyer: C. Vibius Pansa / D. Junius Brutus Albinus
obverse: Bearded head right (Jupiter or Silenus); C.PANSA behind
reverse: Clasped right hands holding a winged caduceus; ALBINVS·BRVTI·F around
orsini_comment: Orsini (p.280, third table, second coin): "Secundus denarius, superato iam ad Mutinam M. Antonio...signatus est: in eoque ad hanc declarandam victoriam Roma sedens, cui in manu dextra Victoriae simulacrum insistit, & Libertatis caput, occiso nuper Caesare recuperatae, impressum est" — reverse shows Roma seated, holding Victory in her right hand, with the head of Libertas (recovered after Caesar's assassination). The obverse carries C. PANSA. This is not a 'clasped hands with winged caduceus' type; that description does not correspond to Orsini's text.

obverse: Head with decorated/styled hair in profile; text around edge
reverse: Second head or bust in profile; text around edge; no PANSA text visible
orsini_comment: Orsini (p.280, third table, first coin): "Primus huius tabellae denarius a C.Panfa, vt opinor, cufus tuc fuit, cum ad eximendum Mutinensi obsidione D. Brutum a Senatu missus est. in eius autem altera parte personae signum ad eaedem indicanda siue Cerealia siue Liberalia." The engraved coin appears as a blank circle in this plate. Orsini does not describe a 'double-mask composition' or call this an aureus. He leaves the reverse figure uncertain between Cerealia and Liberalia symbols.

obverse: Laureate head of Concordia right; CONCORDIAE around
reverse: Victory walking right, carrying palm-branch decorated with four wreaths; L·VINICI
orsini_comment: Orsini: coin 1 shows Concordia's head laureate on one side. He cites Ovid Fasti VI: 'Venit Apollinea longas Concordia lauro / Nexa comas etc.' for the description of Concordia. He adds a Greek diphthong note (CONCORDIAI per Virgilian and Ennian usage). The reverse shows four crowns relating to Augustus's victories. Orsini does not describe this as 'Concordia/Victory' or speak of an 'Augustan ideological program of political harmony.'

obverse: Bare head right
reverse: Rectangular inscribed cippus/tablet with multiple lines of text
orsini_comment: Orsini reads the complex reverse inscription as referring to the restoration of roads from public funds (QVOD VIAE MVNITAE SVNT), citing Suetonius and Dio Cassius on Augustus's road-building program. He identifies L. Vinicius as the moneyer and treats the road restoration inscription as the most explicit coinage statement of Augustan infrastructure policy.

obverse: Inscription in rectangular frame or legend text; multiple lines of text
reverse: Inscription in rectangular frame; multiple lines of text
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses all three road-inscription coins (coins 2, 3, 4) together as documenting Augustus's road restoration program, citing Suetonius lib.ii.cap.iii and Dio lib.LIII. He quotes Dio in Greek to the effect that when Augustus saw roads neglected he distributed them among senators at their own expense, and took the Via Flaminia for himself specifically because he was about to lead an army along it ('Flaminia, quoniam ea ducturus erat exercitum, ipse procurauit'), immediately restoring it, with statues of Augustus placed on arches on the Tiber bridge and at Ariminum. The triumphal arch with statues and the road-inscription reverse (QVOD VIAE MVN. SVNT) refer to this road-restoration program as a group; Orsini does not single out coin 3 as specifically the Flaminia coin — he treats coins 2–4 collectively as road-restoration types, with Flaminia named as one road among others ('reliquas patrum quibusdam, propriis sumptibus reficiendas mandauit').

obverse: Bare male head right
reverse: Triumphal arch surmounted by a quadriga; L·VINICIVS below
orsini_comment: Orsini: the last Vinicius coin shows a triumphal arch with quadriga and the inscription QVOD VIAE MVN. SVNT, i.e. 'quòd uiae munitae sunt.' Orsini reads this in the context of Augustus's road restoration funded from manubial money ("ex ea pecunia, quam ipse ad Aerarium detulisset"). He does not call this 'a standard Augustan commemorative type honoring military or civic achievements' — the specific connection is to road-building, not military triumph.

obverse: Heads of two figures right, bare; legend around border
reverse: Legend in three lines within the field, no figure: M·AGRIPPA COS / DESIG
orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this early joint portrait of Augustus and Agrippa, noting Agrippa's COS DESIG title placing the coin before his first consulship.

obverse: Bare head right; IMP CAESAR DIVI F around
reverse: Legend M AGRIPPA COS DESIG within plain field
orsini_comment: Orsini treats coins 1 and 2 together: both struck when Agrippa was consul designate ("nondum primum Consulatum adeptus, sed designatus tantum fuisset, ut ex eorum inscriptionibus apparet"). The engraving shows M·AGRIPPA·COS·DESIG on both. Orsini does not say coin 2 was struck by 'IIIvir monetalis Platorinus' (that is coin 3), nor does he discuss 'DIVI IVLI FILIVS' or Octavian's claim to divine ancestry in connection with these coins.

obverse: Bare head right; legend CAESAR / AVGVSTVS around
reverse: Bare head right; legend M·AGRIPPA·PLATORINVS·III·VIR around
orsini_comment: Orsini shows Agrippa wearing the rostral crown awarded for his naval victories at Naulochus and Actium, struck by IIIvir monetalis Platorinus.

obverse: Head of Marcus Agrippa left, wearing rostral crown (corona rostrata); legend M AGRIPPA L F COS III around
reverse: Figure of Neptune standing right, holding trident; S C in field
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Quartum aereum nummum...signatos fuisse, ex eorum titulis intelligere possumus. In aereo autem, rostrata Agrippae imagini corona" — the bronze coin (coin 4) carries Agrippa's portrait with the corona rostrata. The reverse shows Neptune: "pertinet Neptuni signum in altera parte aerei nummi expressum" in connection with the Sicilian naval victory over Sex. Pompeius ("naualem de Siculis & Sex.Pompeio victoriam"). He cites Pliny lib.xvi.cap.IV for the corona rostrata. Orsini does NOT say this is a 'posthumous commemorative struck under Caligula,' and does NOT say the crown honours Actian victories — he specifies the Sicilian war.

obverse: Bare head of Augustus right; AVGVSTVS / COS around
reverse: Head of Agrippa right wearing combined mural and rostral crown; M·AGRIPPA·COS·TER / COSS around
orsini_comment: Orsini: "in argenteo rostrata simul & muralis circumdata est" — the silver coin (coin 5) shows Agrippa's portrait with both the corona rostrata and the corona muralis. Orsini does not mention 'IIIvir Cossutius Lentulus' or the legend 'COS XI / COS TER' in connection with this coin.

obverse: Bare youthful male head with flowing hair
reverse: Bull standing right; QVOCONIVS above, VITVLVS Q below, S C in field
orsini_comment: Orsini: "ad quod cognomen respexisse uidetur Q.VOCONIVS is, qui monetam cusit, cum in altera denariorum parte uitulum signauit" — the calf (vitulus) on the reverse echoes the moneyer's cognomen Vitulus. Coin 1 was struck while Julius Caesar was alive ("signauit uiuente adhuc Caesare"). Orsini does not identify the obverse portrait as Augustus.

obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around
reverse: Bull standing right; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Secundus denarius, ut ex titulo DIVI IVL, qui in altera parte adscriptus est, colligitur, interfecto iam a coniuratis Caesare, ab eodem Voconio cusus fuit" — the title DIVI IVL dates this coin to after Caesar's deification; it was struck by the same Voconius after the assassination. Orsini does not discuss 'DIVI F' as Octavian's claim to divine ancestry — he uses DIVI IVL solely to date the coin's striking.

obverse: Bearded head of Jupiter right, laureate
reverse: Temple facade with four columns (tetrastyle); M.VOLTEI.M.F below
orsini_comment: Coin 1: Orsini identifies the temple on coin 1 as Jupiter Capitolinus, hexastyle: 'Templum certè in altera primi denarii parte impressum, quin Iouis sit, dubitari non potest, quamuis eius forma in ueteribus monumentis hexastylos reperiatur.' He cites no specific authority for coin 1 beyond this observation. Coin 3: Orsini identifies Ceres taedifera in a serpent-drawn chariot, noting that he has already written about this in the Vibia section, and cites Ovid Metamorphoses v and Claudianus lib.i de raptu Proserpinae ('De Cerere Taedifera, quae draconum uecta curru in tertio denario signata est, multa in Vibia gente scripta à nobis sunt, quibus adjungi poterunt Ouidii uersus ex lib. v. Metam. & Claudiani, ex lib.i. de raptu Proserpinae'). Varro and Macrobius are NOT cited anywhere in the Volteia section. Any reference to 'Varro and Macrobius' in the concordance coin-comments for coins 1 or 3 must be removed.

obverse: Head of Hercules right; border of dots.
reverse: Erymanthian boar right (one of the Twelve Labors); M·VOLTEI·M·F legend; border of dots.
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Aprum autem, qui est in altera secundi denarii parte notatus, opinor Erymanthium illum repraesentare, quem Hercules interfecisse dicitur" — the animal on the reverse is the Erymanthian Boar killed by Hercules. Orsini does NOT connect coin 2 to the ludi Plebeii, and does NOT describe a 'panther-drawn biga' on this coin.

obverse: Head of Ceres right, wreathed with grain
reverse: Ceres (or Victory) driving a biga drawn by two serpents right; M.VOLTEI.M.F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini connects the ploughing scene on this M. Volteius coin to the ludi Ceriales and the agricultural foundation of the Ceres festival, treating the Ceres head and the ploughman type as directly evoking the goddess of grain and agriculture. He cites Varro and Macrobius for the identification.

obverse: Laureate/wreathed head of Attis (or Bacchus) right
reverse: Cybele (Magna Mater) seated in a chariot drawn by two lions right; M.VOLTEI.M.F in exergue
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coin 4 as a Cybele/Magna Mater type in his opening overview ('in quarto Martis & Cybeles') and discusses it as showing Cybele with turreted crown in a lion-drawn chariot, citing Lucretius lib.ii ('Muralique caput summum cinxere corona... Et iuncti currum dominae subiere leones'), Virgil Aen.vi ('qualis Berecynthia mater / Inuehitur curru Phrygias turrita per urbes'), and Claudianus lib.i de raptu Proserpinae ('Cybelem turrigeam appellauit'). He also cites Diodorus Siculus on lions drawing Cybele's chariot and Varro on their tamed nature. Orsini does NOT name Attis or describe a Phrygian-capped figure anywhere in the Volteia section. The ludi Megalenses connection follows from the overview 'Martis & Cybeles' (Megalesia = Cybele's festival).

obverse: Laureate head right
reverse: Tripod with serpent coiled around it; S·C / D·T in field; M·VOLTEI·M·F below
orsini_comment: Orsini: "Ex tripode autem, qui est in altera quinti denarii parte signatus, propterea quòd Apollini sacer est, cui Saeculares ludi fiebant" — the tripod is Apollo's sacred object, and Orsini connects the coin to the Saeculares ludi (Secular Games), NOT the ludi Apollinares. He notes the letters S.C.D.T on the tripod as unresolved: "Litteras autem S.C.D.T...fateor me...quid significent, nescire." He speculates that M. Volteius was an xvir sacris faciundis (the priestly college overseeing the Secular Games). Orsini does not mention a 'lyre' on this coin, and does not cite Varro or Macrobius.

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; control-mark behind
reverse: Europa seated on bull charging left; behind, winged thunderbolt; L·VLO·L·F·STRB in legend
orsini_comment: Orsini: "L. Volteius. L.F.Strabo in altera sexti denarii parte impressit, quò pertineat certi aliquid afferre possim, nisi quòd suspicor, Iouis templum eius procurationis fuisse: a quo quidem deo in taurum uerso abductam Europam in Cretam insulam poetae fabulantur." The coin is by L. Volteius L.F. Strabo (not M. Volteius). Orsini's legend reading is 'L.Volteius.L.F.Strabo,' not 'L.CO.L.F.S.R.R.' Orsini tentatively connects the Europa/bull to Jupiter's temple procuration. The attribution to Volteia is uncertain ('quò pertineat certi aliquid afferre possim' — he cannot say with certainty what it signifies).

obverse: Bust of Vesta, with stephane and veil, right; lighted torch in front; VESTA·P·R·QVIRTIVM
reverse: Jupiter seated left, holding thunderbolt and sceptre, in distyle temple with wreath in pediment; I·O·MAX·CAPITOLINVS
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses coins 1 and 2 together. He identifies them as struck for the restoration of the temples of Capitoline Jupiter (Optimus Maximus) and Vesta, connecting them to Vitellius: 'Restituta vero eorum templa à Vitellio Imp. fuisse, facile adducor ut credam.' He cites Pliny lib. xxxiv cap. vii and Cornelius Tacitus lib. xix. He does not say he cannot identify the coin; he attributes it to Vitellius's temple restorations. The legend VESTA P R QVIRITIVM is discussed at length as evidence for this.

obverse: Bust of Jupiter, diademed, bearded, draped, left
reverse: Vesta, veiled, seated left on throne, holding patera and torch; VESTA P R QVIRITIVM
orsini_comment: Orsini discusses coins 1 and 2 together as Jupiter/Vesta temple-restoration types attributed to Vitellius: 'Restituta vero eorum templa à Vitellio Imp. fuisse, facile adducor ut credam.' He extends the discussion of POPVLVS ROMANVS QVIRITIVM across most of pp. 288–290. He does not say he cannot identify the coin.

obverse: Laureate head of Italia left; ITALIA legend.
reverse: Oath-taking scene: central standard with a kneeling figure holding a pig, flanked by about four standing soldiers (two on each side) pointing their swords toward the centre; C in exergue.
orsini_comment: Orsini is fully confident in the Social War attribution: 'Tertius tabellae denarius, quin ad Italicorum coniurationem pertineat, dubitari non potest.' He cites Appianus lib. i bel. ciuil. and identifies this as the bellum Italicum, Sociale, & Marsicum. He names the Italian leaders: Velleio, Appian, T. Afranius, C. Pontidius, Marius Egnatius, Q. Popedius Silo, C. Papius Mutilus, M. Lamponius, C. Indacilius, Herius Asinius, T. Vettius Cato, Pontius Telefinus, T. Herennius, A. Cluentius, Iuuentius, P. Praefentius, P. Ventidius. The previous comment's claim that Orsini 'admits he cannot confidently assign' this coin is a direct inversion of the text.

obverse: Diademed head of Bonus Eventus right; BON EVENT
reverse: Roma standing right, holding Victory and eagle-tipped sceptre; ROM RENASC
orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to Galba: 'Quartū denarium ab Imp. Galba cusum esse, ex renascentis Romae simulacro… coniicere possumus.' He then discusses Bonus Eventus at length, citing Varro (lib. i de re rustica), Pliny (lib. xxxv cap. x), and Euphranor. He does not say 'RENASCES ROMA' as an exact legend — he says 'renascentis Romae simulacro.' He does not say he cannot assign the coin; he attributes it to Galba.

obverse: Bust of Hercules seen from behind, head turned left; club over shoulder
reverse: Desultor (rider) left, wearing cuirass; D·S·S and B visible; TI Q text
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse as Hercules (equated with Semo Sancus / Deus Fidius): 'Quinto denario Herculis, ut uidetur, caput signatum est, quē cum Sanco deo, siue Fidio eundem esse, satis demonstrant Varronis uerba.' The reverse legend D.S.S. he expands as 'Deus Fidius Semo Sancus' (p. 290: 'D.S.S. hoc est, Deus Fidius Semo Sancus'). He draws on Varro, Ovid (Fasti lib. vi), Propertius (lib. iv), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (lib. iv), and a Tiberina inscription (SEMONI SANCO DEO.FIDIO SACRVM…). There is no desultor on this coin; the type is Hercules/Sancus, not a rider performing equestrian feats.

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind, ROMA below
reverse: Roma or Minerva seated right on shields, holding spear; birds (eagles) in field
orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the Faustulus type and attributes it to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus: 'Sextus tabellae denarius, in quo Faustulus pastor impressus est cum pico aui, et propè stante cum infantibus lupa, à Sex. Pompeio Fostlo, ut opinor, cusus fuit.' He adds that the Postloria (Frostlora) family took its cognomen from Faustulus. The coin shows a pastor (Faustulus), a woodpecker, and a she-wolf with infants — not an 'early Roma type.' The previous comment's claim that Orsini 'unable to attribute it to a moneyer' is wrong; he attributes it to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus.

obverse: Head of Libertas right, diademed; LEIBERTAS legend
reverse: Prow-stem and anchor arranged upright
orsini_comment: This coin is on the second Incerta plate (p. 291). Orsini attributes the Libertas quinarii on this plate to Caesar's assassins: 'Caesare iam à coniuratis interfecto, libertateq. Reip. restituta, argenteū hunc quinarium à Caesaris percussoribus cusum esse, et ludis Apollinaribus, quos Brutus Praetor populo exhibuit, sparsim fuisse, ex Libertatis signata in eo imagine coniicere facile possumus.' He discusses the PAX ET LIBERTAS legend and the anchor/prow imagery as symbols of recovered liberty. He then discusses Cicero's speech at the temple of Tellus. Attribution is to the percussores of Caesar, not left wholly unidentified.

obverse: Two clasped right hands holding a winged caduceus; PAX·ET above, LIBERTAS in exergue below.
reverse: Text S·P·Q·R in large letters; additional text lines below; wreath or border
orsini_comment: Second Libertas coin on the second Incerta plate. Orsini links the PAX ET LIBERTAS legend to Brutus and the conspirators, citing Cicero's first Philippic ('cuius in lib. i. Philipp. facit his verbis mentionem'). He also notes the corona on the other denarius part as obscure ('mihi quidem obscurum est') since no oak crown is recorded as being decreed to Brutus or Cassius. He does not simply say he cannot assign the coin to a gens; his position is that these coins belong to the percussores of Caesar, with residual uncertainty only about the oak crown motif.

obverse: Victory walking right, holding wreath and palm; SALVS.GENER.HVMANI around
reverse: S.P.Q.R within laurel wreath, rosette above
orsini_comment: Final coin(s) on the second Incerta plate. Orsini closes the entire section by leaving open whether these coins belong to Caesar's assassins or to C. Caesar Triumvir: 'iudicium relinquimus statuendi, sit ne ad Caesaris… interfectores referenda, an ad C. Caesarem Triumuirum R.P.C. qui postea Augustus appellatus fuit.' Earlier he noted that SALVS GENERIS HVMANI appears on an aureus of C. CAESARIS DIVI F. IMP. IIIVIRI R.P.C. and that the Triumviratus-period denarii may be connected. 'Roma Renascens' belongs to coin 4 (Galba), not to this denarius; 'Salus Generis Humani' appears in Orsini only as a comparandum on the gold coin, not as the obverse legend of this denarius.

obverse: Bearded head right with flowing hair (Silenus); T·CARISIVS around
reverse: Recumbent sphinx right, minting implements (anvil, tongs) above
orsini_comment: Orsini places this coin ('sextertius') in the first table of the Carisia gens. He identifies the reverse creature as a tiger sacred to Bacchus ('tigri Baccho sacra'), with thyrsus and other Libera symbols, marking T. Carisius's aedilitas. Modern attribution: Crawford 464/4, reverse is a sphinx — Orsini read the sphinx as a Bacchic tiger.

obverse: Bare head right; IMP·CAESAR
reverse: Standing figure left holding staff; legend around
orsini_comment: Orsini places this denarius in the second table of the Clodia gens and also Iulia, because Caesar's portrait is engraved on the obverse ('quòd in eius altera parte Caesaris imago incifa fit'). He identifies P. Clodius as IIIIvir monetae (not IVvir — his exact phrase is 'Quartumuir monetae cudendae'), who struck the coin under Caesar ('sub quo Clodius, ut opinor, Quartumuir monetae cudendae, denarium signauit'). Note: Orsini places it in the 'secunda tabella gentis Clodiae,' not a general Clodia table.

obverse: Female head right with flowing hair; NT
reverse: Trophy with shields and armor; CAESAR in field
orsini_comment: Orsini places this quinarius ('Quintus huius tabellae quinarius') in the third table of the Iulia gens ('in tertia gentis Iuliae tabella reponendus'). He reads the symbols on both sides as relating to Caesar's victories over the Germans: 'habens in utraque parte eadem ferè fymbola, ad indicandas, ut arbitror, Caesaris uictorias de Germaneis, aliisque gentibus deuictis.' This is the fifth coin described in Orsini's plate-1 text, though it stands third in this concordance's numbering; the description is of the Iulia quinarius.

obverse: Single male head right (NOT Janus); three pellets behind (quadrans mark?)
reverse: Prow right; three pellets before; P·BLAS ROMA legend
orsini_comment: Orsini places this bronze coin ('nummus aereus') in the last table of the Cornelia gens ('in postrema tabella Corneliae gentis reponendus est').

obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; control numeral above, PR·FL below
reverse: Victory driving biga right; L·FLAMINI / CHILO below
orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is the other side ('altera pars') of the L. Flaminius Chilo denarius, which had been badly engraved in the Flaminia gens table ('male incisa'). He republishes it here corrected by comparison with a silver specimen ('ex collatione argentei nummi emendanda').

obverse: Horseman galloping right; P.SEPVLLIVS / MACER around
reverse: Temple of Clementia Caesaris (tetrastyle); CLEMENTIAE / CAESARIS around
orsini_comment: Orsini places this denarius in the last table of the Iulia gens. He notes the reverse shows the temple of Clementia Caesaris ('Clementiae templum'), citing Plutarch and Dio on Caesar's clemency ('de quo Plutarchus, Dio, et alii meminerunt'), and quotes Plutarch in Greek at length on the decree of Caesar's Clementia.

obverse: Head right with wavy hair
reverse: Prow right; P.MAE.ANT.M.F above, ROMA below
orsini_comment: Orsini places this bronze coin ('aereus nummus') as the first of the second plate, in the Maecilia gens ('in Maecilia gente reponendus').

obverse: AVGVSTVS: Bare head of Augustus right; behind, lituus.
reverse: C·MARIVS·C·F TRO·IIIVIR: Augustus, veiled and togate, standing left, extending hand with simpulum/patera.
orsini_comment: Orsini adds this denarius to the silver coins already in the gens Maria ('addendus est argenteis nummis, qui in gente Maria impressi sunt'). The tribal designation Tromentina is unusual on coinage.

obverse: Victory standing right on globe, holding wreath and palm; CAESAR·DIVI·F around
reverse: Open right hand; SCARPVS·IMP around
orsini_comment: Orsini places coins 9 and 10 together ('TERTIVS et QUARTVS reponendi in gente Pinaria'). He says nothing about Octavian vs Antony, command authority, or the open hand symbolism — those are modern identifications not in Orsini's text. Orsini's entire note is: 'TERTIVS et QUARTVS reponendi in gente Pinaria.'

obverse: Victory standing right on globe, holding wreath and palm; AVGVSTVS left, DIVI·F right
reverse: Open right hand; IMP·CAESAR above, SCARPVS·IMP below
orsini_comment: Orsini places coins 9 and 10 together in the Pinaria gens: 'TERTIVS et QUARTVS reponendi in gente Pinaria.' He says nothing about the open hand, Actium, Octavian vs Antony, or Scarpus's allegiance — those are modern numismatic identifications added by the AI. Orsini's note is purely positional.

obverse: Bust of Proserpina right, hair decorated with poppy-heads
reverse: Jug and torch; M·PLAETORI·CEST·EX·S·C around
orsini_comment: Orsini places this coin in the second table of the Plaetoria gens: 'QUINTVS in secunda tabella gentis Plaetoriae.'

obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; acisculus (pick) behind; ACISCVLVS around
reverse: Anguipede giant (snake-legged) right, holding thunderbolt; C·VALERIVS below (Orsini reads L as C)
orsini_comment: Orsini places this denarius in the last table of the Valeria gens, attributing it to the Acisculus branch ('ad familiam Acisculoru'). He misidentifies the types completely: he reads Neptune's head ('Neptuni caput') on the obverse and the sign of Triton ('Tritonis signum') on the reverse, suggesting the coin commemorates either the Acisculus family's curatorship of Neptune's temple or a Roman naval victory. Modern attribution: Jupiter head / anguipede giant (Crawford 474/4).
